<note>Marbled paper like this was traditionally used for the interior covers (endpapers) of high-quality books to hide the construction of the binding and provide a decorative entrance to the text. This specific pattern, often called a "comb" or "nonpareil" marble, is created by dragging a comb-like tool through floating pigments on a liquid bath before laying the paper on top to "lift" the design.</note>

<note>Blank pages at the beginning of a volume are often called "flyleaves." In traditional bookbinding, these pages act as a protective barrier between the decorative endpapers and the actual contents of the manuscript. They also provided historical owners with a space to write shelf marks, signatures, or personal notes.</note>

--- Page 11 ---
<meta>This page follows the archive’s frontispiece and title page. It is the author's official introduction to the sixth volume of his multi-volume effort to transcribe and publish Leonardo da Vinci’s scattered manuscripts.</meta>

## FOREWORD

---

After the publication of the first three volumes of this collection, the French Academy <note>The Académie française, the preeminent French council for matters pertaining to the French language.</note> did me the great honor of awarding me, in its entirety, during its session on November 14, 1889, the Bordin Prize¹ <note>The Bordin Prize is a prestigious academic award established to recognize high-quality works of literature or history.</note>.

I have done everything within my power, in the pursuit and completion of the second part of my undertaking—which concludes with this sixth volume—to ensure that it lives up to such high-level encouragement, according to the measure of my strength.

This volume contains the manuscript from the Institute <note>The Institut de France, which houses many of Leonardo’s notebooks.</note> marked H, which consists of no fewer than 284 pages; to this, I have added the composite notebooks <note>The original French "cahiers factices" refers to notebooks compiled from loose leaves that were not originally bound together.</note>, formed almost entirely of pages removed from manuscripts A and B, which the director of the National Library, Mr. Léopold Delisle, recently saw returned to France <note>Léopold Delisle was a famous librarian and historian known for tracking down and recovering stolen manuscripts.</note>.

The Quantin Publishing House has generously assisted in the creation of this considerable supplement, and I reiterate the thanks that its directors and collaborators deserve.

The small booklet H, scattered throughout with various figures—among which one notices figures, horses, and interlace patterns—offers many allegories to be compared with the "prophecies of Leonardo da Vinci," as well as fables, maxims, and various thoughts. Sometimes in this train of thought, sometimes out of a taste for natural history, and sometimes with an artistic purpose, the author concerns himself with all sorts of animals, moving from fables concerning them to their instincts and their physical structure. Other pages touch upon philosophy, speaking of the progression that leads from matter to spirit, the uselessness of suffering in plants, the end and the first cause, etc.; others relate to various personages, to viols <note>A family of bowed string instruments popular in the Renaissance.</note>, to carriages and harnesses; still others to subjects treated in previous manuscripts, for example, architecture, water, and Latin and Italian grammars², etc.

The first of the two composite notebooks from the National Library, Ashburnham 2, no. 2038 <note>Named after Lord Ashburnham, from whose collection these stolen manuscripts were recovered.</note>, has only 68 pages; but these pages are large and contain very dense texts of exceptional importance for art. It is there, in fact, that one finds many of the principal chapters of the *Treatise on Painting* <note>original: "Traité de la peinture"</note>. Some passages possess a beautiful literary color; others are important for the question of the teaching of drawing, which is so controversial today³!

In this notebook, a host of remarks, whether general and theoretical or detailed and practical, offer much interest. Leonardo treats the honor of art, the study of the masters (which must be followed by the imitation and love of nature), the universality and the specialization of painters, their spirit, and their lives, in...

->## FOREWORD<-

---

...whether in company or solitary, of their despairs, of the games it is good for them to engage in, of time useful for study, of proprieties and harmonies, of forms, contours, contrasts; of backgrounds, draperies, sketches of histories <note>In this context, "histories" refers to narrative scenes, such as those from the Bible or classical mythology</note>, of the representation of the life of a saint, of angels, nymphs, of characters and attitudes, of the balancing and the serpenting <note>Leonardo used the term "serpentinato" to describe figures that appear to twist or turn, giving them a lifelike energy</note> of figures, of relief—"the importance and soul of painting"—of perspective, which is its "bridle and its rudder," of light and shadow—this last part to be compared with the texts of manuscript C (3rd volume)—of the use of the mirror, the "master of painters," of the rule for judging one's own work, of tracing and counter-tracing, of the manner of learning by heart and of inventing, of the stains on walls to be observed <note>Leonardo famously suggested that looking at random stains on walls could help an artist visualize landscapes, battles, or faces</note>, of the utility of carrying a sketchbook and notes, etc., etc.

Alongside the artist, we find in manuscript 2038, as everywhere else, the scientist, preoccupied with verifying through experience the phenomena that authors have described or cited, and with perfecting the instruments used until then; thus, there is mention of levers and what the physician Pelacane <note>Biagio Pelacani of Parma (c. 1345–1416), a physicist and mathematician whose work influenced the development of perspective</note> had written about them, and of an orichalcum <note>a gold-colored alloy, similar to brass, used in the ancient world</note> scale, of suspended bodies, of the sun and the moon, and of a curious visual illusion. In previous manuscripts, we have seen how much optics preoccupied the author; this is because, for Leonardo, as he says here: "The eye, which is called the window of the soul, is the principal path by which the common sense can amply and magnificently consider his infinite works." And to express this grandeur and magnificence, it is above all to painting that one must devote oneself. If painting, says the painter of the *Mona Lisa* <note>original: "la Joconde"</note>, is but "silent poetry," it is nevertheless superior to the "blind painting" of the poet, and it "surpasses all human works." Whoever despises it "does not love the philosophy in Nature," of which it can be rightly called the "granddaughter."

The second notebook, manuscript Ash. I, no. 2037, has only 26 pages, of which 25 were taken from manuscript B of the Institute; but it contains a fine quantity of sketches and drawings, in pen or silverpoint, some of figures—including caricatures—others of weapons and engines, most of churches and ships.

This time, it is primarily a matter of the wars of Antiquity and religious architecture. Some notes offer a special interest, for example, on the use, regarding maritime combat, of an articulated shoe, similar to certain ancient clogs in the Louvre Museum¹, on Archimedes and Tryphon of Alexandria <note>an ancient Greek grammarian</note>, on various names of ancient peoples, as well as a few words that could be in a secret script².

Following these three manuscripts, which together provide 378 facsimiles, and their alphabetical analysis, one will find the errata for the 4th, 5th, and 6th volumes, then an *Appendix* containing, along with a second edition of folio 1 recto of manuscript A—the keys, so to speak, of the work—that is to say, with specimens allowing one to quickly learn to recognize the details of Leonardo da Vinci's handwriting, a directory facilitating the use of the references—tiring by their multiplicity and variety—given by the fourteen individual tables, as well as chronological and concordance essays concerning the manuscripts and biographies of Leonardo and a bibliographic supplement; finally, a few lines to conclude, where mention is made of Italy and England.

---

Olivier, *Revue Bleue*, p. 236, col. I, 1890).

Alongside the artist, we find in manuscript 2038, as everywhere else, the scientist, preoccupied with verifying through experience the phenomena that authors have described or cited, and with perfecting the instruments used until then; thus, there is mention of levers and what the physician Pelacane <note>Biagio Pelacani of Parma (c. 1345–1416), a physicist and mathematician whose work influenced the development of perspective</note> had written about them, and of an orichalcum <note>a gold-colored alloy, similar to brass, used for the construction of scientific instruments</note> used ...

It also identifies Leonardo as a scientist-practitioner who scrutinized the mechanics and instruments of earlier scholars like Biagio Pelacani.</summary>

1. The marks traced from left to right before the texts: "Xe 64", and after (in the other direction): "35", are not by Leonardo da Vinci. The first is likely by Oltrocchi <note>Baldassarre Oltrocchi (1714–1797) was a librarian at the Ambrosiana who cataloged Leonardo's works</note>, and manuscripts G, F, and E bear similar marks (see page 25 of the 1st volume of this publication). The second corresponds to the numbers: "34" on folio 64 [16] verso, and "33" on folio 142 [1] verso (a page that also bears the mark: "NN 48").
On the back of the parchment cover, someone long ago wrote: "Leonardo da Vinci", and on the bottom edge: "Leonardo". On the front cover’s first recto, toward the top, one can read the "H" assigned by Venturi <note>Giambattista Venturi (1746–1822) was an early researcher of Leonardo’s scientific work</note>, and above it, the number 10 [the 10th in the Ambrosian Library collection] replacing 9. (See pages 21 and 25 of the Preface of the 1st volume, which this note corrects.) On the page attached to the first verso of the cover, there is also Venturi’s "H" at the top, with the 10 above it, then lower down, the "Q" (crossed out 4 times) followed by an "a" by Oltrocchi. Next comes a blank leaf, except that on the verso we find the same "Q" without the "a". On the second recto of the cover, this "Q" appears again with the "a", followed by a period; nothing on the outside.
Manuscript H is composed of 3 booklets, each having an old pagination from after Leonardo’s time, together forming 141 folios. The 1st pagination, which begins at the top of this recto, goes from 1 to 48, written in ink by the same hand as the "10" on the cover. The 2nd goes from 17 to 46; it is preceded by 16 leaves added in pencil at the Institute, and then this numbering continues to the number 95. The first 16 leaves of this part, placed upside down from 1 to 15 recto, are also marked at the bottom of the manuscript in reverse, i.e., 16 to 1, from folio 49 [1] verso to folio 64 [16] verso. The 3rd pagination ends on the verso of the first leaf following the 46th of the second, and goes from 47 to 1, the booklet to which it belongs being joined to the others in reverse; between numbers 45 and 44, a leaf is inserted, which was marked in pencil at the Institute: 44 bis.
Although the pages found in disorder (poorly assembled and poorly numbered) are numerous in Manuscript H, it was felt necessary to accept this quirk, just as others were previously, by reproducing these pages as they are, following the uniform method of the entire work.
2. (The rest in ink).
3. Between Turin and Milan, on the Ticino river. Cf. hereafter, folios 38 recto (C. Amoretti, *Historical Memoirs*, p. 29 and 94 [46] verso). — J.-P. Richter, *The Literary Works of Leonardo da Vinci*, vol II, no. 1026. "...in key..." "To lock up a butteris at Vigevano" <note>Richter's original English translation used "butteris," an archaic term for a tool or support, but here refers to hydraulic works</note>. — In the act of donation of 12 manuscripts by Leonardo da Vinci to the Ambrosian Library, the frame panel for painting on the 1st page of the 4th manuscript (Ms A of the Institute, 1st volume) was mistaken for a: "water enclosure" <note>original: incastro d'acqua</note>.

### [ THE CALANDRA LARK AND THE LOVE OF VIRTUE¹ ].

[Upside down:]
->**LOVE OF VIRTUE**<-

The calandra lark <note>original: "calendrino". In medieval bestiaries, this bird—often identified as a lark—possessed the miraculous power to diagnose illness.</note> is a bird of which it is said that, being
brought before a sick person, if the said sick person is to die,
this bird turns its head away from them and never looks at them;
but if the sick person is to escape [death], this bird never
loses sight of them—rather, it is the cause of removing
every illness from them.

Similarly, the love of virtue never looks upon a base
nor a sad [evil] thing; rather, it always dwells
in honest and virtuous things, and finds its
homeland always in noble hearts, just like
birds in the green forests upon the flowering branches.
And this love shows itself more in adversity
than in prosperity, acting like light which shines more
where it finds a darker place.

---

->**LOVE OF VIRTUE.**<-

The calandra lark² is a bird of which it is said that, being
brought before a sick person, if the said sick person is to die,
this bird turns its head [its back] and never
looks at them. And if the sick person is to recover, this bird never
loses sight of them and is the reason that all illness
is taken away from them.
In the same way, the love of virtue never looks at a
vile or sad [evil] thing; on the contrary, it remains
always in honest and virtuous things and
always has its home in noble hearts, in the manner of
birds in the green forests, upon the flowering branches.
And this love shows itself more in adversity than in
prosperity, acting like the light that shines more
where it finds a dark place³.

---

1. Three crosses in grey pencil, reader's marks.

3. J.-P. Richter, vol. II, no. 1220 [translated: "calendrino" as "cardellino" or "goldfinch"].

### — FOLIO 5 (recto). —

<note>In this passage, Leonardo moves from language to natural philosophy, exploring the fundamental principles of dynamics. He argues that the physical world is defined by four interdependent properties.</note>

These four <term>properties of nature</term><note>Leonardo uses "nature" here to mean the physical world</note> are inseparably made together, as if they were a single thing composed of four parts, which are: <term>place</term><note>original: "loco"</note>, <term>motion</term><note>original: "moto"</note>, <term>time</term><note>original: "tẽpo"</note>, and <term>space</term><note>original: "spatio"</note>. And each of these is, in itself, connected to the others, because place will not exist without space, nor time without motion, nor motion without space. By these motions, the distance of places must be measured; and motion, space, and time [exist] together; nor are they measured except through motion, time, place, and space.

And when you find how much portion of time has passed in a certain amount of motion, and in how much space it will have been consumed; then you shall divide by the opposite: that is, you will find how much motion has passed in a certain amount of time and in a certain amount of space. And thus you will do for the remainders; and through this, it shall be found how many parts of motion there are in every [unit of] time.

— how much it may be <note>original: "quanto fia"</note>

Joy.

Sadness.

->[PEACE AND THE BEAVER. ANGER AND THE BEAR].<-

PEACE.
Of the beaver one reads that, when he is pursued, knowing that he is for the virtue of his medicinal testicles, being no longer able to flee, he stops, then, to have peace with his hunters, he detaches with his sharp teeth the testicles, and leaves them to his enemies.
Anger.
Of the bear it is said that, when he goes to the dwellings of the bees to take their honey, the bees begin to sting him, so that he leaves the honey and runs to vengeance; and wishing to take revenge on all those who bite him, he takes revenge on none, so that his way [course] changes into rage; throwing himself to the ground in exasperation, he defends himself in vain with his hands and with his feet $^2$.

### — FOLIO 6 (verso) $^1$. — — FOLIO 7 (recto) $^1$. —

->[GRATITUDE AND HOOPOES. AVARICE AND THE TOAD].<-

[Written upside down:] *mercy* OR GRATITUDE <note>original: "misericordia OVER GRATITUDINE"</note>
The virtue of gratitude is said to be most found in the birds called hoopoes <note>original: "upica [upupe]"</note>; these, recognizing the benefit of the life they received and the nourishment from their father and mother, when they see them old, they make them a nest, brood over them, and feed them; they pluck out their old and bad feathers with their beaks, and with certain herbs they restore their sight, so that they return to a state of prosperity.

Mercy *or* GRATITUDE.
The virtue of gratitude is said to be found especially among the birds called hoopoes; these, knowing the benefit of the life received and of their nourishment by their father and mother, make a nest for them when they see them old, brood them and feed them, take away with their beak the old and bad feathers, and with certain herbs restore their sight, in such a way that they become prosperous again.
Avarice.
The toad feeds on earth and remains always thin, because it does not sate itself, so great is the fear that the earth may fail him $^2$.

<meta>This page transitions from the moral allegories and bestiary entries found on the previous folios of Manuscript H to Leonardo’s rigorous scientific observations on aerodynamics. Having explored the symbolic nature of animals, Leonardo here applies his "analogy of nature" to engineering, comparing the behavior of air to that of water to calculate the requirements for human flight.</meta>

## FOLIO 5 (verso)

<note>Notes on the mechanics of flight and the resistance of air. Leonardo compares the support air provides to a bird or a flying machine to the buoyancy of water for a ship.</note>

On motion <note>original: "motu"</note>

If the falling weight presses below itself as much as its own weight, such motion will be of a slowness almost equal to the movement of birds; and with ribs <note>original: "rami," literally "branches," referring here to the structural struts of the wing</note> that beat the air, and with little force, a man shall be sustained in the air without any hindrance.

->O<-

If the flyer has the weight of 4 men, and its wings are 40 <term>braccia: a Renaissance unit of measurement, approximately 23 inches or 58 cm</term> in length and 8 braccia in width, and they weigh 200 pounds, it shall be so.

->O<-

That the air shall be of such resistance that it can support the bird just as water supports the vessel <note>original: "nauilio," referring to a ship or boat</note> that enters into it with its weight.

->O<-

---

## FOLIO 6 (recto)

<note>Leonardo continues exploring the physical properties of air as a fluid medium, noting its density and the resistance it offers to motion.</note>

The flyer will come apart if the wings are made of ribs <note>original: "rami"</note>, for the air, like water, is composed of a dense substance; because it opens unwillingly before the movement of the vessel, and even more unwillingly closes behind said vessel; and this arises from the difficulty and laziness of the motion of the air that must unite.

->O<-

On motion <note>original: "motu"</note>

That the air moves with almost as much difficulty as water, and is almost of the same nature, because the air moves like water behind the vessel; it is composed of a density and softness such that it cannot close itself above and behind the vessel.

->O<-

---

## FOLIO 6 (verso)

<note>Technical specifications for constructing artificial wings, detailing the use of cane ribs (rami), fustian cloth, and donkey skin.</note>

How the air opens unwillingly in front and even less closes behind the flyer.

->O<-

On motion <note>original: "motu"</note>

One of these wings shall be 40 braccia long and 8 braccia wide, and shall be composed of ribs made of cane with fustian <term>fustian: a heavy, durable cloth usually made of cotton and flax</term> skin over it, and with donkey skins over the fustian; let the fustian be on the underside so that the air, in moving, opens through it and does not pass between the ribs of the flyers; and you shall make sure that said wing is dense <note>meaning airtight or impermeable</note>.

->O<-

---

## FOLIO 7 (recto)

<note>Further details on wing construction, emphasizing the need for an airtight surface to prevent air from passing through the structure.</note>

On motion <note>original: "motu"</note>

The ribs shall be made of cane ribs with fustian skins over them, with donkey skins over the fustian, with donkey skins over that... <note>Leonardo repeats these technical layers to emphasize the need for a non-porous surface</note> let it be of fustian, and for the underside let it be fustian so that the air does not pass through these ribs.

->O<-

And you shall make it so that this wing moves with a velocity of such force that the air does not pass through these ribs, and let it be dense so that it is composed of a nature that cannot open between the ribs of the flyers; and you shall make sure that said wing is dense and that the air closes beneath it, which shall have the strength of fustian and donkey skin.

->O<-

<summary>In these folios, Leonardo da Vinci outlines the physical principles of aerodynamics, comparing air to water to argue that a sufficiently large, airtight wing made of cane, fustian, and donkey skin could support the weight of a human flyer.</summary>
<keywords>aerodynamics, fluid dynamics, flying machine, wing construction, braccia, fustian, air resistance, Leonardo da Vinci</keywords>

<meta>This page transitions from Leonardo’s scientific investigations into the physics of air and flight (found on Folios 5 and 6) back to his interest in moral philosophy and natural allegory. Here, he records a series of "bestiary" entries—moral lessons drawn from the perceived behaviors of animals—a popular literary genre in the Middle Ages and Renaissance which Leonardo used to explore human virtues and vices.</meta>

### [ LIBERALITY AND THE EAGLE. CORRECTION AND THE WOLF ].

[Written upside down:] **LIBERALITY**
Of the eagle it is said that it is never so hungry that it does not leave a part of its prey to those birds that are around it; these birds, being unable to provide food for themselves, must necessarily be courtiers to this eagle, because in this way they are fed.
**CORRECTION**
When the wolf goes stealthily around some livestock stall, and if by chance it places its foot wrongly so that it makes a noise, it bites its own foot to correct such an error.

**LIBERALITY.**
Of the eagle it is said that it never has such great hunger that it does not leave a part of its prey to the birds that are around it; these, being unable to have pasture by themselves, find it necessary to form a retinue for the eagle, so that in this way they may nourish themselves.
**CORRECTION.**
When the wolf goes with circumspection around some stable of cattle, and if by chance it sets its foot falsely, in such a way that it makes a noise, it bites its foot to correct itself for such an error <note>Leonardo often uses animal behavior as a direct model for human discipline; here, the wolf represents the rigorous self-correction required of a wise person.</note>.

### [ FLATTERIES AND SIRENS. PRUDENCE AND ANTS. FOLLY AND BULLS ].

[Written upside down:] **FLATTERIES OR ADULATION**
The siren sings so sweetly that she puts the mariners to sleep; then she climbs upon the ships and kills the sleeping mariners.
**PRUDENCE**
The ant, by natural counsel, provides in the summer for the winter, killing the gathered seeds so that they do not sprout again, and they nourish themselves on these in due time.
**FOLLY**
The wild ox <note>original: "bo salvatico," referring here to a wild bull</note>, having a hatred for the color red, hunters dress the trunk of a tree in red; the ox runs at it and with great fury strikes it with its horns, whereby the hunters kill it.

**FLATTERIES OR ADULATIONS.**
The siren sings so sweetly that she puts the mariners to sleep, and she climbs upon the vessels and kills the sleeping mariners.
**PRUDENCE.**
The ant, by natural instinct, provides in the summer for the winter by killing the harvested seeds <note>Ancient and medieval naturalists believed ants bit the germ out of seeds to prevent them from growing in the damp underground nests.</note>, so that they do not grow again; and they feed on them at the [appointed] time.
**FOLLY.**
The wild bull having a hatred for the color red, hunters cover the foot of a plant with red; the bull runs against it and pins its horns there with great violence, and then the hunters kill it.

### [ JUSTICE AND BEES. TRUTH AND THE PARTRIDGE ].

[Written upside down:] **JUSTICE**
And one can liken the virtue of justice to the king of the bees <note>At the time, the leader of the hive was thought to be a king rather than a queen.</note>, who orders and disposes every thing with reason; for some bees are ordered to go for flowers, others ordered to work, others to fight with wasps, others to remove the filth, others to accompany and court the king; and when he is old and without wings, they carry him; and if one fails in its duty, it is punished without any remission.
**TRUTH**
Although partridges steal eggs from one another, nonetheless the children born of those eggs always return to their true mother.

**JUSTICE.**
And one can assimilate the virtue of justice to the king of the bees, who orders and disposes each thing with reason, seeing that some bees are ordered to [tasked with] going among the flowers, others are ordered to work, others to fight with the wasps, others to remove the filth, others to accompany their king and form his retinue; and when he is old and without wings, they carry him, and if one of them fails in its office, it is punished without any mercy.
**TRUTH.**
Though partridges steal eggs from one another, nevertheless the young born of these eggs always return to their true mother.

### [ FIDELITY AND CRANES. FALSEHOOD AND THE FOX ].

[Written upside down:] **FIDELITY OR LOYALTY**
Cranes are so faithful and loyal to their king that at night, when he sleeps, some go around the field to guard from afar; others stay close by and each holds a stone in its foot, so that if sleep should overcome them, the stone would fall and make such a noise that they would wake up; and there are others who sleep together around the king, and they do this every night, taking turns so that their king shall not be found wanting.
**FALSEHOOD**
The fox, when it sees a flock of magpies or jackdaws or similar birds, suddenly throws itself on the ground with its mouth open so that it appears dead; the birds want to peck at its tongue, and it grabs them by the head.

**FIDELITY OR LOYALTY.**
Cranes are so faithful and loyal to their king that at night, when he sleeps, some go around the meadow to guard [him] from afar; others hold themselves near and each holds a stone in its claw, so that if sleep should master them, the stone would fall and make a noise such that they would wake. There are others who sleep together around the king, and they do this every night, alternately, so that their king does not come to be left alone.
**FALSEHOOD.**
The fox, when it sees some troop of magpies or jackdaws, or similar birds, immediately throws itself to the ground in a manner that, with its mouth open, it appears dead; the birds want to peck at its tongue and it takes them by the head.

### [ LIE AND MOLE. VALOR AND LION. COWARDICE AND HARE ].

[Upside down:] LIE
The mole has very small eyes and always remains underground; it lives as long as it stays hidden, but as soon as it comes into the light, it dies immediately because it becomes known—so it is with a lie.

VALOR
The lion never fears; on the contrary, with a brave spirit, it engages in fierce battle against a multitude of hunters, always seeking to attack the first one who attacked it.

FEAR OR COWARDICE
The hare is always afraid; the leaves that fall from the plants in autumn keep it in a constant state of terror, and most of the time, it is in flight <note>original: "infuga"</note>.

### [ MAGNANIMITY AND FALCON. VAIN GLORY AND PEACOCK ].

[Upside down:] MAGNANIMITY
The falcon <note>original: "falcone"</note> never hunts anything but large birds, and it would sooner let itself die than feed on small ones or eat foul-smelling <term>fetid</term> <note>Decaying or stinking meat.</note> flesh.

VAIN GLORY
Regarding this vice, one reads that the peacock is more subject to it than any other animal; this is because it is always contemplating the beauty of its tail, spreading it out in the shape of a wheel, and with its cry, it draws the attention of the surrounding animals to itself.
And this is the last vice that can be conquered.

### [ CONSTANCY AND PHOENIX. INCONSTANCY AND SWIFT. TEMPERANCE AND CAMEL ].

[Upside down:] CONSTANCY
The phoenix is likened to constancy; because it understands by its nature its own renewal, it is constant in enduring the searing flames that consume it, and then it is born anew.

INCONSTANCY
The swift <note>original: "martinet" / "rondone". A bird known for its constant, rapid flight.</note> is associated with inconstancy, as it is always in motion and cannot endure the slightest discomfort.

TEMPERANCE [CONTINENCE]
The camel is the most <term>lustful</term> <note>original: "lussurioso", meaning driven by sexual desire.</note> animal there is, and it would follow a female for a thousand miles; yet, if it lived continually with its mother or sisters, it would never touch them, so well does it know how to restrain itself <note>original: "tempere", meaning to practice temperance or self-control.</note>.

### [ INTEMPERANCE AND UNICORN. HUMILITY AND LAMB ].

[Upside down:] INTEMPERANCE
The unicorn, because of its intemperance <note>A lack of self-control, particularly regarding pleasures.</note> and its inability to conquer itself, forgets its ferocity and wildness for the delight it takes in <term>damsels</term> <note>original: "donzelle", referring to young maidens.</note>. Casting aside all suspicion, it goes to the seated maiden and falls asleep in her lap, and in this manner, the hunters capture it.

HUMILITY
One sees the greatest experience of humility in the lamb, which submits itself to every animal. When lambs are given as food to caged lions, they submit to them as if to their own mother, so much so that many times the lions have been seen refusing to kill them.

-> [PRIDE AND FALCON. ABSTINENCE AND DONKEY. GLUTTONY AND VULTURE] <-

[Upside down:] PRIDE <note>original: "SUPERBIA"</note>
The falcon, because of its arrogance and pride, wishes to lord over and overcome all other birds of prey, desiring to be alone; and many times the falcon has been seen attacking the eagle, the queen of birds.

-> ABSTINENCE <-
The wild donkey, when it goes to the spring to drink and finds the water muddied, never has such a great thirst that it does not abstain from drinking and wait for the water to clear.

-> GLUTTONY <-
The vulture is so subject to its gluttony that it would go a thousand miles to eat a carcass, and for this reason, it follows armies. <note>Leonardo notes the vulture’s association with battlefields.</note>

***

-> PRIDE <-
The falcon, with its height and pride, wants to dominate and surpass all other birds of prey, and this is because it desires to be alone; and many times one has seen the falcon assail the eagle, king of birds.

-> ABSTINENCE <-
The wild donkey, when it goes to the fountain to drink and finds the water troubled, never has so great a thirst that it does not abstain from drinking and wait until the water clears.

-> GLUTTONY <-
The vulture is so submitted to its gluttony that it would go a thousand miles to eat a carcass, and that is why it pursues armies.

-> [EAGLE. LUMERPA AND FAME] <-

[Upside down:] EAGLE
The eagle, when it is old, flies so high that it burns its feathers, and Nature allows it to be renewed in youth by falling into shallow water.
And if its young cannot keep their gaze upon the sun, it does not feed them. Let no bird that does not wish to die approach its nest! The animals fear it greatly, but it does not always harm them; it always leaves the remains of its prey for them.

-> LUMERPA Fame <-
This is born in Greater Asia and shines so brightly that it removes its own shadows. In dying, it does not lose this light, and its feathers never fall out; but a feather that is plucked out no longer shines. <note>The "Lumerpa" is a legendary bird used here to represent the concept of Fame, which illuminates and persists after death.</note>

***

-> EAGLE <-
The eagle, when it is old, flies so high that it burns its feathers; and Nature consents to them being renewed in youth by falling into a little water.
And if its young cannot hold their sight to the sun, it does not feed them. Let no bird that does not want to die approach its nest! Animals fear it much, but it does not harm them; always it leaves them a remainder of its hunt.

-> LUMERPA-Fame <-
This one is born in Greater Asia and shines so strongly that it removes its shadows. In dying, it does not lose this light, and the feathers never fall from it again; the feather that detaches no longer shines.

<meta>This page marks a transition in Manuscript H. While the preceding folios focused on a bestiary (using animals as moral allegories), these folios (11v through 13r) shift toward Leonardo’s fascination with the mechanics of the human voice, phonetics, and the limitations of language compared to sight. <meta>Continuity Note: Following the previous folios on phonetics and the mechanics of the voice, Leonardo shifts here to a bestiary—a collection of short descriptions of animals used as moral allegories. This was a common literary genre in the Middle Ages and Renaissance, which Leonardo uses to explore themes of virtue, vice, and human behavior through the supposed "nature" of animals.</meta>

-> - FOLIO 13 (*verso*). - <-

### [ALÈPE. OSTRICH AND CAPTAINS. SWAN. STORK].

[Written upside down:] ALEPO FISH <note>original: "ALEPO PESSCIE." The "alèpe" is difficult to identify precisely; it may refer to a type of shad or a legendary fish described in medieval bestiaries.</note>
The alèpe does not live outside of the water —

OSTRICH <margin>(For heraldry: nourishment / of captains)</margin>
This bird converts iron into its nourishment; it hatches its eggs with its gaze. <note>In Leonardo’s time, it was widely believed that ostriches could digest metal and that the heat of their stare was enough to incubate eggs.</note>

SWAN
The swan is white without any spot, and sweetly sings while dying; this song ends its life.

STORK
By drinking salt water, this bird rids itself of illness. If it finds its mate in fault <note>original: "infallo," referring to adultery.</note>, it abandons her. When the parent is old, its children brood over and feed it until it dies —

**ALÈPE, FISH.**
The alèpe does not live out of the water.

**OSTRICH.** — For coats of arms; the nourishment of captains.
This bird changes iron into its food; it broods its eggs with its sight.

**SWAN.**
The swan is white without any blemish, and sings sweetly when dying; this song ends its life.

**STORK.**
This bird rids itself of evil by drinking salt water; if it finds its mate in fault, it abandons her. When she is old, her children brood over and feed her until she dies <margin>1. J.-P. Richter, Vol. II, no. 1237.</margin>.

-> - FOLIO 14 (*recto*). - <-

### [CICADA. BAT AND VICE. PARTRIDGE. SWALLOW].

[Written upside down:] CICADA
With its song, this one makes the cuckoo fall silent; it dies in oil and revives in vinegar; it sings during the burning heat.

BAT <margin>For the vice that cannot stay / where virtue is —</margin>
The more light there is, the more this creature becomes blind; and the more it looks at the sun, the more it is blinded.

PARTRIDGE
This bird transforms from female to male and forgets its former sex. Out of envy, it steals the eggs of others and broods them, but the hatchlings follow their true mother —

SWALLOW
With <term>celandine</term> <note>original: "celidonia." A plant long associated with the swallow (Greek: khelidōn); folklore held that swallows used the sap of this herb to restore sight to their blind chicks.</note>, this bird gives sight to its blind-born young —

**CICADA.**
With its song, this one makes the cuckoo keep silent; it dies in oil and is resurrected in vinegar; it sings through the burning heat.

**BAT.** — For the vice which cannot remain where virtue is.
This creature loses more of its sight where the light has more brilliance, and blinds itself as much as it looks more at the sun.

**PARTRIDGE.**
This bird transforms itself from female to male and forgets the first sex. Out of envy, it steals eggs from others and broods them, but the young <note>The translator clarifies that the chicks follow the mother, even if hatched by a thief.</note> follow their true mother.

**SWALLOW.**
With the celandine, this bird gives light to its young, who are born blind <margin>1. J.-P. Richter, no. 1238.</margin>.

-> - FOLIO 14 (*verso*). - <-

### [OYSTER AND TREACHERY. BASILISK AND CRUELTY. RUE AND VIRTUE. ASP]

[Written upside down:] OYSTER <margin>For treachery</margin>
When the moon is full, this one opens completely; when the crab sees it, it throws a stone or a piece of straw inside so that the oyster cannot close itself, and thus becomes the food of that crab. So it is for the mouth that speaks its secret: it becomes the prey of the indiscreet listener.

BASILISK <margin>Cruelty</margin>
This creature is fled by all serpents; the weasel <note>original: "donola."</note> fights it with the help of <term>rue</term> <note>original: "ruta." A bitter herb believed to be an antidote to poison and a symbol of grace or virtue.</note> and kills it — <margin>(Rue for virtue)</margin>

THE ASP
This one carries sudden death in its teeth; and so as not to hear incantations, it stops up its ears with its tail — <note>A reference to the "deaf adder" of the Psalms, often used as an allegory for those who refuse to hear the truth.</note>

**OYSTER.** — For treachery.
This one opens wide when the moon is full; and when the crab sees it inside, he throws in some stone or straw, and the oyster cannot close, so that it is the food of that crab. Let it be so for the mouth that tells its secret, which makes itself the prey of the indiscreet listener.

**BASILISK.** — Cruelty.
This one is shunned by all serpents; the weasel in the middle of the rue [plant] fights with it [and] kills it. — (The rue for virtue) <margin>1. See folios 7 recto and 27 recto (Weasel). 2. J.-P. Richter, Vol. II, no. 1239.</margin>.

**THE ASP.**
This one carries sudden death in its teeth; and in order not to hear the enchantments, it plugs its ears with its tail.

### [DRAGON AND AVENGED DEATH. VIPER. SCORPION AND THE PATH OF VIRTUE].

[Written upside down:] DRAGON
This creature ties the legs of the elephant, and the elephant falls upon it, and both of them die — <margin>(And in dying it takes its revenge)</margin>

VIPER
In the act of mating, she covers <note>original: "copre bocha," likely meaning she bites or swallows the male's head.</note> his mouth, and at the end she clenches her teeth and kills her husband; then the children, having grown inside her body, tear open her belly and kill the mother —

SCORPION
Saliva spat upon a scorpion while one is fasting kills it. This is a likeness of the abstinence from gluttony, which takes away and kills the illnesses that depend on that gluttony and opens the path to the virtues <margin>(For the path of virtues)</margin>.

**DRAGON.**
It binds the legs of the elephant and the elephant falls upon it; both die. — (And in dying it takes its revenge.)

**VIPER.**
This one, in its mating, covers [the] mouth, and at the end clenches its teeth, and kills the husband; then its young, grown in its body, tear the belly there and kill the mother.

**SCORPION.**
Saliva, spat upon the scorpion when one is fasting, kills it. — In the likeness of abstinence from gluttony, which takes away and kills the diseases that depend on that gluttony and opens, etc. — (For the path of the virtues) <margin>1. J.-P. Richter, Vol. II, no. 1240 ("opens the mouth").</margin>.

### FOLIO 17 (recto)

->[ THE CROCODILE AND HYPOCRISY.
THE TOAD AND THE ENEMY OF VIRTUE ].<-

<note>Translation of Leonardo's Italian text</note>

[Written upside down:] **CROCODILE.** — Hypocrisy.
This animal catches a man and kills him immediately. After he is dead, it mourns him with a sorrowful voice and many tears; but when the lamentation is finished, it cruelly devours him. — So does the hypocrite, whose face fills with tears for every slight thing, while showing the heart of a tiger; he rejoices in his heart at the misfortune of others while maintaining a weeping countenance.

->TOAD<-

The toad flees the light of the sun; if, however, it is held there by force, it puffs itself up so much that it hides its head low and deprives itself of the sun's rays. — So does the enemy of clear and shining virtue, who cannot stand before it except by force, and with a puffed-up spirit.

<margin>1. J.-P. Richter, Vol. II, no. 1241.</margin>

# — FOLIO 17 (verso). — — FOLIO 18 (recto). —

[ THE CATERPILLAR AND VIRTUE. THE SPIDER. REPUTATION ].

[*Written upside down:*] ->THE CATERPILLAR<-
->On virtue in general<-
The caterpillar, through the practiced diligence of weaving its new dwelling with admirable art and subtle work, later emerges from it with beautiful, painted wings, rising toward heaven with them.
->THE SPIDER<-
The spider gives birth to an artful and masterly web, which returns a benefit to it by catching prey.
Nothing is to be feared more than a foul reputation.
[*Written in red pencil:*] Toil flees with Fame, almost hidden in her arms, c... <note>original: "fame" here refers to "Renommée" or reputation/glory, not hunger.</note>

<margin>1. J.-P. Richter, Vol. II, No. 1242.</margin>

---

[ LION CUBS AND THE CHILDREN OF VIRTUE. LIONS AND CAPTAINS ].

[*Written upside down:*] ->THE LION<-
This animal awakens its cubs with its thundering roar three days after they are born, teaching them the use of all their dormant senses; and all the animals—the wild beasts that are in the forest—flee.
This can be compared to the children of Virtue, who awaken through the cry of praise; their honorable studies grow, raising them ever higher, and all the wicked flee at that cry, withdrawing from the virtuous.
Furthermore, the lion covers its tracks so that the path of its journey is not known to its enemies.
This is well-suited for captains, to hide the secrets of their minds so that the enemy does not recognize their strategies.

<margin>
1. A gray cross, a reader's mark, appears before the texts.
2. J.-P. Richter, Vol. II, No. 1243.
</margin>

[ THE ELEPHANTS ].

[*Written upside down:*] ->THE ELEPHANT<-
The great elephant has by nature that which is rarely found in men: namely probity, prudence, equity, and religious observance. Indeed, when the moon is new, these animals go to the rivers and, solemnly purifying themselves, they wash there; having thus saluted the planet, they return to the forests. And when they are sick, lying on their backs, they throw herbs toward the sky as if they wished to offer a sacrifice.
They bury their tusks when they fall out due to old age. Of their two tusks, they use one to dig up roots for food, and for the other, they keep the point sharp for fighting.
When they are overcome by hunters and exhaustion masters them, the elephants strike their tusks [against trees], and having removed them, they ransom themselves with them <note>Leonardo references the ancient myth that elephants would shed their own ivory to satisfy hunters and save their lives.</note> [Continued on folio 19 verso].

<margin>1. J.-P. Richter, Vol. II, No. 1245.</margin>

# [ THE ELEPHANTS ].

[Upside down (Continuation from folio 19 recto):] They are merciful and they recognize dangers. If it finds a man alone and lost, it kindly puts him back on the path he had lost. If it finds the footprints of a man before seeing the man himself, it fears treachery, so it stops and blows, showing them to the other elephants; then they form a troop and proceed with caution. These always travel in troops; the oldest goes in front and the second-oldest remains last, thus closing the line of the troop. They fear shame. They do not engage in coitus except at night and in secret, and they do not return to the herds after coitus without first washing themselves in the river. They do not fight over females <note>original: "non conbattano me [mezzo] femine"</note> as other animals do. 
And it is so merciful that by nature it does not willingly harm those less powerful than itself. If it encounters a flock or crowd of sheep [The continuation on folio 20 recto].

<margin>1. See Pliny, *Natural History*, Book VIII, chapter 1 and following. — J.-P. Richter, vol. II, no. 1246 ("The females do not fight...") — See Pliny, chapter v, "nor do they have battles among themselves because of females, which are destructive to other animals."</margin>

---

# [ THE ELEPHANTS ].

[Upside down (Continuation from folio 19 verso):] ...it moves them aside with its hand <note>original: "mano" — Leonardo likely refers to the trunk here, which he elsewhere calls a "hand."</note> so as not to trample them underfoot. They never harm unless they are provoked. When one of them has fallen into a pit, the others fill the pit with branches, earth, and stones, so as to raise the bottom so that it may easily become free. They greatly fear the squealing of pigs, and in fleeing backward, they do no less harm with their feet to their own kind than to their enemies. They greatly enjoy rivers and are always wandering near them; but, because of their great weight, they cannot swim. They devour stones, and the trunks of trees are a very pleasant food for them. They hold rats in hatred. Flies greatly love their scent and, if they land on the elephant, it twitches its skin, and by tightening its deep, narrow folds, it kills them <note>Leonardo describes the elephant's ability to crush insects within the wrinkles of its skin.</note>. [The continuation on folio 20 verso].

# [ ELEPHANTS AND DRAGONS. REVENGE AND UNITY ].

[Upside down (Continuation from folio 20 recto):] When they cross rivers, they send their young toward the downstream side, and staying themselves upstream, they break the unified force of the water so that the current does not carry them away. 
The dragon <note>In the tradition of Pliny, the "dragon" refers to a giant serpent or python, the natural enemy of the elephant.</note> throws itself under the elephant's body, knots its legs with its tail, and with its wings and claws, it encircles its ribs and slashes its throat with its teeth; the elephant falls upon it and the dragon bursts; thus, with its own death, it is revenged upon its enemy.

-> THE DRAGON <-
These go in company; they weave themselves together like roots, and with their heads raised, they cross marshes and swim to where they find better pasture; and if they did not unite in this way [The continuation on folio 21 recto].

<margin>1. See Pliny, Book VIII, chapter I and following. — J.-P. Richter, vol. II, no. 1248.</margin>

# [ SERPENT OF MARCUS REGULUS. BOA OF CLAUDIUS ].

[Upside down (Continuation from folio 20 verso):] ...they would drown. Thus does unity.

-> SERPENTS <-
The serpent, a very large animal, when it sees any bird in the air, draws its breath so strongly that it pulls the birds into its mouth. Marcus Regulus, consul of the Roman army, was, with his army, attacked by such an animal and almost put to flight; this animal, having been killed by a wall-breaking engine <note>original: "macina mvrale" — likely a ballista or catapult used to hurl stones during sieges.</note>, was measured at 125 feet, that is, 64 and a half cubits <note>original: "braccia"</note>; with its head, it surpassed all the trees of a forest.

-> BOA, BOAS <-
This is a large snake which wraps itself around the legs of a cow so that she cannot move, then it suckles her in such a way that it almost dries her up; one of this species was killed in the time of Emperor Claudius on the Vatican Hill [The continuation on folio 21 verso].

<margin>1. See Pliny, Book VIII, chapter XIV. "They are given credit in Italy by those called boas..." — J.-P. Richter, vol. II, no. 1249, "The Boa(?)."</margin>

### [ Serpents — The Achlis and sleep ]

<note>This first section is written upside down in the original manuscript.</note>
...one which had an entire child in its body, which it had swallowed <note>This fragment likely refers to a large serpent described on the preceding page. Compare Pliny, Natural History, Book VIII, paragraph XIV.</note>.

**THE ACHLIS** <note>The Elk</note> — (Caught through sleep).
This beast is born in the island of Scandinavia. It has the form of a large horse, except that the great length of its neck and ears makes it different. It grazes on grass by moving backward, because it has such a long upper lip that if it grazed forward, the lip would cover the grass. Its legs are of a single piece <note>meaning they have no joints</note>; for this reason, when it wishes to sleep, it leans against a tree. Hunters, having seen in advance the place where it is accustomed to sleep, saw almost all the way through the tree; and when it later leans against it while sleeping, it falls down in its sleep, and the hunters capture it in this way. Every other way of taking it is in vain, because it is of incredible speed in running <note>Compare Pliny, Natural History, Book VIII, chapter XVI. J.-P. Richter, Volume II, No. 1250, mistakenly titles this "The Macli."</note>.

---

### [ Bonases — Lions, leopards, etc. ]

<note>Written upside down in the manuscript.</note>
**THE BONASE** <note>The Bonnacon or Bison; harms with its flight.</note>
This animal is born in Paeonia; it has a neck with a mane similar to a horse; in all other parts it is similar to a bull, except that its horns are curved inward in such a way that it cannot butt with them. Because of this, it has no other escape than flight, during which it throws out dung for a distance of 400 cubits <note>original: "braccia"; approximately 230 meters</note> along its path, which burns like fire wherever it touches <note>Compare Pliny, Natural History, Book VIII, chapters XVI, XVII, XIX: "They say that in Paeonia there is a wild beast called the bonasus..."</note>.

**LIONS, LEOPARDS, PANTHERS, TIGERS.**
These animals keep their claws within sheaths and never draw them out except when they are upon their prey or an enemy.

**THE LIONESS.**
When the lioness sees that she must defend her cubs from the hands of hunters, so as not to be frightened by the spears, she lowers her eyes to the ground so that her cubs will not be taken prisoner because of her flight <note>J.-P. Richter, Volume II, No. 1251. Richter mistakenly identifies this as a bison, but the text clearly describes the lioness.</note>.

### [ Fears of lions — Beauty of panthers ]

<note>Written upside down in the manuscript.</note>
**THE LION.**
This animal, so terrible, fears nothing more than the noise of empty carts, and likewise the crowing of roosters. It feels great fear upon seeing them, and with a frightened expression looks at the rooster's comb; it loses its courage when its face is covered.

**PANTHERS IN AFRICA.**
The panther has the form of a lioness, but it is higher on its legs and more slender and long. It is all white and marked with black spots in the manner of rosettes. All animals delight in looking at it, and they would always remain around it were it not for the terribleness of its face. [Continued on folio 23 recto].

### [ Beauty of panthers — Character of camels ]

[Continued from folio 22 verso:] ...therefore, knowing this, the panther hides its face, and the surrounding animals feel secure and draw near so that they can better enjoy such great beauty; then the panther suddenly seizes the nearest one and immediately devours it <note>Compare Pliny, Book VIII, chapters XIX and XXIII. J.-P. Richter, Volume II, No. 1252.</note>.

**CAMELS.**
The Bactrians have two humps, the Arabians have one. They are fast in battle and very useful for carrying loads. This animal is a most observant follower of rule and measure, for it will not move if it has a load larger than usual; and if it travels a longer distance [than its custom], it does the same: it stops immediately, so that it is necessary for the merchants to lodge there <note>Compare Pliny, Book VIII, chapter XXVI. J.-P. Richter, Volume II, No. 1253.</note>.

<meta>Continuing from the previous folios where Leonardo recorded proverbs and fables about human nature, he now transitions into a "Bestiary"—a collection of descriptions of animals, both real and mythical. These entries are heavily influenced by classical sources like Pliny the Elder’s *Natural History*, but Leonardo often adapts them to explore themes of deception, specialized anatomy, and the relentless nature of the animal world.</meta>

### [THE HYRCANIAN TIGER AND THE HUNT WITH MIRRORS]
### [THE ETHIOPIAN CATOBLEPAS — THE BASILISK OF CYRENAICA]

[Written upside down:] **THE TIGER**
This animal is born in Hyrcania <note>A region south of the Caspian Sea, legendary in the Renaissance for its fierce tigers.</note>; it is somewhat similar to the panther because of the various spots on its skin. It is an animal of terrifying speed. When the hunter finds its young, he snatches them away immediately, placing mirrors in the spot from which he took them; he then flees quickly upon a fast horse. The panther <note>Leonardo or the source likely uses "panther" and "tiger" interchangeably here.</note>, returning, finds the mirrors fixed to the ground, and seeing herself in them, she believes she is seeing her cubs. Scratching at the glass with her paws, she discovers the deception. Then, by the scent of her children, she follows the hunter. When the hunter sees the tigress approaching, he drops one of the cubs; she takes it, carries it back to the nest, and immediately catches up with the hunter again, and does [Continued on folio 24 recto].

**THE TIGER**
This one is born in Hyrcania; it is somewhat similar to the panther by the diverse spots of its skin; it is an animal of frightening rapidity. When the hunter finds its young, he carries them off at once, having placed mirrors at the place from which he took them, and then flees immediately on a swift horse. The panther, returning, finds the mirrors fixed to the ground, and seeing herself there, believes she sees her young; then, striking them with her paws, she discovers her error, and by means of the scent of her children, follows the hunter. When the hunter sees the tigress, he leaves one of the young; she takes it, carries it to the nest, rejoins the hunter immediately, and does [Continued on folio 24 recto].

<meta>Following the descriptions of animals like the tiger and the basilisk on the preceding pages, Leonardo shifts his focus on these folios toward physics, optics, and botany. He explores the phenomenon of parallax—how objects appear to move differently based on their distance from a moving observer—and transitions into observations on the structural growth of trees, which he categorizes under "painting" as these are essential principles for a painter to depict nature accurately.</meta>

-> - FOLIO 23 (verso). - <-

In what way the being that is in the air moves, not moving of its own accord, but through its medium, which is moved by the one who moves; and this is the eye, which, when it moves, it seems to it that every object moves contrary to its own motion; and that which is very far away seems to follow the motion, but that which is near the eye seems to flee in the opposite direction to its motion; and the reason for this will be given. And this happens also when sailing in a ship, where the stones at the bottom of the earth <note>Leonardo refers here to the seabed or riverbed seen through the water.</note> seem to flee backward, and the highest mountains seem to follow the motion of the sailor; and the reason for this will be given in the [study of the] motion of the eye.

### [ Ichneumons and Egyptian crocodiles <note>original title: "Ichneumons et crocodiles d’Égypte"</note> ].

<note>The following sections were written upside down in the original manuscript.</note>
-> ICHNEUMON <-
This animal is the mortal enemy of the asp. It is born in Egypt, and when it sees an asp near its place, it immediately runs to the mud or slime of the Nile and covers itself entirely with it. Then, dried by the sun, it smears itself again with mud, and drying one layer after another, it forms three or four coats like a suit of armor. Then it attacks the asp and struggles well with it, so that, seizing the right moment, it leaps at its throat and suffocates it.

-> CROCODILE <-
This creature is born in the Nile; it has four feet, and lives on land and in water. It is the only land animal found without a tongue, and it bites only by moving its upper jaw. It grows up to 40 feet long; it has claws and is covered in a hide like armor capable of withstanding any blow. By day it remains on land, and at night in the water. Having fed on fish, it falls asleep on the bank of the Nile with its mouth open, and the bird called... [Continued on folio 26 recto].

<margin>
1. See Pliny, *Natural History*, Book VIII, chapters 35 to 37.
2. J.P. Richter, vol. II, no. 1258. (Richter mistakenly translated "lita" [mud] as "to the bed".)
</margin>

---

### [ Crocodiles, trochilus, dolphins ].

<note>Upside down (continued from folio 25 verso):</note>
The trochilus <note>A small bird, often identified as the Egyptian plover.</note>, a very tiny bird, immediately runs to its mouth, hops between its teeth, and goes about pecking the remains of food both inside and out. By hopping and pecking thus with delightful pleasure, it invites the crocodile to open its mouth wide, and so the crocodile falls asleep. Seeing this, the ichneumon <note>a type of mongoose</note> immediately flings itself into the mouth, pierces the stomach and intestines, and finally kills it. It is similar to the green lizard.

-> OF THE DOLPHIN <-
Nature has given such knowledge to animals that, beyond knowing what is useful to them, they also know the weaknesses of their enemies. Thus, the dolphin understands how powerful the sharp edges of the fins on its back are, and how tender the belly of the crocodile is. Therefore, in their combat, it dives beneath the crocodile, slits its belly open, and so kills it.

The crocodile is terrifying to those who flee and most cowardly toward those who hunt it. <margin>1. See Pliny, Book VIII, chapters 37 and 38. — J.P. Richter, vol. II, no. 1259.</margin>

---

### [ Hippopotamus, ibis, stags ].

<note>Written upside down:</note>
-> HIPPOPOTAMUS <-
When this animal feels weighed down <note>likely referring to an excess of blood or "humors"</note>, it goes searching for thorns or places where there are remains of cut reeds. It rubs a vein against them so much that it cuts it, and having drawn the blood it needs, it smears the wound with mud and seals the injury. It has a form much like a horse, with cloven hooves, a twisted tail, and the teeth of a wild boar, with a maned neck. Its skin cannot be pierced unless it is wet. It feeds on grain in the fields, entering them backward so that it appears to have left them.

-> IBIS <-
This bird resembles a stork, and when it feels sick, it fills its crop with water and gives itself an enema with its beak.

-> STAGS <-
When the stag feels bitten by the spider called a phalangium <note>a venomous spider mentioned by Pliny</note>, it eats crabs and is freed from such poison.

<margin>
1. See Pliny, Book VIII, chapters 40 and 41. — J.P. Richter, vol. II, no. 1260. (Richter mistakenly translated "l'unghia fessa" [cloven hoof] as "with long haunches".)

-> SWALLOW <-
The swallow restores sight to its blind chicks with the juice of the celandine <note>a flowering plant in the poppy family long associated with eye health in folklore</note>.

-> WEASEL <-
When this animal hunts rats, it first eats rue <note>a bitter herb used as an antidote to poison</note>.

-> WILD BOAR <-
This animal cures its ailments by eating ivy.

-> SNAKE <-
When the snake wishes to renew itself, it sheds its old skin, starting from the head; the change takes a day and a night.

-> PANTHER <-
Even after its entrails have spilled out, the panther continues to fight against dogs and hunters.

<meta>The previous folios concluded the descriptions of the crocodile and the ichneumon, moving from specific animal behaviors to broader philosophical reflections. These pages represent a shift into Leonardo’s deeper meditations on the nature of life, death, and the interconnectedness of living beings—specifically how one life is sustained by the destruction of another, a theme that led to his well-known advocacy for vegetarianism.</meta>

## Folio 25 (verso)

Many fish of one water approach the one who knows them, and similarly, the birds of the woods. If, in truth, they lived on the death of others and lived with that body which has departed from one life—and death could not be escaped without passing through the stomach of another—then man and animals would be a true desire for death, by being a vehicle and a place of burial <note>Leonardo frequently used the metaphor of the body as a "tomb" or "sepulcher" for the animals consumed by humans.</note>.

Although nature has moved them to go from one place to another, and they are therefore nourished by various other substances, it does not seem wrong if they shared the living company of their own kind; and so the fish of a single body of water are similar to those fishing for one another, not for any other truth than that they are of one nature—one living by the life of the other—as has been seen many times through the deposits <note>original: "dafforti," likely meaning "d’apporti" or alluvial deposits</note> that are seen similarly through the lowering of rivers.

---

## Folio 26 (recto)

If a voice, if a sight, and of waters of one place, of a stream... through the verses. Certain things are similar in one virtue, that is, fish of one water; but when one from another water runs after another, one chases the other, and there is not one of them who does not clothe himself in another garment <note>Leonardo often uses "garment" or "clothing" as a metaphor for the physical form or the qualities that envelop a soul or essence.</note>. Whence it seems that this being of one water clothes the animals in one garment and one motion. I mean of various, varied qualities, the same thing of one and the same life, and when the body is alive.

Many and varied pursuits of what was said will be made with the coming of one water from one nature into another. The voice being in the ear, and so the smelling in the nostrils, and thus the odor of every substance of one life; but in the sense, the smelling is of one essence, of one nature, of a **vital wind** <term>Vital wind: A Renaissance concept referring to the breath or pneuma that carries life and sensory information through the body.</term>.

### [ WATER. — ARTIFICIAL WINGS ].

Once a year, the amount of water that rises will be as much as that which descends in the rivers and in the air. <note>Leonardo is describing the concept of the hydrological cycle: the balance between evaporation and precipitation.</note>

For the wing, let a cord be made that can endure fatigue, and in the same place a looser one, so that if the one under strain breaks, the other remains to perform the same duty. <note>An early principle of mechanical redundancy for safety in flight.</note>

->is that which descends, in the rivers and in the air.<-

->That to the wings one should make a cord that endures fatigue<-
->and in the same place a looser one, so that if the one,<-
->fatigued, breaks, the other remains in the same duty.<-

### [ WAVES IN WATER. — DEAD BODIES IN WATER ].

A stone thrown into still <note>original: "acqua morta"; literally "dead water," referring to stagnant or perfectly calm water</note> water will create a perfectly circular expansion of motion, provided that the water is of equal depth.

If two stones are thrown near one another within the space of one <term>cubit</term><note>original: "braccio"; a Florentine unit of measurement approximately equal to 23 inches</note>, the circles of the water will grow equally, one into the body of the other, without one ruining the other. 

But if the bottom is not level, the circulation will not be equal, except on the surface.

Every man, in his third year, is half of his final height.

The bodies of males who have died in the water remain on their backs <note>original: "supini"</note>, and the females face down <note>original: "bocconi"</note>.

A long-shaped object thrown upon the water will create an oval-shaped wave.

A round object thrown into running water will create an oval-shaped wave of two movements.

<margin>
1 and 3. Some emblematic sketches and several words were traced in red chalk before the ink texts. Near the first line of the manuscript, one reads: "mulberry" <note>original: "more" or "moro"; may refer to the mulberry tree, a common symbol in Leonardo's work</note>, and near the 10th line: "sweet and sour, and slow..."
2. See F. Cardinali, p. 333, book I, ch. LIII and ch. XII.
4. J.-P. Richter, Vol. I, no. 308.
</margin>

### [ ANTITHESES. — PERSPECTIVE ].

Lust is the cause of generation.
Gluttony is the maintenance of life.
Fear or dread is the prolongation of life.
Deceit is the preservation of the instrument <note>Leonardo often refers to the body or the living organism as an "instrument" or machine</note>.

[Figure: T V R N A M T O S]

*T - S* represents how the eye has seen a circular wall equidistant to the eye. The wall *V - S* constrains the perspective to be viewed through a single hole.

### [POWDER — EVILS AND DEATH. INCIDENCE AND REFLECTION.]

<margin>thin copper</margin>
To dampen the powder when it is swept. <note>original: "dadaquare [di adaquare] lapolvere quando siscoua." Leonardo is likely advising on how to prevent dust from rising while cleaning a workspace.</note>

Every injury leaves a sense of regret in the memory, except for the supreme injury—that is, death—which kills the memory along with life itself. <note>This is a famous philosophical fragment from Leonardo's journals (Richter §1164), reflecting his view that death is an absolute end to the conscious experience of pain or regret.</note>

The descent of birds, or the rebound taken by any object, will never rise as high as the initial descent, nor will it surpass it. <note>Leonardo applies the same physical principle to both the flight of birds and the motion of inanimate objects: energy is lost during the "rebound," preventing it from reaching its original height.</note>

[Figure 1:] Thin copper.
To dampen the powder when it is uncovered.
Every evil leaves displeasure in the memory, except the supreme evil, that is to say, death, which kills this memory at the same time as life.
The descent [climb] of birds, or the rebound near any thing, will never rise as much as the descent or will not exceed it.

### [ Arcs. — Watercourses ].

->A continuous body <note>original: *quantità continua*; refers to a solid, unified material like a wooden beam</note> that is forcibly bent into an arch pushes toward the line where it desires to return.<-

### [ Supports. — Water ].

->The sides of any discrete quantity <note>such as sand or gravel</note> that has been piled up in a pyramidal heap will have the slant of the diagonal of a perfect square. <note>Leonardo is describing the "angle of repose," observing that a pile of loose material naturally forms a 45-degree angle.</note><-

<meta>Building on the previous discussions regarding the center of gravity and the mechanics of arches (discrete vs. continuous bodies), these folios transition into specific calculations for structural stability, the physics of leverage, and the practical application of geometry to quantify military munitions like cannonball stacks.</meta>

### [Folio 35 verso]

<note>Structural study of an arch, analyzing how its weight pushes outwards.</note>

This arch, through its own weight, pushes outwards as much as its parts weigh.

Let the arch be half as wide on the outside at the top as it is on the inside; the same shall apply to the height.

The reason is this: because when an arch breaks <note>fails under stress</note>, it divides itself into 4 parts, and the parts at the bottom are the ones that push <note>referring to lateral thrust, the outward force that can cause walls to buckle</note>.

---

### [Folio 36 recto]

<note>Continuation of structural arch studies, exploring the effect of a heavy vertical load on lateral thrust.</note>

Because this arch has more weight above than at the sides, it does not push [outwards] as much as it would if it did not have such weight. <note>Leonardo observes that a heavy vertical load—like a wall or tower—can actually help stabilize an arch by pinning the stones down and counteracting the tendency to spread.</note>

---

### [Folio 36 verso]

<note>Mechanical study of leverage and the direction of motion/force. Includes a diagram with an eye observing the mechanics.</note>

There will be as much force here as here.

It shows how the force is directed along the path it is moved, because the line of its motion is a straight line.

Just as if it were placed, it does not employ much force; if you draw a line from the moving element to the center of its balance <term>bilancia; here meaning the fulcrum or axis of a scale</term>, that will be the length of its arm <note>the "lever arm" in modern physics</note>, because if you draw a line from itself to its center...

---

### [Folio 37 recto]

<note>Mathematical and ballistic study concerning the weight of spheres (such as cannonballs) stacked in a pyramid.</note>

If you wish to know how much balls <note>likely stone or iron cannonballs</note> arranged in a pyramid or mound will weigh, you must multiply what is in that line...

These balls must be weighed by the length of the diameter of the ball, multiplied by the lines with which they are woven to form the pyramids, and the remainder should be divided by half. <note>Leonardo is attempting to find a geometric formula to calculate the total mass of a stockpile without weighing every individual ball.</note>

<summary>Leonardo analyzes the physics of arches, noting that vertical loads can prevent lateral collapse, and provides geometric methods for calculating the weight of piled cannonballs.</summary>
<keywords>structural engineering, lateral thrust, arch stability, leverage, ballistics, sphere packing, geometry of weight</keywords>

## — FOLIO 41 (verso)¹ . —

[1st fig.:] mirror &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; light

If a whole man were at the bottom of a well that had 20,000 braccia <term>braccia: an Italian unit of measurement, literally "arms," approximately 23 inches or 58 cm</term> of water, he would not support any weight from it. <note>Leonardo is correctly observing that a submerged body does not feel the "weight" of the water above it in the way a person on dry land feels a heavy object, due to the principles of buoyancy and hydrostatic pressure.</note>

### [ THE OYSTER AND THE RAT (A FABLE). — WATER ].

[Upside down:]
**FABLE**
An oyster, being unloaded along with other fish at a fisherman’s house near the sea, begged a rat to lead it back to the water. The rat, having formed a plan to eat the oyster, made it open up; but as the rat bit into it, the oyster snapped shut, pinning the rat’s head and holding him fast. Then, a cat arrived and killed the rat. <note>original: "FAVOLA sen/do lostriga..." Leonardo often used fables to illustrate moral lessons or the dangers of deception.</note>

Measure the water that falls by its height and multiply it by the height to which you wish to raise it (and however many times the fall of the water fits into the height of its elevation, it will be that much thinner <term>sottile: in this context, Leonardo refers to the volume or "thinness" of the stream relative to its velocity and pressure</term> than the water that rises). And this is the final, greatest amount that can be raised.

---

**FABLE.**
The oyster being unloaded at the same time as the other fish, at the fisherman's dwelling near the sea, begs the rat to lead it to the sea; the rat, having formed the design of eating it, makes it open, and the oyster, biting him, squeezes his head and holds him; the cat comes and kills him.

Measure the water that falls by its height and multiply it by the height to which you want to raise it (and as many times as the fall of the water enters into the height of its elevation, so much more subtle [lighter] it is than that which rises). And this is the final greatest sum that can be raised.

<margin>
1. Written in red chalk, except for the first 8 lines and the numbers 26.
2. J.-P. Richter, i. n° 1265.
</margin>

---

### [ RISES AND FALLS OF WATER ].

[Upside down:]
The water that rises continually because of the movement of another water will be as much thinner <note>original: "sottile"</note> than the water that moves it as it is higher and longer.
[Figure:] m n a q p o
If the water *n a — p o* has a fall of 2 braces <term>braccia: an Italian unit of measurement, approximately 23 inches or 58 cm</term>, and you add water *n m, p q* above it, it does not fall with as much of a drop.

---

Water that rises continuously because of the movement of other water will be as much thinner than that which moves it as it is *higher and longer*.
[Fig.:] m n a q p o
If the water *n a p o* has a fall of 2 braces, and you add over it the water *n m, p q*, it does not fall with as much of a drop.

<margin>
1. Written in red chalk.
</margin>

### [ MOVEMENT (THE SIEVE, GOLD OF THE TICINO, GOLDSMITHS). — TURBID WATER ].

[Upside down:]
Why does the movement made by the sieve gather all the lightest parts together at the top, to one side? The same thing happens with the small boat <term>navetta: a shuttle-shaped vessel or tray</term> where they fish for gold in the Ticino <note>The Ticino is a river in northern Italy known historically for small amounts of gold in its sands.</note> by means of the impact; and also with the sweepings of goldsmiths, which are washed.

Turbid water <term>acqua turba: muddy or sediment-heavy water</term> harms the banks more than clear water, and more at the bottom than at the top, because it is heavier and thicker.

---

Why does the movement made by the sieve gather all the lightest parts together on top, separately? And the same is done by the small boat where gold is fished in the Ticino, by means of the blow, and also the sweepings of the goldsmiths, which are washed.
Turbid water harms the banks more than clear water, and more at the bottom than at the top, because it is heavier and thicker.

1. Written in red chalk.
2. See F. Cardinali, p. 380, book six, chapter xiv.
</margin>

### [ FALLS OF WATER ].

[Upside down:]
[Figure:] a b
The line of water that has the greater movement breaks that of the lesser movement, and plunges beneath it.

The part of the sand that is closest to the impact <note>original: "perchusione"</note> of the falling water will be finer than the rest.
The heavy gravel will be further away from the impact.

---

[Figure:] a b
The line of the water which has the greatest movement breaks that of the lesser movement, and sinks beneath it.
The part of the sand which is closer to the impact of the falling water will be smaller than the other.
The coarse gravel will be further from the blow.

--- Page 68 ---
<meta>Following the previous exploration of air as a fluid medium and the resistance encountered by moving bodies, Leonardo here shifts his focus specifically to hydraulics and the mechanics of watercourses. These folios contain his observations on how water behaves when it falls, turns in eddies, or flows through channels of varying widths and slopes. He is particularly interested in the "inversion" of water layers during a fall—how the top becomes the bottom.</meta>

If Nature has ordained suffering in the vegetative souls [endowed with] movement, for [the] preservation of the organs which might be diminished and spoiled by movement, the vegetative souls without movement do not have to run against opposing objects; therefore, suffering is not necessary in plants, so that in breaking them, they do not feel pain like those of animals.

->[HYDRAULIC WHEEL]<-

[2nd figure:] f n a r m
If **a n** receives 100 pounds of weight from **f n**, then **a m**—because it is half as long on the lever—will lift 200; and **a r**—because it is similar to **n a** on the lever—will lift 100. But it is just as effective to use **a r** as **a m**, because if **a m** lifts 200, it lifts them half as high as **a r** lifts its 100; I conclude, therefore, that each performs the same operation <note>original: "pari operatione," meaning they produce the same total work or result</note>.

[1st figure:]
No mounting <note>original: "incasstro," referring to the frame or gate of a lock</note> should be narrower than the general width of its canal, because the water then creates eddies and breaks the embankment.

### PERSPECTIVE
Shadows or things reflected in moving water—that is, water with small waves—will always appear larger than the actual object outside the water from which they originate.

[2nd figure:]
The eye cannot judge the exact point where a high object must descend.

The derived shadow <note>the shadow cast by an object onto a surface</note> is never similar to the body from which it originates unless the light source is the same shape and size as the shaded body.

The derived shadow cannot be similar in shape to the original <note>primitive</note> shadow if it does not strike the surface at equal angles.
