— FOLIO 77 [29] (*recto*) <note>The figures are in red pencil.</note> —

->[NATURE IN MOUNTAINS, MAN, WATER, AND BLOOD]<-

The water that springs in the mountains is the blood that keeps that mountain alive. If one of its veins is opened, either within it or across it <note>on its sides</note>, Nature—which assists her living beings—being eager to abundantly overcome the lack of the spilled fluid <note>original: "omore," or "humor," referring to vital fluids</note>, flows there with a curious haste. This is just as it happens with a wounded spot in a man: one sees, by the help provided, the blood multiply under the skin in the form of a swelling, to open itself to the infected place <note>the wound</note>. Similarly, if a vine is cut at its highest extremity, Nature sends its fluid from the lowest roots to the greatest height of the severed spot; and once this is poured out, she does not leave it without vital fluid until the end of its life.

<summary>This section covers mechanical calculations for water wheels, the behavior of water currents and reflections, and concludes with Leonardo's "macrocosm-microcosm" theory, comparing the Earth's hydrology to the human circulatory system.</summary>

### Ms H (2) — FOLIO 77 [29] (verso) — FOLIO 78 [30] (recto)

->[Water. — Blue of the air. — Movement].<-

Water that flows near the bottom between the banks will be slower than the rest, because of the disturbances <note>original: "perclussioni," referring to the water striking the banks or floor</note> that create eddies.

The air is blue <note>original: "azurra"</note> because of the darkness that is above it, because black and white make blue. <note>Leonardo believed the sky's color was not inherent, but resulted from the "white" light of the sun illuminating the atmosphere against the "black" vacuum of space.</note>

All violent movements weaken the more they depart from their cause. <note>In Leonardo’s physics, a "violent" motion is one caused by an external force (like a thrown stone), which loses energy over time, as opposed to "natural" motion like gravity.</note>

<margin>1. Written in red pencil.</margin>
<margin>2. Reference to Jean-Paul Richter’s compilation of Leonardo’s notebooks, Vol. I, No. 304.</margin>

---

->[Error on purchased water. — Natural movement].<-

You who buy water by the ounce <note>The "ounce" (oncia) was a standard unit for measuring water flow in Renaissance Italy, usually determined by the size of the opening through which the water passed.</note>, know that you may be greatly deceived. This is because if you take an ounce of still water and an ounce of running water against the opening of your measure—one ounce near the surface, one near the bottom, or one across the current—[the volume delivered will differ].

As much as natural movement departs from its origin <note>original: "cavsa"</note>, so much faster it becomes. <note>This refers to acceleration due to gravity; the further an object falls from its starting point, the faster it travels.</note>

<margin>1. Written in red pencil.</margin>

---

## [WATER].

[1st fig. :] 40 20 20
[2nd fig. :] a i t r o n s m
13 THE LINES WHICH REBOUND FROM THE WATER AFTER ITS IMPACT WILL NOT HAVE A STRAIGHT COURSE; INSTEAD, THEY WILL INCLINE IN A CURVE.

The impact made by the water from **s** at **a** would desire to rebound toward **m**, but the obstructions of the other lines that strike it—namely **t**, **r**, and **o**—twist it downward <note>The French translation adds: "push and turn it"</note> toward **n**.

## [CHANNELS].

11 — A straight channel of equal depth and slope will, in a short time, create a deeper hollow in the middle than near the bank.

— In the middle of straight channels, the water flows more rapidly than at the sides.

— Where the water moves more, it is lighter, given equal heights. <note>Leonardo is observing an early intuition of fluid pressure: faster-moving water appears to exert less weight or pressure than still water of the same height.</note>

12 — Water that is constricted will break the bank and the bed after its fall.

## [CHANNELS].

10 EVERY WATER CHANNEL OF EQUAL SLOPE, DEPTH, AND WIDTH WHICH IS CONSTRICTED IN ANY PLACE WILL BREAK THE BED AND THE BANK AFTER PASSING THAT NARROWING.

This happens because where the water is constricted, it rises behind that narrowing; and passing through that narrow place, it passes with fury because it descends. It finds the water below which is not moving and meets an obstruction; consequently, it follows the line of its descent, goes to the bottom, digs there, and with circular movements <term>retrose</term> <note>original: "retrose," referring to eddies or back-currents that swirl against the main flow.</note> turns toward the banks; by hollowing them from below, it makes them collapse, as is shown in the drawing above.

<margin>In red pencil, except for the numbers.</margin>

### [Optics (The Man and the Owl)].

— **All things seen will appear larger at midnight than at midday, and larger in the morning than at midday.** —
This happens because the pupil of the eye is much smaller at midday than at any other time. —
In the same proportion that the eye or pupil of the owl is larger relative to its body than that of a man, it sees that much more light at night than the man does. For this reason, at midday it sees nothing if it does not diminish its pupil; and likewise, it sees things larger at night than by day. <note>Leonardo is observing how the dilation of the pupil affects the perceived size and clarity of objects in different lighting conditions.</note>

<margin>Below the first text, there is a figure in red chalk.</margin>

--- Page 101 ---
<meta>Continuing from the previous pages, which shifted from hydraulic observations to optics and mechanics, these folios transition into a deeply philosophical and metaphysical exploration. Leonardo uses geometric and mechanical concepts—specifically the "point" and "unity"—as metaphors to argue for the indivisibility and immortality of the soul in relation to the physical body.</meta>

**FOLIO 85 [37] (verso)**

<note>Perspective study of an interior corner with geometric lines. This diagram illustrates Leonardo’s attempt to map the non-physical "point" of the soul onto a three-dimensional space.</note>

The soul cannot operate if it does not originate from a point, and it is present in its entirety in every part of that body. It is not diminished by the mutilating or breaking of the limbs, because in that loss, only the senses <note>The physical faculties of perception.</note> would suffer, but not the soul, which is not diminished in any point. The soul, therefore, does not fear the loss of the body, because the soul has nothing to lose from any sense of that body; for the soul neither thinks, nor sees, nor feels by means of the quantity <note>The physical size or mass.</note> of that body.

The soul cannot be mutilated, nor does it fear diminution <note>The state of being made smaller or less.</note> through the diminution of the body, because it is indivisible.

---

**FOLIO 86 [38] (recto)**

Every reason <term>reason: *ragione*, here meaning the underlying logic, nature, or governing principle</term> in the point has no point, so that it has no point by reason of any point; because unity is not a deficiency, because unity is the reason for being.

Therefore, by reason it has none, and reason is not a lack of unity; nor is unity diminished by the loss of a limb. Now see if reason is within the point: every reason in the point is transformed, so that it can only fail along with the failure of the body itself. And if it is a point of unity, then it cannot be diminished by the loss of the body, nor fail through the loss of that body, because it is within the point of unity.

---

**FOLIO 86 [38] (verso)**

<note>Mechanical diagrams of toothed wheels or pin-drums on a vertical axle. Leonardo uses these mechanical labels (K and F) to provide a visual anchor for his abstract logic.</note>

**K** within point **K** has no reason of unity, and is therefore indivisible, as it possesses no nature of diminution through the diminution or loss of any limb of that body; therefore, it has neither reason nor diminution.

**F**, but by reason of a point **X**, has no reason; but by the loss of a point, there is neither reason nor diminution. By the loss of a point, neither reason nor unity is diminished. It exists by reason of a point of unity, but by reason of a point of diminution, it is not diminished.

---

**FOLIO 87 [39] (recto)**

The point has no point; it has neither reason nor diminution because it is indivisible, for unity has no point.

<note>Wavy lines depicting fluid patterns or architectural molding profiles. These lines reflect Leonardo's constant habit of observing natural flow, even amidst abstract philosophical writing.</note>

Every loss of a point, or reason of a point, or reason through diminution, has no reason of unity; of unity, it has no diminution, but by reason of a point—of the reason of a point—it has neither reason nor diminution.

<summary>In these folios, Leonardo argues for the indivisibility of the soul, comparing it to a geometric point that exists within the body but is not subject to physical decay or mutilation. He uses the concept of "unity" to explain how the soul remains whole regardless of what happens to the physical limbs.</summary>
<keywords>soul, indivisibility, geometry, the point, unity, metaphysics, mechanics, anatomy, philosophy of mind</keywords>

->[Optics]<-

THE EYE WHOSE PUPIL IS LARGER WILL SEE THINGS AS LARGER FIGURES.
This is demonstrated by the sight of luminous bodies, and especially celestial ones; when the eye leaves the darkness and suddenly looks at these bodies, they appear larger <note>original: "magiori"</note> and then they diminish. And if you look at these bodies through a small hole, you will see them as smaller, because a smaller part of the pupil <note>original: "popilla"</note> is employed for that task <note>Leonardo is observing how the pupil dilates in the dark, which affects the perceived size of stars before the eye adjusts to the light.</note>.

<margin>J.-P. Richter, volume I, no. 32.</margin>

<note>Sketch of a horizontal lever or balance beam with points marked M, A, and N.</note>

The weight, as it moves along its straight surface, or in a straight line from whatever side it is moved, moves as much as its <term>motor|The force or object initiating the movement</term> moves. **m** or **n** in **m n** under **n**.

Because weights that move here or there <note>that is, horizontally or laterally</note> have no regard for the center of the earth, but only insofar as they approach or move away from the center of the earth <note>Leonardo is observing that gravity only acts on the vertical component of movement; purely horizontal movement does not change the weight's relationship to the earth's gravitational center</note>.

### FOLIO 88 [40] (recto)

<note>Sketch of a screw-like mechanical device.</note>

Why the tide <note>original: "marea"</note> moves more in channels than in the wide sea or in the ocean.

Liquids that approach the bottom of a vessel through a pipe: why they keep that motion which the <term>impetus|The momentum or driving force of the water</term> sent into them gives to the bottom of said water, so that it tends to follow the tide; and suddenly it approaches the bottom of the sea, and the impetus of said water in the channels pushes the water more toward the shore because of the motion of the water of the tide, and it rises higher toward the shore because of the impetus of said water.

# — FOLIO 90 [42] (verso) —

### [Optics. — Hydraulic machine].

ON PAINTING
The light of lights—that is, the luster <note>original: "lustro"; the specular highlight or the brightest point of reflection on a surface</note> of any object—will not be located in the middle of the illuminated part; instead, it will change position as many times as the eye of the viewer changes.

If 12 ounces of water make a <term>millstone|original: "macina"; a grinding wheel or the engine of a mill</term> turn 30,000 times per hour, we believe that 24 ounces will make the same millstone turn 60,000 times per hour, the fall of the water being the same, and that it will grind twice as much as the first.

<margin>
1. J.-P. Richter, Vol. I, no. 134.

# — FOLIO 91 [43] (recto) —

### [Cost of a canal].

The <term>canal|original: "navilio"; a navigable waterway</term> that is 16 <term>braccia|A Renaissance unit of length, approximately 23 inches</term> wide at the bottom and 20 at the mouth [the top], can be said, in short, to be 18 braccia wide on average. And if it is 4 braccia deep, at 4 <term>denari|A small unit of currency</term> per <term>quadretto|A cubic measurement in this context, roughly a cubic braccio</term>, the excavation alone will cost 900 <term>ducats|Gold currency</term> per mile, the *quadretti* being of the common braccio. 

But if the braccia used are the "land measurement" <note>original: "misura di terra"; standard units often varied between commercial use and land surveying</note>, where every 4 units are equal to 4 and 1/2; and if the mile is understood to be 3,000 common braccia which are converted into land-measure braccia, its 3,000 braccia lose 1/4 of their number, so that 2,250 braccia remain. Thus, at 4 denari per braccio, the mile comes to 675 ducats. At 3 denari per *quadretto*, the mile comes to 506 1/4 ducats, so that the excavation of 30 miles of canal comes to 15,187 1/2 ducats.

<margin>
1. Cf. C. Amoretti, *Mem. stor.*, p. 104, and *Saggio del. op. di L. da V.*, plate VI.
2. J.-P. Richter, Vol. II, no. 1014.
</margin>

### [OPTICS. — LUMINOUS BODIES].

The eye which, emerging from the darkness, suddenly sees a luminous body, will find it appears much larger at the first glance than after looking at it for a while.
A luminous body will appear larger and more luminous with two eyes than with only one. 
That luminous body will show itself to be of a smaller shape when it is seen by the eye through a smaller <term>aperture<note>original: "spirachulo"; a small opening or pinhole</note></term>.
That luminous body of an elongated shape will show itself as a rounder body the further it is situated from the eye.

---

The eye which, emerging from darkness, suddenly sees a luminous body, will find it appears much larger at the first glance than after continuing to see it.
The luminous body will appear larger and more luminous with two eyes than with only one.
This luminous thing will show itself as a body of lesser form when it is seen by the eye through a smaller aperture.
This luminous body of elongated shape will show itself as a rounder body when it is situated at a greater distance from the eye.

### [THE CIRCULATION OF WATER]

<margin>Upside down:</margin>
The water which, entering from the deepest depths of the sea into the powers of its motor <note>Leonardo often theorized a "vital force" or heat within the Earth that acted as a "motor" to push water upward, much like the heart in a human body.</note> to the high peaks of the mountains, is pushed; there, finding the cut veins *low down*, it rushes down and returns by the shortest route to the low sea; it rises again through the branching veins *and is* and then falls back. And thus, moving up and down, turning now inside, now outside, circling with natural or accidental motion, in the likeness of a vine <note>The Italian word "vite" can mean both "vine" and "screw." Given the mention of "cut branches," Leonardo is likely comparing the Earth's hydrology to the sap in a grapevine.</note>—from which the water pours through the cut branches and falls back upon its roots, then rises again through the passages and returns by similar descents. <note>original Italian: "lacqua. chedalinfima profondita. delmare entrando nelle forze del- suo motore..."</note>

The water which, entering from the extreme depth of the sea into the forces of its motor, is pushed to the high summits of the mountains, where it finds cut veins *descending, low* and precipitates there, returning by the shortest way to the low sea; it rises again through the ramified veins *and is* and then falls back, and going and coming thus, between the high and the low, sometimes inside, sometimes outside, turning thus in the manner of a screw <note>Here, the translator interprets "vite" as "screw," referring to the mechanical motion of water.</note>, the water of which flows through the cut branches and falls back on its [?], rises again through [its] passages and returns by similar descents.

1. The figure is in red crayon. <note>Refers to a drawing in the original manuscript not captured in the text transcription.</note>
2. See above, folio 77 [29] recto.

### — FOLIO 101 [42 recto] (verso). — — FOLIO 102 [41 verso] (recto). —
### — FOLIO 102 [41 recto] (verso). — — FOLIO 103 [40 verso] (recto). —

### FOLIO 101 [42 recto] (verso)

<note>Drawing of a structural frame or arched bridge truss at the top of the folio, illustrating the text below.</note>

If two <term>beams<note>original: "piche." This term refers to structural supports or pillars, likely related to the construction of bridges or scaffolding.</note></term> were of the same height, length, and thickness—one being made of a single piece, and the other of several pieces interlocked and bound together—it follows that the one composed of several pieces will be much weaker than the one made of a single piece. And the reason for this is that the single piece, when bent, cannot <term>slide<note>original: "sscorrere." Leonardo observes that a solid beam resists internal displacement, whereas a composite beam suffers from the parts shifting against one another.</note></term> in any of its parts, neither lengthwise nor crosswise; which does not happen in the one composed of several pieces, because they will never be so tightly bound together that one does not slide some small amount over the other at its joint, whereby it becomes more flexible.

---

### [ACCOUNTS OF GIULIO AND MASTER THOMAS, 1493].

->centered text<-
1493
On the first day of November we made an account. Giulio had 4 months remaining to be paid — and Master Thomas 9 months. Master Thomas then made 6 candlesticks: 10 days; Giulio certain springs <note>original: "molli." These could be pincers or mechanical springs.</note>: 15 days; then Giulio worked for himself until the 27th of May, and worked for me on a <term>jack</term> <note>original: "martinetto." A mechanical device for lifting weights or spanning a heavy crossbow.</note> until the 18th of July, then for himself until the 7th of August, and in this period one day for a lady, then for me on 2 locks until the 20th of August.

->centered text<-
1493.
On the first day of November, we made an account. Giulio had 4 months to settle, and Master Thomas 9 months. [So that] the corner of the walls may be broken to provide a <term>joint</term> <note>original: "commetitura" - a structural connection between two masonry elements.</note> for the new wall; that is, let the <term>tooth</term> <note>original: "dente" - a stone or brick left projecting from the face of a wall to allow for a future connection, known today as "toothing."</note> be of such a size that it can be inserted into the old wall. The tooth of the wall that receives it should be of a size similar to the new wall, and for every tooth let there be a corresponding tooth. The tooth of the old wall shall be [recessed] into the space of the new wall's tooth, and the tooth of the new wall shall be set into the old wall where a tooth or void has been removed.

-> FOLIO 113 [30 recto] (verso) ¹. <-

-> [Mechanics. — Movement]. <-

---

[Upside down:]
If the contact *made* by a unified object with the earth that supports it is not along the line of its mover, [the movement] *will be* rendered more difficult the further it is from the line of the mover.
<note>In this context, Leonardo uses the term "motor" (mover) to describe the source of force or the person/machine applying pressure. He is observing that if the point of contact with the ground is not aligned with the direction of the force, friction increases and efficiency drops.</note>

> If the contact *made* by a unified object with the earth that supports it is not according to the line of its mover, it will be rendered [become] all the more difficult as it is more distant from the line of its mover.

->**FOLIO 113 [30 *recto*] (*verso*).**<-

<note>Mechanical diagram of a ratchet and pawl mechanism designed to ensure unidirectional motion.</note>

To ensure that the wheel which is moved 
by the weight does not turn backward
but always goes in one direction,
this method is to be followed: the tooth
of the wheel must always engage.
<note>Leonardo is describing a ratchet mechanism. The "tooth" refers to a pawl or a catch that falls into the gaps between the gear teeth, allowing rotation in one direction while physically blocking it in the reverse.</note>

a small wheel
that acts as the counterweight
to the weight for doing it.
<note>Leonardo appears to be sketching a method of regulating motion. By using a "small wheel" as a counterweight, he is exploring how to balance the force of gravity to achieve a steady or controlled release of energy, a principle essential for clockwork escapements.</note>

In gold: 15 soldi.
I estimate [this azure and gold]: 2 ½ lire².

The narrow <term>gronda</term>² [coving] above the hall: 30 lire.
For the coving below this, I estimate each panel at 7 lire, and in expenses, as much for azure as for gold, white lead, plaster, indigo, and glue: 3 lire; in time, 3 days.
The histories [subjects] under these covings, with their pilasters: 12 lire for each.
I estimate the expense for enamel, azure, and gold, and other colors, at 1 ½ lire.
I estimate the days at 5 for the investigation of the composition <note>The "investigation" refers to the preparatory phase: sketching and designing the layout.</note>, the small pilaster, and other things.

<margin>
1. See folios 121 [22 recto] verso and 129 [14 recto] verso.
2. "Gronda" usually means: gutter. This word was translated in the work of Mr. J-P. Richter, vol. II, no. 1515: "cornice," and: "moulding." Here is what Mr. H. de Geymüller, a collaborator of Mr. Richter, now thinks: "As it concerns an interior, *gronda* can hardly be translated otherwise than by: *coving* (voussure): *The narrow coving above the hall*, 30 lire. *The coving below this one* [that is to say, below that coving...]. I estimate each picture [painted in the coving] at 7 lire." See folio 124 [19 recto] verso, 2nd line (small vault).
</margin>

It also contains brief notes on hydraulic mechanics, questioning the pressure of water at different depths.</summary>

### [LATIN-ITALIAN GLOSSARY].

<note>Here, Leonardo practices the various forms of the Latin verb "amare" (to love). He provides the Italian equivalent for each Latin grammatical form to help him understand how infinitives, gerunds, and participles function.</note>

**Amare**: To love <note>original: Amare [Aimer]</note>
**Amavisse**: To have loved <note>original: Avere amato [Avoir aimé]</note>
**Amatum ire [iri]**: To be about to love <note>original: Dovere amare [Devoir aimer]</note>
***
**Amandi**: Of loving <note>original: Da mare [D’aimer]</note>
**Amando**: By loving <note>original: Amando [En aimant]</note>
**Amandum**: To love <note>original: [A] amare [A aimer]</note>
***
**Amatum**: To love <note>original: Io voglio amare [Je veux aimer] — used to express purpose</note>
**Amatu**: From loving <note>original: Io vengo d'amare [Je viens d’aimer] — the Latin supine used with verbs of motion</note>
***
**Amans**: Loving <note>original: Amare [Aiming]; present participle</note>
**Amaturus**: About to love <note>original: Da amare [Devant aimer]; future participle</note>
***
**Amari**: To be loved <note>original: Amarsi [S’aimer]</note>
**Amatum esse, fuisse**: To have been loved <note>original: Essersi amati [Avoir été aimés]</note>
**Amatum iri**: To be about to be loved <note>original: Doversi amare [Devoir être aimés]</note>

### [LATIN GRAMMAR].

<note>Leonardo continues his grammar drills, focusing here on the endings for the passive voice of "amare." He lists the person and number suffixes for various tenses.</note>

*Amor, ris, re, tur, mur, mini, antur.* <note>Present Passive: I am loved, you are loved, etc.</note>
*Amabar, ris, re, tur, mur, mini, antur.* <note>Imperfect Passive: I was being loved</note>

*Amarer, ris, re, tur, mur, mini, tur.* <note>Imperfect Subjunctive Passive</note>
*Amer, ris, re, tur, mur, mini, tur.* <note>Present Subjunctive Passive</note>
*Amer, ris, re, tur, mur, mini, tur.* <note>Repeating the subjunctive forms</note>
*Amarer, ris, re, tur, mur, mini, tur.*
**Amatus sum, fui, es, sti, est, sunt.** <note>Perfect Passive: I have been loved</note>
**Amatus eram, fueram, as, at, fuerant.** <note>Pluperfect Passive: I had been loved</note>
**Amatus fuerim, is, it, mus, tis, int.** <note>Perfect Subjunctive Passive</note>
**Amatus fueram, as, at, mus, tis, ant.**
**Amatus fuissem, es, et, mus, tis, ent.** <note>Pluperfect Subjunctive Passive</note>

**Amatus fuissem, es, et, mus, tis, en [ent].**

### [LATIN GRAMMAR. — MOTION AND LIFE].

I am loved, you are, he is, we are, you all are, he is. <note>Leonardo is mixing personal endings here.</note>
I was loved, you were, he was, we were, you all were, he was.
Having been loved, I have been, I was, to be, to have been, he was.

Having been loved, I had been, I had been, you had been, you had been, he had been, he had been.
I will be loved.

[In red chalk:] **Motion is the cause of all life.** ¹
<note>original Italian: "Il moto e chausa dogni vita"</note>

### MS 2038 NATIONAL LIBRARY — FOLIO 1 (recto). — [VISUAL POWER, EXPERIENCE. — SHADOW, LIGHT, DRAWING].

-> THE EYE THAT IS STRUCK OR PUSHED FROM BELOW UPWARD WILL PRODUCE A CONTRARY MOVEMENT FROM ITS CENTER BACKWARD; AND BECAUSE OF THIS, IT WILL SEEM TO MOVE STABLE AND FIXED OBJECTS FROM THEIR PLACES AND CARRY THEM FROM ABOVE TO BELOW <-

This effect occurs because the eye, when struck and moved from below upward or from above downward, moves by shifting or pushing its eyelids, which are joined to the surface skin of the eye at their origin. If you push the lower lid upward, it will pull the eye back and raise the pupil upward; the part of the eye located behind the center will make the contrary movement. From these contrary movements, the images of objects are imprinted on that posterior part of the eye where the power of the <term>impressiva</term> <note>Leonardo’s term for the "perceptive faculty," the specific area of the brain or eye where he believed sensory impressions were collected and processed.</note> is founded. This effect happens while keeping both eyes open, because the eye that is not moved sees the object in its true position, while the eye that is moved shifts the image of the object imprinted in its *impressiva*. The object seen by the moved eye will never have that clear form possessed by the one seen by the unmoved eye; this is because, being moved, it does not see the image of the object through the central line by which things are best judged. Instead, it sees through those parts that surround the center, and because these are of a less transparent fluid, objects are seen more confusedly.

It is impossible for the eye to send out from itself the visual power through visual rays <note>Leonardo is refuting the ancient "extramission theory," which suggested that the eye emitted rays to "touch" objects.</note>. This is because, upon opening the eye, the first part of that power that would begin the exit and have to travel to the object could not do so without time. Being so, it could not travel in a month to the height of the sun when the eye wishes to see it. And if it did travel and arrive there, it would be necessary for it to be continually maintained along the entire path from the eye to the sun, and for it to always broaden in such a way that the sun and the eye formed the base and the point of a pyramid. If this were the case, even if the eye were as large as a million worlds, it would not be enough to avoid being entirely consumed in providing said power. And if this power had to travel through the air as scent does, the winds would twist it and carry it to another place; yet we see the body of the sun with the same speed that we see a distance of one <term>braccio</term> <note>An Italian unit of length, roughly the length of an arm (approx. 23 inches or 58 cm).</note>, and it is not changed by the blowing of winds or any other accident.

-> WHICH IS MORE DIFFICULT: SHADOW AND LIGHT, OR RATHER GOOD DRAWING? <-

I say that a thing which is constrained to a limit is more difficult than one which is free. Shadows have their limits at certain degrees, and for one who is ignorant of them, their work will be without relief; this relief is the most important part and the soul of painting. Drawing is free, in that if you see an infinite number of faces, they will all be different—some with a long nose, some with a short one... . . — 5 —

<margin> [In the margin:] 5 Therefore, the painter can also take this liberty, and where there is liberty, there is no rule. </margin>

Let there be an eye, and let it be **.a.**, which looks through the surface **.b c.** at the interior of a ball of water; and let **.d d.** be the said ball, and let the eye be **.a.**, and the eye inside the middle of the ball be **.e.** I say that the eye **.a.** will see inside the ball, and the vision will be **.e d.**, which will be represented at point **.e.** in the center of the ball. And this vision will not be straight, because air is of less density than water. Wherefore the <term>visual ray</term> <note>Leonardo’s term for the path light takes to the eye, often treated as a physical line in his geometric proofs.</note> departing from the eye **.a.** and touching the surface of the water at **.d.** will not go straight to **.e.**, because, according to what was said previously, every visual ray that departs from a thinner medium and enters a thicker medium bends toward the <term>line of incidence</term> <note>The perpendicular line at the point where the ray enters the new medium.</note>—as is the line **.h d.** here. For this reason, the ray **.a d.** entering the water will not go to **.e.**, but will go to **.f.** Consequently, the eye **.a.** will not see the center **.e.** through the straight path **.a d e.**, but will see it at **.f.** through the path **.a d f.** Because the eye never judges seeing inside <term>mirrors</term> <note>original: "spechi"; here Leonardo uses the term to refer to any refracting surface, such as the boundary between air and water.</note> except by a straight line, therefore, the eye seeing through the path **.f d.**, it will seem to see in the straight line **.a d.**; and thus it will appear to it that the center of the ball was at **.k.**—if it should be that the visual ray passes through the air and the eye is inside the water.

<note>A small circular diagram illustrates the refraction of light rays passing from air into a sphere of water, showing how the focal point or perceived position of the center is displaced.</note>

Let there be an eye **.m.** which sees the sphere of the Earth inside the surface **.s t.**, which Earth is **.a b.** I say that the eye **.m.** will see at point **.c.** of the surface the likeness of the pole **.a.**, and at point **.d.** of the surface the likeness of the pole **.b.**, because the ray **.m c.** reflected at **.c.** goes to the pole **.a.**, and the ray **.m d.** reflected at **.d.** goes to the pole **.b.** And to the eye **.m.**, it will appear to see the pole **.a.** at **.x.** and the pole **.b.** at **.y.** And thus it will appear to see the diameter of the Earth as **.x y.** Therefore, the Earth will appear to it to be as much larger as **.x y.** is greater than **.a b.** Now you see, if our eye were outside the atmosphere of the Earth, what would happen inside it—how much larger the sphere of the Earth would appear to us! Would it not be larger than the moon? I believe so.

If the eye **.m.** sees in the surface **.r d.** the truth of a thing—or to put it better, the sphere of the Earth **.n o p q r.**—I say that the eye **.m.** will see at point **.c.** of the surface the likeness of the pole **.n.**, and at point **.d.** it will see the pole **.r.** Because the ray **.m c.** reflected at **.c.** goes to the pole **.n.**, and the ray **.m d.** reflected at **.d.** goes to the pole **.r.** And the eye **.m.**, judging by a straight line, will seem to see the pole **.n.** at **.f.** and the pole **.r.** at **.h.** And thus the diameter of the Earth will appear to it to be **.f h.** Therefore, the Earth will appear to it larger than it truly is, by as much space as **.f h.** is greater than **.n r.**

And if it happened that the eye **.m.** were inside the water of the sea or another deep body of water, seeing through the surface of the water outside of it, such as the air and the stars [...]

<meta>Following the optical studies on Folio 1 (recto) regarding the refraction of light through water, this verso page transitions into Leonardo’s studies of mechanics. The text focuses on the laws of motion and the geometry of impact—specifically how objects behave when thrown or struck. This is a common theme in Leonardo's work, where he seeks to find universal geometric rules that apply to both light and physical matter.</meta>

— FOLIO 1 (verso). —

<meta>This page from a 19th-century scholarly edition presents Leonardo's original 15th-century Italian (transcribed from his mirror-writing) followed by a French translation. Both have been translated here into English.</meta>

## [MOTION AND IMPACT]

<note>original: "MOUVEMENT ET PERCUSSION"</note>

— Every object moved with force will follow through the air the line of the movement of its <term>mover</term> <note>The "mover" (motore) is the source of the force, such as a hand, a bowstring, or a catapult.</note>. —

If that which moves the object [moves it] in a circle, and if it is released during that motion, its motion will be curved; and if the motion is begun in a circle and finished in a straight line, its course will be in a straight line; and likewise, being begun straight and finished curved, its path will be curved.

<note>Leonardo is grappling here with the principles of inertia. While modern physics states an object released from circular motion travels in a straight tangent, Leonardo is observing the complex "impetus" or follow-through of the movement.</note>

— Every object moved *parts* from the blow; it parts between equal angles of its mover. —

That is, if you move a <term>ball</term> <note>original: "balla"</note> with the blow of a <term>stick</term> <note>original: "basstone"</note>, it will depart from the stick along such a line that it leaves, at its start, equal angles upon that stick.

---

<note>The following is the English translation of the French translation provided in the original scholarly manuscript.</note>

Every object moved with violence will follow in the air the line of movement of its mover.

If someone moves the object in a circle and it is released in this movement, its movement is curved; and if the movement is begun in a circle and finished in straightness, its course will be in straightness; and similarly, being begun straight and finished twisted, it will have a twisted path.

Every moved object *separates* by the blow [and] separates according to equal angles from its mover.

That is to say, if you move a ball with the blow of a stick, it will separate from the stick by such a line that it will leave at its birth equal angles on the stick.

<vocab>motion, impact, mover, line, ball, stick, impact, angles</vocab>

<summary>Leonardo describes the trajectories of objects set in motion, attempting to establish a rule that an object's path mimics the final motion of its mover and departs at symmetrical angles upon impact.</summary>
<keywords>mechanics, trajectory, impetus, inertia, geometry of motion, ballistics, Leonardo da Vinci</keywords>

## FOLIO 2 (recto)

->[ THE MIND OF THE PAINTER ]<-

**PAINTING**

The mind of the painter should be like a mirror, which always transforms itself into the color of whatever object it faces, and is filled with as many images as there are things placed before it. Therefore, knowing that you, painter, cannot be good unless you are a universal master <note>Leonardo uses "universal" to mean someone capable of depicting everything in the natural world, not just a specialist in one subject like portraits or landscapes.</note> capable of imitating with your art all the qualities of the forms that Nature produces—which you will not know how to do unless you see them and retain them in your mind—ensure that when you go through the countryside, your judgment turns to various objects. Look at one thing and then another from time to time, making a bundle <note>original: "vnfascio"; a metaphor for gathering and grouping different observations to be studied later.</note> of various things, selected and chosen from among those that are less good. 

And do not do as some painters do who, becoming weary in their imagination, abandon their work and take exercise by going out for amusement, yet keep a weariness in their minds which prevents them from truly seeing or perceiving the various things they encounter. Indeed, many times when meeting their friends or relatives and being greeted by them, though they may see or hear them, they do not truly recognize them, as if they had encountered nothing more than so much air. <note>original: "altretantaria"; Leonardo is describing a state of mental exhaustion where the eyes see but the brain does not process, rendering people as invisible as air.</note>

* The edge of the shadow will always be in a straight line with the center <margin>2</margin> of its light and with the edges of the **opaque body** <term>opaque body: an object that does not allow light to pass through it, such as a solid figure.</term> that produces it. Let **A** be the light and **BC** be the opaque body, and **e** be the center of the light. Let **d f g** be the shadow, which will have its edges **d** and **g** in a straight line with the center **e** and with the edges of the opaque body **B** and **C**.

The shadow will be as much larger in thickness than the body that produces it as it is further away from that same body, which shall be proven. Let **d g** be the shadow and **BC** be the opaque body and **e** be the center of the light. I say that if you draw the line **e B**, it will reach **d**, and the line **e C** will reach **g**. **d** will be one edge of the shadow and **g** will be the other edge. Therefore, **d g** will be the width of the shadow and **BC** will be the width of the body.

A shadow will be of equal thickness to its body when it is seen between **parallel lines** <note>original: "linia equidistante"; literally "equidistant lines," which Leonardo uses to describe parallel paths of light.</note>, and this will be proven. Let the light be **a b** and the opaque body **c d** and the shadow **f g**. I say that if the light **a b** is of equal thickness to the opaque body **c d**, then the shadow **f g** will be of equal thickness to the said body.

<summary>Leonardo explains the geometric principles of shadow formation, demonstrating how the size of a shadow is determined by the relationship between the center of the light source and the edges of the object. ## FOLIO 2 (verso)

# [ LEVERS — THE OPINION OF PELACANE ]

[Figure in the margin:] n m

Pelacane <note>original: "il pelachane"; referring to Biagio Pelacani of Parma (c. 1345–1416), a famous Italian mathematician and philosopher whose views on mechanics Leonardo often challenged.</note> says that the longer arm of this balance will fall *because it is* faster than the shorter one. Because its descent describes its quarter-circle in a way that is straighter than that of the shorter one; and because *pr the weights* <note>The scribe or Leonardo likely started writing "p" for "pesi" (weights) and corrected it.</note> desire to fall in a perpendicular line, the more that circle twists [curves], the more the motion will be delayed. Figure **m n** casts down [refutes] this reasoning, because the descent of its weights does not follow circles, and yet the weight of the longer arm **m** sinks down.

That thing which is further from its support <note>original: "firmamento"; referring to the pivot or fulcrum of the lever.</note> will be less sustained by it. Being less sustained, it will partake more of its liberty <note>In Leonardo’s mechanics, "liberty" refers to the degree to which a weight is free to follow its natural inclination to fall toward the center of the earth.</note>. And because a free weight always descends, therefore that extremity of the beam of this balance which is further from its support, because it is more ponderous [heavy] than it is fast, will descend of its own accord more quickly than any other part of it.

[Figure before the final text:] o m q r s z p n

*the weight*

Because the wheel has its extremities equally distant from its center, all weights placed upon its circumference will exert such a force upon it as would similar weights placed under their perpendicular line upon the line of equality <note>original: "linea delle qualita"; likely a transcription error for "equalità," referring to the horizontal level.</note> **q z**.

---

<note>The following section translates the 19th-century French commentary included in the transcription.</note>

[Figure in the margin:] n m

Pelacane¹ says that the larger arm of this balance will fall *because it is* faster than the small one, because its descent describes its quarter-circle straighter than the small one does; and [that] because *the pr the* weights desire to fall by a perpendicular line, it will slow down more as the circle curves more. Figure **m n** casts to the ground [refutes] this reason, because the descent of its weights does not go by circles and yet the weight of the large arm **m** lowers itself.

The thing which is further from its point of support is less supported by it; being less supported, it keeps more of its liberty, and because the free weight always descends, necessarily the extremity of the beam of the balance which is more distant from its point of support, because it is heavier *than*, will descend of itself faster than any [other] part.

[Figure before the last text:] o m q r s z p n

*The weight...*

Because the wheel has its extremities equally distant from its center, all the weights placed on its circumference will have a force there such as that which similar weights placed under their perpendicular [vertical] line would have, on the line of equality **q z**.

1. Probably Biagio Pelacani, a physician from Parma († 1416), whom Tiraboschi (*History of Italian Literature*, VI, p. 1ª, § 6) calls an "illustrious philosopher and mathematician."

<summary>Leonardo critiques the mechanical theories of Biagio Pelacani regarding the motion of levers, arguing that the distance from the fulcrum determines how much "liberty" a weight has to fall. # Ms 2038 BIB. NAT.

## FOLIO 2 (verso)

Why the shadow does not separate from the base of the opaque body <note>original: "corpo onbroso"; an object that blocks light to create a shadow.</note> unless the light is lower <note>original: "ūmile"; literally 'humble', used here in a spatial sense to mean 'low' or 'at a lesser height'.</note> than that base. This is proven by the seventh [proposition] of this work, which says: all parts of opaque bodies that see the light are illuminated. Therefore, if it is true that the base of the opaque body sees the light, it will be illuminated; and if it is illuminated, it cannot possess a shadow; and not possessing a shadow, it cannot cast one onto the flat wall <note>original: "pariete"; refers to the surface upon which the shadow falls.</note>. Thus, the proposition remains <unclear>proven</unclear>.

---

<note>Central diagram: A complex study of light and shadow projection. A source of light at points 'a' and 'b' projects through an aperture (line 'x-y') onto a spherical body 'o-p' and a background surface 'c-d'.</note>

The shadow in its entirety is always the same length as the opaque body itself, provided the distance between the light and the wall where the shadow is received is equal, if those walls are equidistant <note>Parallel.</note> to the motion of the light. I say that in this case the light moves from the center **a** to **b**. When it is at **a**, the shadow is at **c**; when it is at **b**, the shadow is at **d**. Then the length of the shadow **c-d** will be the same as the length of the wall of the housing <term>albergo</term> <note>original: "albergo"; literally 'lodging', here referring to the chamber or the aperture through which light passes in his optical experiments.</note> **x-y**, just as **a-b** is the motion of the light. And the wall of the housing **x-y** is as large as the interval between the wall and the light. And the shadow **c-d** is as long as the length of the opaque body **o-p**, assuming you wish to make the shadow as long as the opaque body.

---

Why the shadow is longer than the opaque body: when the light is closer to the wall where the shadow is received than the light is to the opaque body; and the shadow is longer in proportion to how much closer the light is to the wall than to the body. And so, conversely, when the light is further from the wall than from the body, the shadow of that body will be shorter <note>original: "brieve"; brief or short.</note> than the body itself.

**Vocabulary:** shadow, opaque body, light, wall/surface, illuminated, equidistant, length, short, housing/chamber.

<summary>Leonardo explains the geometric relationship between a light source, an object, and the resulting shadow, proving that shadow length is determined by the proportional distances between the light and the receiving surface.</summary>

### ->[SUSPENDED BODIES].<-

A suspended body which is of a flat roundness <note>original: "piana retondita"; likely referring to a disk or a two-dimensional circular object.</note> will fall according to its center and will come to rest directly below the center of the cord that suspends it. —

The center of the weight—the <term>ponderosity<note>original: "ponderosita"; Leonardo's term for the quality of having weight or the force of gravity acting on a body.</note></term> of any suspended body—will come to rest *on* a perpendicular line below *the center* the middle of its support. —

---

A suspended body which is of a flat roundness will fall with [according to] its center, and will stop under the center of the cord which suspends it.

The center of gravity <note>original French: "pesanteur"</note> of any suspended body will stop *on* a perpendicular line under the *center* the middle of its support.

That object will be closer to the **truth** <term>truth of its form<note>original: "uerità della sua forma"; Leonardo uses this to mean the objective reality of an object's shape as opposed to its distorted appearance.</note></term> which is seen through multiple **apertures** <note>original: "busi"; literally 'holes.' Leonardo suggests that viewing an object through small openings can refine the visual rays.</note> and is seen under a more **acute angle**.

<margin>intersection</margin>
That part of the **intersection** will provide a **clearer knowledge** <note>original: "notitia"; refers to the cognitive recognition or perception of the image.</note> of its true form which is intersected under more **acute angles**.

<note>A vertical column of diagrams on the right illustrates these optical principles:
1. Lines of sight intersecting at a specific point, demonstrating a study in optics.

**Technical Vocabulary**
*   **Truth/Reality** <note>original: "uerità"</note> — the actual geometric shape of the object.
*   **Apertures** <note>original: "busi"</note> — small holes or openings through which light or sight passes.
*   **Acute Angle** <note>original: "angolo acuto"</note> — an angle less than 90 degrees, here used to describe the convergence of visual rays.
*   **Intersection** <note>original: "intersegatione"</note> — the point where lines of sight or light rays cross.
*   **Knowledge/Perception** <note>original: "notitia"</note> — the clarity with which the mind perceives the form.

# FOLIO 4 (recto). — Ms 2038 BIB. NAT.

-># [PAINTING (CONTRASTS, DRAPERY, AND BOARDS)]<-

---

->ON PAINTING<-

The various comparisons of the different qualities of shadows and lights often make the painter, who wishes to imitate and replicate the things he sees, appear hesitant and confused. The reason is this: if you see a white cloth compared to <note>original: "a paragone di"</note> a black one, it is certain that the part of the white cloth bordering the black will appear much whiter than the part bordering a greater whiteness. The reason for this is proven in my *Perspective* <note>Leonardo refers here to his own lost or projected treatise on the science of optics, specifically the phenomenon of "simultaneous contrast" where colors appear different based on their neighbors.</note>.

->### ON THE NATURE OF FOLDS IN DRAPERY<-

### THAT PART OF THE FOLD WHICH IS FOUND FARTHEST FROM ITS CONSTRAINED ENDS WILL RETURN MORE TO ITS ORIGINAL NATURE.

[2nd figure:] **a b c**
Naturally, everything desires to maintain itself in its own state of being. Drapery, because it is of equal density and thickness on its reverse side as on its front, desires to remain flat. Therefore, when it is constrained by some folds or creases to leave that flatness, it observes the nature of the force in that part of itself where it is most constrained; and you will find that the part farthest from those constraints returns more to its original nature—that is, being spread out and wide <note>without folds</note>.

->### EXAMPLE:<-
Let **a b c** be the fold of the drapery mentioned above. Let **a** and **c** be the places where this cloth is folded and constrained. I proposed to you that the part of the cloth farthest from the constrained ends returns more to its original nature; therefore, **b**, being located farthest from **a** and **c**, the fold **a b c** will be wider there than in any other of its parts.

->### ALWAYS TO THE ABOVE PURPOSE:<-
I told you that a width which had its front side of the same breadth as its reverse could not, by nature, stay anything but flat; and so, conversely, it follows for unequal surfaces. Take, then, a board <term>ais<note>A thin wooden plank or board, often used as a support for painting.</note></term> and heat it on one of its sides; you will immediately see it hollow itself and curve with a convex twist toward the fire. And this arises because the heat moves the moisture—every body being held together by the moisture infused within it. Part of that moisture flees from the surface turned toward the fire, and part of it penetrates into the opposite surface. That part which flees toward the fire leaves its surface diminished; the other part, which flees to the opposite surface, remains there, and by remaining, increases and swells it. This makes these two surfaces unequal and warped, so that the larger side bends over the smaller.

---

<note>
1. Three barred ovals appear as marks before the 2nd and 3rd paragraphs in the original manuscript.
2. This section corresponds to J.-P. Richter, Vol. I, No. 560.
3. Figures and text related to drapery correspond to G. Manzi, p. 267 and J.-P. Richter, Vol. I, No. 390.
</note>

<summary>Leonardo explains how visual contrast affects a painter's perception of color and describes the physical mechanics of drapery folds and the warping of wood due to heat and moisture.</summary>

# FOLIO 4 (recto) — Ms 2038 BIB. NAT.

<margin>
Because the weight
</margin>

Which is of greater power: that which falls straight or that which falls obliquely? <note>Leonardo is comparing a vertical impact (perpendicular to the surface) with a slanted or diagonal one.</note>
The weight that falls straight strikes the center of the impact <note>original: "ochio della percussione"; literally the "eye" or focal point of the collision</note> with all its weight <note>original: "graueza"; referring to the force of gravity/weight</note>.
And that which falls obliquely does not strike with its full weight, except along the line leading straight to the impact; rather, it strikes with that portion of such weight that is directed through a straight descent <note>original: "p rāpito dj dritto"; Leonardo uses "rapito" or "rapina" to describe the momentum or swiftness of a force</note> over the part of the object being struck.

### On the weight that falls straight and that which falls obliquely
The weight that falls straight strikes the center of the impact with all its weight.

If you strike straight upon the object being struck, it will strike straight; but if you strike obliquely <note>at an angle</note> upon the object, the part of the blow that strikes obliquely will strike along an oblique line, as will be shown straight ahead in this figure here below. That which strikes straight strikes with all its momentum <note>original: "rapina"</note> straight on and with all its weight; but that which strikes obliquely strikes with half-straight and half-oblique force, as is seen straight ahead in this figure placed below, which rushes straight along a straight path.

<note>Drawing of a rectangular weight in two orientations (vertical and tilted) impacting a horizontal surface, illustrating the physics of percussion.</note>

Because **d. n.** strikes with one force, but in the impact of **a. d. n.** with oblique momentum, it strikes with the portion of the weight having oblique momentum; as can be seen from **a. d. n.**, it will only strike through oblique momentum.

<note>Diagram showing force lines (rapina) emanating from a point of impact on a surface.</note>

Furthermore, it can be said that oblique momentum is of greater force than that which falls straight, because if the oblique part rushes over a longer path, it will strike more swiftly; and that which strikes more swiftly exerts greater force. But it will not strike with all its gravity as it would straight on, because it does not fall along the line of gravity, but falls with an oblique, rushing line. Said velocity will be sent straight, but it will rush obliquely; it will carry the part of the momentum with oblique velocity, but it will not rush with the gravity of the momentum as it would straight on, as will be seen straight ahead in the figure below, rushing straight and obliquely. But it will not deliver a straight impact; rather, it will rush with its oblique force, like a spear that strikes obliquely: it does not strike with all its force, but strikes with half-straight and half-oblique force, because it strikes with its momentum straight.

<note>Translator's note on technical vocabulary: Leonardo uses "percussione" for impact, "gravezza" for the force of weight/gravity, and "rapina" for the impetus or momentum of a moving object. His conclusion balances the gain in speed from a longer slanted path against the loss of direct gravitational force.</note>

<summary>This page contains Leonardo’s analysis of the physics of impact, comparing the force generated by objects falling vertically versus those falling at an angle. He concludes that while oblique motion might gain velocity over a longer distance, it loses the full direct force of its weight upon impact.</summary>
<keywords>mechanics, percussion, gravity, momentum, oblique force, physics of impact, velocity, Leonardo's diagrams</keywords>

### THE METHOD OF DRAWING FROM NATURE

A small square pane of glass should be made, about the size of a sheet of paper. Fix it well in front of your eyes—that is, at the point from which you wish to draw. Then, facing this glass at a distance of one <term>braccio<note>A Florentine unit of measurement, approximately 23 inches or 58 centimeters.</note></term> from it,
-> place your head in a fixed part of an <-
instrument which holds the head so still that it cannot move. Finally, transfer this from the glass onto paper using <term>tracing paper<note>original: "lucido"; transparent paper treated with oil or resin to make it see-through.</note></term> and <unclear>powder</unclear> <note>original: "polvere"; likely referring to the "pouncing" technique where charcoal dust is pressed through pinpricks in a drawing to transfer the outline.</note>.

# MS 2038 NATIONAL LIBRARY — FOLIO 5 (recto)

<note>Leonardo's mirror script, transcribed left-to-right. These notes concern the physics of light, optics, and shadow projection.</note>

<margin>
The shadow
</margin>

That part of the <term>surface<note>original: "pariete", referring to the wall or plane where light and shadow are projected</note></term> which is closer to the cause of the light will be more luminous. The shadow will be so much darker as it is closer to the shadow <unclear>shadow</unclear> that is beneath; the light will be behind the light.

---

If the distance of the <term>opaque body<note>original: "corpo onbroso", an object that blocks light to cast a shadow</note></term> from the light is doubled, the width of the shadow will be doubled; and the same will occur if the distance of the surface from the opaque body is doubled.

---

If the light is smaller than the opaque body, the shadow will be more "doubled" <note>likely referring to the widening of the penumbra or the blurring of the shadow's edges</note> at its boundaries. If the light is equal to the opaque body, the shadow will be equal. If the light is larger, the shadow will be smaller.

In the same way that the shadow went on narrowing according to the distance from the luminous body to the surface.

---

In whatever distance the shadow is more or less "of a shadow" <note>referring to the varying degrees of intensity or density within the shadow</note>, the shadow will be so much darker in one part than in the other; in whatever proportion the shadow is closer to the light <note>referring to the shadow's proximity to the object's base or the source</note>, the shadow made by a light will be darker at that point, and it will be of "higher quality" because it is more unified <note>original: "unita", meaning the shadow is more concentrated and less diluted by secondary reflections</note>.

In whatever distance the shadow moves away from the light, it will go on losing its darkness.

<summary>Leonardo outlines the geometric and physical principles of shadows, explaining how their size and darkness are determined by the distance and relative scale of the light source, the object, and the surface.</summary>
<keywords>shadow projection, optics, chiaroscuro, light intensity, geometry, opaque body, penumbra</keywords>

### Manuscript 2038 NATIONAL LIBRARY — FOLIO 6 (back side<note>original: "verso"</note>) —

->[PYRAMIDS, VISUAL RAYS¹].<-

[Figure:] a b g f e d c
Every pyramid composed of a long convergence of rays contains within itself infinite pyramids; and each has the power of all, and all the power of each.

Every shadowy body <note>Leonardo uses "corpo ombroso" (shadowy body) to refer to any opaque object that blocks light and thus has a visible form.</note> fills the surrounding air with infinite likenesses of itself; which, through infinite infused pyramids, represent that body, the whole in the whole, and the whole in every part.

The equidistant circuit of pyramids from the point of convergence will give to its object an equal quality of angles, and the thing will be received by the object in equal size.

*Every radiant pyramid of length...*

The body of the air is full of infinite pyramids, composed of radiant and rectilinear lines, which are generated from the edges of the surfaces of shadowy bodies placed in that air. The further they move from their cause <note>The "cause" here refers to the physical object reflecting light or the light source itself.</note>, the more acute they become. And although their convergences are intersected and interwoven, they nevertheless do not become confused with one another; with a spreading convergence, they go on amplifying and infusing themselves through all the surrounding air. They are of equal power among themselves—all as much as each, and each as much as all. Through them, the likeness of the body is carried; it is carried the whole in the whole, and the whole in the part. Each pyramid by itself receives in every smallest part of itself the entire form of its cause.

---

[Figure:] a b g f e d c
<note>The following section is a translation of the French scholarly commentary provided in the source text.</note>
Every pyramid composed by a long convergence of rays contains in itself infinite pyramids; and each has power for all, and all for each. The equidistant circuit [of rays] of pyramidal convergence will give to its object an equal sort of angles, and of equal size the thing will be received [perceived in each of the angles] by the object [the eye] ².

Every shadowy body fills the surrounding air with an infinity of its resemblances [images], which, from infinite pyramids that are infused there, represent this body the whole in the whole and the whole in each part ³.

*Every radiating pyramid of length...*

The body of the air is full of infinite pyramids, composed of radiating and straight lines, which are caused by the superficial extremities of the shadowy bodies found in this air; and the further they move from their cause, the more acute they become. And although their convergence is intersected and woven, nevertheless they do not confound one another; they go in a divergent convergence, amplifying and infusing themselves in all the surrounding air; they are between them of equal powers, and all as much as each, and each as much as all. By them the image of the body is carried, and carried the whole in the whole and the whole in the part; and each pyramid by itself receives in each of its smallest parts the whole form of its cause ⁴.

---

1. See manuscript A, 1st volume of this publication, folio 2 back side.
2, 3, 4. J.-P. Richter, volume I, no. 63 ("27b").

<term>pyramid: the cone-like shape Leonardo used to describe how light rays converge from an object to a single point (the eye) or diverge from a source</term>
<term>likeness: (Italian: *similitudine*) the visual information or "species" of an object that travels through the air to the eye</term>
<term>rectilinear: moving in a straight line; Leonardo believed light always traveled in straight lines</term>

<summary>Leonardo explains his "pyramidal" theory of optics, arguing that every point in the air contains the complete visual information of surrounding objects through converging rays of light. This concept is a precursor to the modern understanding of how light waves carry information and how the eye perceives perspective.</summary>

->### [ THE BRASS SCALE-WEIGHT ]<-

<margin>[Second figure:] 1 2 3 . . . 9 [?]</margin>
<margin>[Upside down:]</margin>
This method of weighing is very efficient, because the plumb line immediately shows the true weight of the object by touching the letter on the <term>abacus</term> <note>original: "abacho." Here, Leonardo refers to the graduated scale or calculating plate on the instrument.</note>. It removes the confusion felt by those who weigh goods for retail sale—that is, the trouble of testing so many different weights, taking one off and trying another, and never finding the true weight. 

Wherefore, with this device—which is constructed through experience—you can immediately read the letter on the scale plate that is touched by the wire, and you will know the precise weight. But know that this instrument must be made of <term>orichalcum</term> <note>original: "richalcho." A golden-colored alloy, typically brass or a similar copper-based metal, valued for its durability.</note>, so that moisture does not alter it. It should be half a <term>braccio</term> <note>original: "braccio." An Italian unit of measure (literally "arm") equivalent to approximately 58 centimeters or 23 inches.</note> in diameter, and as thick as the back of a knife.

<margin>[Third figure:] Wedges [?] <note>original: "coni" / French: "coins". This likely refers to the shape of the component parts or the pointers on the scale.</note></margin>

<margin>[Second figure:] 1 2 3 . . . 9 [?]</margin>
This means of weighing is very prompt, given that the plumb line immediately shows the true weight of the thing by touching the letter of the abacus, and removes the embarrassment [the difficulty] of those who weigh when selling by retail—that is to say, of checking so many weights, removing one, checking with another, and never finding the truth of the weight.

Consequently, with that which is made through experience, read immediately after the letter of the abacus which is touched by the thread, and you know the truth of the weight exactly. ### PRECEPTS OF PAINTING

Let the <term>sketching</term> <note>original: "bozare." The initial process of blocking out a composition.</note> of <term>narratives</term> <note>original: "storie." ### PRECEPTS OF PAINTING.

<meta>This page transitions from the geometric theories of light and shadow on Folio 9 verso to practical applications for the painter. It discusses how distance and shadow obscure color, the proper perspective for drawing from life, and the optical reasons why a flat painting can never fully replicate the three-dimensional depth perceived by two human eyes.</meta>

FOLIO 10 (recto).
Ms 2038 BIB. NAT.

->[DISTANT COLORS. — PAINTING, DRAWING, MIRRORS].<-

### ALL COLORS IN DISTANT SHADOWS ARE UNKNOWN AND INDISCERNIBLE

All colors in the distance will be unknown in the shadows, because an object that is not touched by the primary light does not have the power to send its form and similitude <note>original: "similitudine"; in Renaissance optics, this refers to the visual "species" or image of an object traveling through the air to the eye</note> to the eye through the more luminous air, because the lesser light is overcome by the greater. EXAMPLE: We see, when we are inside a house, that all the colors on the surfaces of the walls are seen clearly and distinctly when the windows of said dwelling are open; but if we go outside of that house and look from a little distance through said windows to see the paintings made on those walls, instead of those paintings we will see a continuous darkness.

An object which, through its brightness, is closer in appearance to the light will be seen from further away, and will appear of a larger form than is required by the quality of the body at that distance.

### PRECEPTS OF PAINTING

The painter must first train his hand by copying drawings by the hand of good masters; and having achieved this habituation, under the judgment of his teacher, he must then practice by drawing good things in relief <note>original: "di rilievo"; referring to three-dimensional objects or sculptures</note> following the rules that will be stated below.

### ON DRAWING FROM RELIEF

He who draws from relief should position himself in such a way that the eye of the figure being drawn is level with the eye of the one who is drawing. And this should be done for a head that you have to draw from nature <note>original: "di naturale"; drawing from a live model</note>, because generally, the figures or people you encounter in the streets all have their eyes at your same height; and if you made them higher or lower, you would cause your portrait to lose its resemblance.

### ON THE MANNER OF DRAWING FIGURES FOR NARRATIVES

The painter must always consider, on the wall which he is to paint with a history <note>original: "istoria"; a narrative painting depicting a specific scene or event, considered the highest form of art</note>, the height of the site where he wants to place his figures. This is so that when he draws from nature for that purpose, he keeps his eye as much lower than the object he is drawing as that object will be placed higher than the eye of the spectator; otherwise, the work will be blameworthy.

### WHY PAINTING CAN NEVER APPEAR AS PROMINENT AS NATURAL THINGS

<margin>
[1st fig.:] a b n m
[2nd fig.:] s f r
</margin>
Painters often fall into despair in their imitation of nature, seeing that their paintings do not have that relief and that vivacity that things seen in a mirror have. They argue that they have colors which, in brightness or darkness, far surpass the quality of the lights and shadows of the thing seen in the mirror, accusing their own ignorance in this case and not the true reason, because they do not understand it. It is impossible for a painted thing to appear with such relief as to equal things in a mirror—even though both are on a flat surface—unless it is viewed with only one eye. The reason is that two eyes see one thing after another, as **a** and **b** see **n** and **m**. **m** cannot entirely block **n**, because the base of the visual lines is so wide that it sees the second body behind the first. But if you close one eye, as at **s**, the body **f** will block **r**, because the visual line originates in a single point and makes its base at the first body, so that the second body of equal size is never seen.

---

### ON THE SHADOW

If the shadow exists because the pupil <note>original: "luscina"; literally "the light" or aperture of the eye</note> of the eye is a single thing, the further that pupil is from said shadow, the smaller it will be; and the closer it is, the larger it will be. And this proceeds because the pupil of the eye is not a single thing, but is made of many images; and the further the pupil is from that shadow, the more images of that shadow come to the pupil.

---

### THE PUPIL OF THE EYE

The pupil of the eye moves by itself according to whether the eye sees bright or dark things. If they are bright, the pupil constricts, and if they are dark, the pupil expands. And this is seen in nocturnal animals such as cats and owls and similar animals, which have small pupils by day and very large ones by night.

---

### On the pupil of the eye

<margin>
If the pupil of the eye is smaller than the object that is interposed
</margin>

The pupil of the eye will be seen through the object that is interposed; and the smaller the pupil is compared to the object, the more images it will be seen through; and the larger the pupil is compared to the object, the fewer images it will be seen through. And if the pupil is equal to the object, it will be seen through a single image. And if the pupil is larger than the object, it will be seen through fewer images; and if the pupil is smaller, it will be seen through more images; and if the pupil is equal, it will be seen through a single image. If the pupil is smaller than the object seen, the shadow of that object will be made of more images; and the further it is from that pupil, the smaller it will be; and the closer it is, the larger it will be.

### THOSE BODIES WHICH ARE CLOSER TO OR FURTHER FROM THEIR ORIGINAL LIGHT WILL PRODUCE A LONGER OR SHORTER DERIVATIVE SHADOW.

[Figure:] a c v s     b d t x     m n o     p q     r

> Among bodies of equal size, the one which is illuminated by a larger light will have its shadow of lesser length.

In experimenting, the aforementioned proposition is confirmed, because the body *m n* is embraced <note>surrounded or struck</note> by a larger portion of light than the body *p q*, as is shown above. Let us say that *v c a b d x* is the sky which creates the original light <term>original light: the primary source of illumination, such as the open sky</term>, and that *s t* is a window through which the luminous species <note>original: "spetie"; in Renaissance optics, these are the formal images or rays of light emitted by an object</note> enter; and likewise let *m n* and *p q* be the shadowy bodies placed against said light. *M n* will have a smaller derivative shadow <term>derivative shadow: the shadow cast by an object onto a surface, extending through space</term> because its original shadow <term>original shadow: the shadow attached to the dark side of the object itself</term> will be small, and the derivative light will be large because the original light *c d* is also large. *P q* will have more derivative shadow because its original shadow will be greater, and its derivative light will be less than that of the body *m n*, because the hemisphere—that part of the hemisphere *a b* that illuminates it—is smaller than the hemisphere *c c d* which illuminates the body *m n*. <note>The author uses "hemisphere" to refer to the arc of the sky providing light.</note>

---

### THOSE BODIES WHICH ARE CLOSER OR MORE DISTANT FROM THEIR ORIGINAL LIGHT WILL MAKE THEIR DERIVATIVE [derived] SHADOW SHORTER OR LONGER. <note>original: "dérivée"</note>

[Figure:] a c v s     b d t x     m n o     p q     r

(Among bodies of equal size, that which is illuminated by a greater light will have its shadow of lesser length.)

Through experiment, the aforementioned proposition is confirmed, because the body *m n* is embraced by a larger portion of light than the body *p q*, as is shown above. Let us say that *v c a b d x* be the sky which creates the original light, and that *s t* be a window through which the luminous species enter; and that likewise *m n* and *p q* be the shadowy bodies placed opposite to the said light. *M n* will have a smaller derivative shadow, because its original shadow is small; and the derivative light will be large, because the original light *c d* is also large. *P q* will have more derivative shadow, because its original shadow is larger; its derivative light will be less than that of the body *m n*, because the hemisphere—the part of the hemisphere *a b* which illuminates it—is less than the hemisphere *c c d*, which illuminates the body *m n*.

<header>Ms 2038 NATIONAL LIBRARY — FOLIO 11 (recto). —</header>

->[ LIGHT AND SHADOW ].<-

---

THOSE separate BODIES that are found scattered and LOCATED IN A DWELLING ILLUMINATED BY A SINGLE WINDOW WILL PRODUCE A DERIVATIVE SHADOW <term>derivative shadow: the cast shadow that extends from an object onto a surface</term> THAT IS MORE OR LESS SHORT DEPENDING ON WHETHER IT IS MORE OR LESS DIRECTLY IN FRONT OF THAT WINDOW.

->[ Figure: ] a e b c f d &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; s n v m t &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; WINDOW m. e n &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; x &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; x o g p 4 &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; k q l r h &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; y<-

The reason why the shaded bodies located more directly in front of the middle of the window produce shorter shadows than those located in a transverse [oblique] position is this: the central body sees the window in its true shape, while the transverse bodies see it in foreshortening <note>original: "iscorto"</note>. To the one in the middle, the window appears large; to the transverse ones, it appears small. The one in the middle sees a large hemisphere <note>Leonardo uses "hemisphere" here to describe the broad arc of light coming from the sky through the window</note>, namely **e. f.**, and those on the sides see it small, namely **q. r.** sees **a. b.**, and likewise **m. n.** sees **c. d.** The body in the middle, because it receives a greater quantity of light than those on the sides, is illuminated much lower than its center, and therefore the shadow is shorter. And just as much as **a. b.** enters into **e. f.**, so the pyramid **g. 4** enters into **l. y.** exactly.

Every center of a derivative shadow passes through the $\frac{1}{2}$ [midpoint] and aligns with the center of the original shadow <term>original shadow: the part of the object itself that is not reached by light</term>, with the center of the shaded body and of the derivative light, with the empty middle of the window, and finally with the middle of that part of the hemisphere of original light produced by the celestial hemisphere.

**y. h.** is the middle of the derivative shadow; **l. h.** of the original shadow. **l.** is the center of the shaded body; **l. k.** of the derivative light. **v.** is the middle of the window. **e.** is the final middle of the original light produced by that part of the hemisphere of the sky that illuminates the shaded body.

<margin>[ In the margin: ] Among shadows produced by equal bodies at equal distances from the opening <term>spiraculo: a small window or vent used as a light source</term> that illuminates them, the one that is longer will come from the less luminous body. And one body will be as much more luminous than another as its shadow is shorter than the other.</margin>

->[ Figure: ] a e b c f d &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; s n v m t &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; m e n &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; X &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; x o g p 4 &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; k q l r h &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; y<-

The reason why the shaded bodies located more directly in front of [directly before] the middle of the window produce shorter shadows than those situated in a transverse [oblique] position, is that they see the window larger in [its] own shape, and the transverse bodies see it in foreshortening. To the one in the middle of the window, it appears large; to the transverse ones, it appears small. The one in the middle sees the hemisphere large, that is to say [at] **e f**, and those on the side see it small, that is to say that **q r** sees **a b**, and likewise **m n** sees **c d**. The body in the middle, because it has a greater quantity of light than those on the side, is lit much lower than its center, and for that reason the shadow is shorter. And just as much as **a b** enters into **e f**, so much does the pyramid **g 4** enter into **e f**, between **l y**, exactly.

**Y h** is the middle of the derivative shadow, **l h** of the original shadow; **l** is the center of the shaded body, **l k** of the derivative light; **v** is the middle of the window; **e** is the final middle of the original light, produced by the part of the hemisphere of the sky that illuminates the shaded body.
