# FOLIO 12 (verso) — Manuscript 2038 National Library

### [LIGHT AND SHADOW, OPTICS]

---

->*The resemblance of bodies*<-

EVERY PHYSICAL FORM, AS FAR AS THE FUNCTION OF THE EYE IS CONCERNED, IS DIVIDED INTO 3 PARTS: THAT IS, **BODY**, **SHAPE**, AND **COLOR**. THE PHYSICAL RESEMBLANCE <note>original: "similitudine." In Leonardo's theory of optics, "similitudes" or "species" are the invisible images that emanate from an object to the eye.</note> [of the volume] EXTENDS FURTHER FROM ITS ORIGIN THAN DO COLOR OR SHAPE; NEXT, COLOR EXTENDS FURTHER THAN SHAPE; BUT THIS RULE IS NOT OBSERVED FOR LUMINOUS BODIES.

[Figure:] a &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; b c &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; d

The proposition above is very well demonstrated and confirmed by experience; for if you see a man from nearby, you will recognize the quality [nature] of the body, the quality of the shape, and likewise the color; and if he moves some distance away from you, you will no longer recognize who he is, because the quality of the shape is lost; if he goes even further away, you will not be able to discern his color, and indeed he will appear to you as a dark body; from further still, he will appear to you as a tiny, dark, round body *of almost round shape*. He will appear round because distance diminishes the individual members [limbs] so much that only the greatest mass appears; the reason for this is as follows:

We know clearly that all the resemblances of things enter the <term>imprensiva<note>The *imprensiva* was a term used by Leonardo to describe a specific part of the brain—the "intellectual receptor"—where sensory impressions (like sight) are first received and processed before being passed to the "common sense."</note></term> through a small aperture <note>original: "spiraculo," literally a breathing hole or vent.</note> of the eye; therefore, if the whole horizon **a b** [d] enters through such an aperture, and the body **b c** is a very tiny part of that horizon, what portion will it occupy in the minute representation of such a vast hemisphere? And because luminous bodies are more powerful in the darkness than any other body, it is necessary—since the aperture of the vision <insert>the sight</insert> is quite dark, as is the nature of all holes—that the "species" <note>Images or visual rays.</note> of distant bodies are blended into so much bright light from the sky; and if they do appear, they appear obscure and black, as does any small body seen in the brightness of the air.

---

<note>1. An oval mark appears before the first paragraph in the original manuscript.</note>
<note>2. Regarding the *imprensiva*, see the discussion on folio 1 recto, note 1.</note>
<note>3. This text corresponds to J.-P. Richter, Vol. I, No. 224 ("23a") and Plate VI, No. 4.</note>

<summary>Leonardo explains the hierarchy of visual perception, noting that an object's volume remains visible at greater distances than its color or its specific shape. He provides a physiological explanation for why distant objects eventually appear as small dark circles, centered on how the eye's aperture processes light and "similitudes."</summary>
<keywords>optics, perception, imprensiva, visual perspective, light and shadow, anatomy of the eye, distance</keywords>

--- Page 207 ---
<meta>This page, folio 12 verso, continues the optical investigations from the previous page. While the recto side dealt with the physical recognition of bodies and shapes as they recede into the distance, this verso side focuses specifically on the phenomenon of atmospheric perspective—how the "thickness" of air, smoke, and clouds alters our perception of color, particularly the transition between blue and white.</meta>

— FOLIO 12 (verso). — Ms 2038 BIB. NAT.

The eye is more tinted by the color of the object it observes as the air between the eye and the object becomes thinner.

The color of the object will be that much weaker in the eye as the color of the intervening air becomes more powerful. <note>Leonardo is observing that as the volume of air between the viewer and a distant object increases, the air's own color—usually a hazy blue—begins to overwhelm the true color of the object.</note>

The color of the air between the eye and the object will be tinted by the rays of another body that, from above, is more powerful in color than the air itself.

Between two objects in which the light is more powerful.

<note>Geometric diagram illustrating optics and atmospheric perspective, showing an eye (right) observing an object (left) through a cone-shaped field of vision with several labeled points.</note>

The air is illuminated by the rays of the sun; this air is between the eye and the dark object, and the color of that same air will be tinted by the rays of said sun.

A dark object will appear more blue in the eye as the whiteness of the air interposed between the eye and it becomes of greater thickness. <note>This is Leonardo’s fundamental theory of the "blue of the sky": that blue is not an inherent color of the atmosphere, but the result of illuminated "thin" air seen against the darkness of outer space.</note>

As appears in smoke which is interposed between the eye and the flue of a chimney; if the flue is dark, the smoke will seem blue.

But if such smoke is between the eye and the illuminated sky, that smoke will be dark in color and will tend toward reddish due to its thickness. <note>In this instance, the smoke is backlit, which changes the optical effect from scattering to absorption/blocking of light.</note>

But if that smoke is thin and is between the eye and the illuminated air, then it will be blue in color because of the air seen beyond it.

The air will be blue in color the deeper it is; and if a cloud is interposed between that air and the sun, that cloud will appear white.

If that cloud is thin and light, then it will tend toward blue; but it will be thin—and thus appear bluer—the thinner it is and when it is between the eye and the darkness of celestial space. And as that cloud becomes thicker and denser, it will be that much whiter, because the multitude of its minute particles yields so much light that the darkness of the space positioned behind it is not powerful enough to pass through. It is similar to the foam of water: the thinner it is, the bluer it will seem, and the denser it is, the whiter it will be; just as when it is between the eye and the darkness of the space between the eye and the bottom of the water, which water will appear blue because of the air <note>original: "aria." Leonardo sometimes uses "aria" (air) interchangeably with the medium or the reflected light of the sky when discussing the color of water.</note> seen through it.

Let the air be illuminated, and the darkness behind it will be blue; and through the thickness of that air, it will be blue.

That air will be blue because of its thinness, and the thicker it is, the whiter it will be.

<summary>Leonardo explains the science of atmospheric perspective, detailing how the density of air, smoke, and clouds creates the visual sensation of blue when viewed against a dark background, or white when the medium is dense enough to reflect light.</summary>
<keywords>atmospheric perspective, optics, blue of the sky, scattering of light, smoke, clouds, sfumato, color theory</keywords>

# Ms 2038 BIB. NAT. — FOLIO 13 (recto). —

A thousand lights equally distant from a single eye will illuminate that body equally, provided that such lights are of the same size, the same power <term>virtù: the physical potency or efficacy of a light source</term>, and the same color.

->**[DIAGRAM]**<-
<note>The diagram shows three circular light sources projecting rays through a single point to an object or surface below. The circles are labeled as follows:</note>

Yellow
Green
Red

The light in front will be overcome in brightness <note>original: "albore", literally "whiteness," used here to denote the intensity of light</note> by the lights that surround that part of the body which was made shadowy by that same light; and it will seem that it is confused with those parts that were illuminated by that same light. 

And this happens because the air, overcome by the surrounding bright parts, seems to cover the dark parts of that shadow.

### Note
That which is more overcome by a deficiency <note>original: "māchamento", a failing or lack</note> of light will be less visible.

### Furthermore
The deficiency of light in an eye will be the cause of losing the color of the body that is illuminated by such light.

# MS 2038 NATIONAL LIBRARY — FOLIO 13 (verso). —

### [LIGHT AND SHADOW].

EVERY SHADOW MADE BY AN OPAQUE BODY <term>corpo onbroso: an object that blocks light</term> SMALLER THAN THE ORIGINAL LIGHT SOURCE WILL PROJECT DERIVATIVE SHADOWS <term>onbre derivative: secondary shadows that extend into space from the object</term> TINTED WITH THE COLOR OF THEIR ORIGIN.
The origin of the shadow *e f* is *n*, and it will be tinted with its color. The origin of *h e* is *o*, and it will likewise be tinted with its color; and thus the color of *v h* will be tinted with the color of *p*, because it is born from it—and the shadow of the triangle *z k y* will be tinted with the color of *q*, because it derives from it.

[Figure:] a b c d g z m n o p q k y r s t v x h e f

<margin>To the degree that <note>original: "tanto quanto"</note> *c d* is contained within *a d*, the area *n r s* is that much darker than *m*; and all the rest of the field is without shadow.</margin>

[Below the figure:] *f g* is the first degree of light because here the entire window *a d* illuminates; and likewise on the opaque body, *m* is of similar brightness. *e f z k y* is a triangle that contains within itself the first degree of shadow, because the light *a d* does not reach into this triangle. *x h* is the second degree of shadow because it is illuminated by only 1/3 of the window—that is, *c d*. *h e* is the third degree of shadow because it "sees" <note>Leonardo often uses the verb "to see" (vedere) to describe the geometric path of light rays</note> two-thirds of the window, *b d*. *e f* is the final degree of shadow because the last degree of light from the window illuminates at the location of *f*.

THAT PART OF THE OPAQUE BODY WILL BE LESS LUMINOUS WHICH IS SEEN BY A SMALLER QUANTITY OF LIGHT.
The part of the body *m* is the first degree of light because it sees the entire window *a d* along the line *a f*. The second degree is *n* <note>The letter 'n' is omitted in the Italian text but supplied by context and the French translation</note> because it sees the light *b d* along the line *b e*. *o* is the third degree because it sees the light *c d* along the line *c h*. *p* is the penultimate degree because it sees *c d* along the line *d v*. *q* is the final degree because it sees no part of the window whatsoever.

EVERY SHADOW MADE BY AN OPAQUE BODY SMALLER THAN THE ORIGINAL LIGHT SOURCE WILL PROJECT DERIVATIVE SHADOWS TINTED WITH THE COLOR OF THEIR ORIGIN.

The origin of *h e* is *o* and it is likewise tinted in its color; and so the color of *v h* is tinted in the color of *p*, because it is born from it. And the shadow of the triangle *z k y* is tinted in the color of *q*, because it derives from it.

# FOLIO 13 (verso). — Ms 2038 NATIONAL LIBRARY

### [ON THE ILLUMINATION OF THE MOON]

Why the moon is not illuminated over the entirety of its half-sphere:
If the air [atmosphere] is that which illuminates it, let it be the air between us and the moon itself. This is because the air between us and the moon is illuminated by the sun, just like the air over fields and mountains is illuminated from below by the light of that same moon. For the moon is not otherwise brightened <note>original: "rischiarata"</note> except by the air, as will be proven below, because she partakes of the nature of bodies like riverbeds and mountains—in that she is [inherently] shadowy <term>onbrosa: Leonardo believes the moon's surface is naturally dark and rugged, like the Earth, rather than a smooth, self-luminous crystal</term>.

<margin>
And the shadows of such a moon will be more or less dark according to whether they are seen through more or less of the illuminated air.
</margin>

<note>Geometric diagram exploring optical effects on the moon's surface, specifically the illumination of its dark side by light reflected from the Earth's atmosphere (the phenomenon of 'earthshine'). Rays originate from source points a, b, c, d, e, passing through a sphere representing the moon, with a base line labeled t, n, m, r, x, o, f, s representing the terrestrial atmosphere or observer's plane.</note>

If *p n m* were air illuminated by the sun and were brightened from the lower part, then *t n m r x o f s* would be the region from which such brightened air descends. And because the part of the air labeled *o* is seen from a greater expanse of the illuminated air than part *n* is, it follows that part *o* will be more luminous <note>original: "più luminosa"</note> than part *n*. And thus, degree by degree, such air below the moon will be brightened.
Below *p r n f* will be the brightened air; and [looking through] this brightened air, the shadow of the moon will appear darker than it actually is.

This is proven because she [the moon] partakes of the nature of bodies like riverbeds and mountains, and is naturally shadowy.

If the moon brightens the air below it, this occurs because of its own luminosity. And because it [a specific point in the atmosphere] is seen from more of the illuminated air, it will be more brightened than the moon’s shadow will be; this is because the air between the eye and that shadow brightens [the view] from below. It brightens that shadow more or less according to how much the air itself is more or less brightened, and it brightens the air that is within the shadow.

<summary>Leonardo analyzes 'earthshine,' concluding that the moon's dark side is partially visible because it is illuminated by the Earth's atmosphere. He argues that the moon's surface is naturally dark and rugged like the Earth's mountains and riverbeds, rather than being a perfect, polished sphere.</summary>

# FOLIO 14 (recto) — MS 2038 NATIONAL LIBRARY

->[LIGHT AND SHADOW]<-

EVERY LIGHT THAT FALLS UPON SHADOWY BODIES <note>original: "corpi onbrosi"—referring to opaque objects that cast shadows</note> AT EQUAL ANGLES HOLDS THE FIRST DEGREE OF BRIGHTNESS, AND THAT AREA SHALL BE DARKER WHICH RECEIVES LESS EQUAL ANGLES. AND LIGHT OR SHADOWS PERFORM THEIR OFFICE BY MEANS OF PYRAMIDS <term>pyramids: Leonardo's term for the conical way light rays and shadows radiate from a point or source</term>.

[Figure:] m z p s &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; t &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; v &nbsp; p [q] y x &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; a &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; b &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; o k i h c d e f g
4 &nbsp;&nbsp; 1 7 8 &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; 6 &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; horizon

Angle *c* holds the first degree of brightness because it "sees" <note>Leonardo often uses the verb "to see" (vedere) for surfaces to describe their exposure to a light source</note> the entire window *a b* and the entire horizon of the sky *m x*. Angle *d* has little difference from *c* because the angles that surround it are not so different in proportion as the others below; it lacks only that part of the horizon between *y* and *x*. Although it acquires just as much from the opposite side, nevertheless its line is of little power because its angle is smaller than its companion.

Angles *e* and *i* have less light because the light from *m s* and the light from *v x* do not "see" them, and their angles are quite unequal. Angle *k* and angle *f* are each placed between angles very different from one another, and therefore will have little light, because at *k* it only sees the light *p t*, and at *f* it only sees *t q*.

*O g* shall be the last degree of light, because there it sees no part of the light of the horizon; these are the lines that once again reconstruct a pyramid similar to pyramid *c*. This pyramid *l* will be found at the first degree of shadow, because it too falls between equal angles. These angles are directed and face each other along a straight line that passes through the center of the shadowy body and reaches the middle of the light source.

The luminous species <term>species: an Aristotelian concept used by Leonardo to describe the "likeness" or visual information of an object traveling through space</term> multiplied at the edges of the window at points *a* and *b* create a brightness that surrounds the derivative shadow <note>the secondary shadow cast by an object, as opposed to the "attached" shadow on the object itself</note> created by the shadowy body at places 4 and 6. The dark species multiply in *o* and *g* and end in 7 and 8.

# FOLIO 14 (recto). — MS 2038 NAT. LIB.

Every shadow cast by one and the same object grows larger <note>original: "s’ingrossa"—literally "thickens" or "swells," referring to the widening of the shadow cone as it moves away from the object</note> in proportion to its distance from the object that produces it. That part of the shadow shall be of greater darkness.

<note>A large, precise geometric diagram illustrating the physics of light and shadow. A curved light source at the top (marked R, S) sends rays through an opening. These rays strike a spherical body (labeled n, o, p, q), which casts a shadow onto a flat surface below. Points on the surface are marked a, b, c, d to show the varying intensity of the shadow.</note>

That shadow shall be of less darkness which is "seen" <note>Leonardo frequently uses the verb "to see" (vedere) to describe how a surface is exposed to a light source; if a point can "see" the light, it is illuminated</note> by more of the light source; and likewise, on the contrary, that shadow shall be of greater darkness which is seen by a smaller part of the light source. This happens because if you look at mark **a**, you will see that the shadow-body **n o p q** cannot see any part of the front of the light source **r s**, because the object itself stands between the shadow and the lights. And if you look at mark **b**, you will see that the shadow-body **n o p q** sees only a small part of the light source **s r**, namely <note>original Latin: "scilicet"</note> **s x**; and for this reason, it sees little light and the shadow is powerful <note>In this context, "powerful" means dense or very dark</note>. And if you look at mark **c**, you will see that the shadow-body **n o p q** sees a more luminous part, namely **s y**; and for this reason, shadow **c** is less dark than **b**. And if you look at mark **d**, you will see that the shadow-body **n o p q** sees even more of the light, namely **s z**; and for this reason, shadow **d** is lighter than **c**. And so, step by step, the shadow comes to fade away until it merges with the primary light <term>primary light: the direct, unobstructed light from the source</term>. And this happens because angle **s n b** is larger than angle **s n c**, and angle **s n c** is larger than angle **s n d**; and for this reason, at mark **b** one sees less light than at mark **c**, and so it is seen in the other marks by reason of the angles.

<summary>Leonardo uses geometric proofs to explain the penumbra, demonstrating that shadow intensity decreases as a point on the ground "sees" more of the light source. He concludes that the graduation of shadow darkness is strictly governed by the geometry of the angles between the light source and the object.</summary>

<keywords>optics, shadow intensity, penumbra, geometry of light, primary light, angular perspective, Leonardo da Vinci physics</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Leonardo’s technical instructions for painters, shifting from the geometry of shadows (on the previous page) to the practical application of light, reflections, and the effects of distance on human perception. It maintains the same analytical tone, treating the act of seeing as a physical science.</meta>

<page-num>f. 14v</page-num>
<header>Ms 2038 — FOLIO 14 (verso). — NATIONAL LIBRARY.</header>

## [CONTOURS, REFLECTIONS, ERRORS IN SMALL THINGS].

### ON LINEAR PAINTING.
<margin>note</margin>
Let extreme care be taken when considering the boundaries <note>original: "termini"—referring to the edges or contours of a shape</note> of any body, and the way they "snake" [curve]. One must judge if the turns of these curves partake of a circular semi-curvature or of an angular concavity.

### ON PAINTING.
The shadows which you discern with difficulty, and whose boundaries you cannot distinguish or recognize, but rather accept and transfer into your work with a confused judgment—you shall not make them finished or defined, or else your work will result in a "woody" appearance <note>original: "legniosa"—meaning stiff, dry, or lacking the softness of life</note>.

### ON REVERBERATION.
Reverberations <term>reverberation: in Leonardo's usage, this refers to "reflex" or reflected light that bounces off one surface onto another</term> are caused by bodies of a brighter quality, with flat and semi-dense surfaces. When these are struck by light, they strike it back toward the first object, much like the bounce of a ball.

### WHERE LUMINOUS REVERBERATION CANNOT BE.
All dense bodies have their surfaces covered by various qualities of lights and shadows. Lights are of two natures: one is called "original," the other "derivative." I say "original" is that which derives from a flame of fire, or from the light of the sun or the air. Derivative light is reflected light. But to return to the promised definition, I say that luminous reverberation will not exist on that part of a body that is turned toward shadowy bodies, such as dark places, meadows of various heights of grass, or green or dry woods. Although the part of each branch turned toward the original light is clothed in the quality of that light, nevertheless there are so many shadows made by each individual branch, and so many shadows cast by one branch onto another, that in the end, such darkness results that the light is as nothing. Therefore, such objects cannot give any reflected light to opposing bodies.

### HOW ERRORS ARE NOT PERCEIVED IN SMALL THINGS AS THEY ARE IN LARGE ONES.
In things of minute form, one cannot comprehend the quality of an error as one can in large things. The reason is that if this small thing is made in the likeness of a man or another animal, its parts—because of their immense reduction—cannot be searched out by the creator with that proper finish <note>original: "fine"—referring to the level of detail or completion</note> that would be appropriate. Since it remains unfinished, you cannot comprehend its errors. 

**EXAMPLE:** Look from a distance at a man from 300 cubits <term>braccia: an Italian unit of measurement, literally "arms," roughly 23 inches</term> and judge with care whether he is handsome or ugly, or if he is monstrous or of common quality. You will see that despite your greatest effort, you cannot persuade yourself to make such a judgment. The reason is that at the aforementioned distance, this man diminishes so much that the qualities of his parts cannot be comprehended. If you want to clearly see this reduction of the man, place a finger near your eye at the distance of a palm’s width <note>original: "span palmo"</note>, and move that finger up and down so that its upper tip ends below the feet of the figure you are watching. You will see an incredible reduction appear, and for this reason, one often doubts the form <note>meaning the identity</note> of a friend from a distance.

<page-num>f. 14v</page-num>
<header>- FOLIO 14 (verso). -</header>

<margin>On landscapes. Note.</margin>

Before you attempt anything in landscapes, first ensure you have practiced well the air, buildings, branches, and foliage of different trees, as well as stones, rivers, and grasses, testing each thing on its own before you put them together.

<margin>On shadow</margin>

The shadow will always be between the light and the object that creates it; this shadow is shorter and darker the closer the object is to the place where it falls.

<margin>On the shadow of trees</margin>

The shadow of trees is darker the darker and thicker the foliage of the tree itself; if you are to paint an isolated tree with the air surrounding it, it will have one character, and if you are to paint a dense forest, it will have another.

<margin>On lights and the air</margin>

The air should be practiced before you create the narrative scene <note>original: "storia"—referring to the main subject or composition of the painting</note>. That air which is closer to the earth will be brighter than that which is further away; the buildings and trees within it will be increasingly "lost" <term>lost: the softening of edges and colors as objects recede into the distance, a core part of Leonardo's "sfumato" and aerial perspective</term> the further away they are, due to the thickness of the air placed between them.

<margin>On smoke</margin>

Smoke will appear bluer the thinner it is; it will be lighter or darker depending on whether the light comes from above or below. It will be darker toward its beginning than toward its end, and wider at the end than at the beginning. It will be thinner at the edges than in the middle, and it should move in every direction, just like the smoke from wet straw.

<margin>How the air should be made whiter toward the horizon</margin>

The air should be made whiter toward the horizon because smoke and thin, dusty mists lie between the eye and the sky itself, and therefore it will be whiter there. Buildings, mountains, and trees will appear lighter and more "lost" because of this intervening air. Be aware that trees, stones, or other objects that are further from you will appear lighter in both their shadow and their light because of the air between you. If you must make one object darker than another, do so because it is closer to you than the others, or because it is naturally darker in its own character. For every object that is near, the light and shadow must be well-defined. If you must make one tree darker than another, see that you make it more green, red, or yellow according to the specific type of tree; if you have to paint many together, it is better to make those shadows from the same mixture.

<summary>Leonardo provides practical advice for landscape painters, emphasizing the importance of studying individual natural elements like trees, smoke, and air before composing a full scene. He explains the principles of aerial perspective, noting how distance and atmosphere blur the edges of objects and change their colors and values.</summary>
<keywords>landscape painting, aerial perspective, atmospheric effects, shadows, foliage, smoke, horizons, artistic practice</keywords>

### FOLIO 15 (recto). — Ms 2038 NATIONAL LIBRARY

The movement of vision together with the <term>spirits<note>In Renaissance science, "animal spirits" were believed to be a subtle fluid that traveled through the hollow tubes of the nerves to carry sensory information to the brain.</note></term> and through the nerves; one must observe whether vision—one must observe whether the interposition of a wall, whether straight or nearby, causes the <term>spirits</term> to change at the extremes of sight in such a way that...

Ms 2038 BIB. NAT. — FOLIO 15 (verso). —

# [LIGHT AND SHADOW]

EVERY SHADOW, WITH ALL ITS VARIATIONS WHICH GROWS IN WIDTH BY DISTANCE *g* MORE THAN ITS CAUSE, HAS ITS *outer* <note>original: "i strc/extr", referring to the external or boundary lines of the shadow</note> LINES JOINING TOGETHER BETWEEN THE LIGHT AND THE SHADED BODY.

[First diagram:] ->East [Rising]: a  West [Setting]: b  m  c  d<-

This proposition clearly appears and is confirmed by experience; because if **a b** is a window without any divider, the luminous air that is on the right, in **a**, is seen on the left in **d**, and the air that is on the left illuminates the right at point **c**; and the said lines intersect at point **m**. <note>Leonardo is describing how light rays cross when passing through a narrow opening, effectively explaining the principle of the camera obscura.</note>

EVERY SHADED BODY IS FOUND BETWEEN 2 <term>PYRAMIDS<note>In Renaissance optics, light was envisioned as traveling in "pyramids" or cones, with the base at the light source or object and the apex at the eye or a point of intersection.</note></term>, ONE DARK AND THE OTHER LUMINOUS. ONE IS SEEN AND THE OTHER IS NOT. AND THIS ONLY HAPPENS WHEN THE LIGHT ENTERS THROUGH A WINDOW.

[Second diagram:] z y h k a b c i r g f s m n o p x

Suppose that **a b** is the window and that **r** is the <term>shaded body<note>original: "corpo onbroso", an opaque object that blocks light to create a shadow.</note></term>. The right-side light **h z h** passes the body on the left side of the shaded body at **g** and goes to **p**; the left-side light **k** passes the said body on the right side at **i** and goes to **m**, and these two lines intersect at **c**, and there they form a pyramid. Furthermore, the edges of the window **a** and **b** touch the shaded body at **i** and **g**, and form their pyramid at **f i g**. **F** will be dark because the light can never reach there; **i g c** will always be luminous because the light reaches it.

<meta>Following the previous page's discussion on how light rays intersect when passing through windows, Leonardo now moves to the specific mathematical relationships between distance and the intensity of light and shadow. He continues to use geometric proofs to explain visual phenomena, a hallmark of his scientific approach to painting.</meta>

FOLIO 15 (verso). Ms 2038 BIB. NAT.

Every <term>opaque body<note>original: "chorpo opacho"; an object that does not allow light to pass through it.</note></term> will be of so much less brightness as it is more remote from the light that illuminates it; and this will be in such proportion as that of the space that separates it from its light.

<note>Geometric diagram illustrating a sphere (labeled "corpo" or body) situated between two light sources (each labeled "lume"), with rays defining the areas of illumination and shadow.</note>

Every shadow will be of so much less darkness as it is more remote from the opaque body that produces it; and this will be in such proportion as that of the space that separates it from that very opaque body which causes it. For example, shadow **n** will be less [dark] than shadow **m** in such proportion as the space **m-o** is to the space **n-o**; [likewise for] the other mark **s**.

<note>Geometric diagram of shadow projection on a plane. It shows light sources at points 'd' and 'c' illuminating an object 'o', casting shadows at points 'm', 'n', and 's' on a base line.</note>

Shadow **m** will be of a given darkness, and so will shadow **n**, even though one is closer to the opaque body than the other. The reason is this: because light **d** sees **n** across a large space, but does not see **m** in such a large part because the body **o** takes away a part of it; and the same happens with light **c**. Thus, **c m** will be of greater unity <note>original: "magior d'unita"; in Leonardo's optics, "unity" often refers to the density or concentration of the shadow, where it is not diluted by secondary light sources.</note> than shadow **n**. For this reason, it is concluded that a shadow becomes lighter the further it is removed from its opaque body, and so forth.

<summary>Leonardo explains the mathematical relationship between distance and the intensity of light and shadow, demonstrating that both brightness on an object and the darkness of its cast shadow diminish in proportion to their distance from the source or the object.</summary>
<keywords>optics, geometry, light intensity, shadow density, opaque body, proportions, chiaroscuro theory</keywords>

*as it b* <note>The scribe appears to have started a sentence and then struck it out.</note> WHY THE SERIES OF FIGURES ONE ABOVE THE OTHER IS A WORK TO BE AVOIDED.

This universal custom, which is practiced by painters on the walls of chapels, is reasonably to be much blamed, given that they make one <term>history<note>original: "storia"; in Renaissance art, this refers to a narrative scene or a multi-figure composition illustrating a specific event.</note></term> on one level with its landscape and buildings, and then they rise up another level and make another history, changing the <term>point [of view]<note>original: "punto"; the vanishing point in linear perspective, which should ideally align with the viewer's eye level.</note></term> from the first, and then a third and a fourth, so that on one wall a work is seen with four points of view; this is the height of folly for such masters. We know that the point of view is placed at the eye of the one who looks at the narrative; and if you should ask, "In what way then should I depict the life of a <insert>saint</insert> divided into many narratives on the same wall?" to this I answer you: that you must place the first level with the point of view at the height of the eye of the spectators of that narrative; and on said level, represent the first history on a large scale. Then, by diminishing the figures and houses little by little upon various hills and plains, you will create the entire setting of that narrative. For the rest of the wall, in its upper part, you shall make trees that are large in comparison to the figures, or angels if they suit the subject of the history, or perhaps birds, or clouds, or similar things. Otherwise, do not trouble yourself with it, for your entire work will be false. <note>Leonardo is arguing for a single, unified perspective on a wall rather than the traditional "stacked" registers common in Gothic and early Renaissance fresco cycles.</note>

<meta>Following the previous page’s discussion on the technical challenges of perspective in large-scale chapel paintings, Leonardo transitions from the external world of art and landscape into a scientific investigation of biology and optics. He begins to explore the physiology of the eye, specifically comparing animal and human vision to understand how light is processed internally.</meta>

# FOLIO 16 (recto). — Ms 2038 BIB. NAT.

<margin>
Why the eyes of animals travel through the darkness.
</margin>

Whoever wishes to see by experience how the eyes of animals possess in themselves, of their own accord, a certain light, should look at the eyes of cats and other animals that roam by night; you will see that their eyes glow like flames of fire. This is because nature has given such animals night vision to enable them to find their prey. And if you say to me that this is a reflection of external <note>original: "istrinseca" (extrinsic); light coming from outside the eye.</note> light, I tell you that this cannot be; for if you look at them in a place that is completely dark, where there is no light at all, you will still see the eyes of these animals glowing. This occurs because the pupil dilates so much that it occupies almost the entire eye, and that part inside the eye called the <term>uvea<note>original: "uuea"; Leonardo uses this term to describe the inner lining of the eye. In nocturnal animals, he is observing the "tapetum lucidum," a reflective layer that creates the "eyeshine" effect.</note></term> is of a white and shiny color like a mirror; it receives the light that is inside that eye and reflects it, sending it out through the pupil. For this reason, the eyes of these animals glow and give back the light that they have received. This also happens with the eyes of men: when the pupils are very dilated, they seem to glow.

-> ### [THE SUN OVER THE SEA, THE MOON. — LIGHTS AND SHADOWS, PARTS AND WHOLES, FACES AND LIMBS]. <-

The minor details must correspond well to their parts, and the parts must correspond to the whole.

**PROOF: HOW THE CLOSER YOU ARE TO THE SOURCE OF THE SUN'S RAYS, THE LARGER THE SUN REFLECTED ON THE SEA WILL APPEAR TO YOU.**

<margin>[1st fig.:] a n</margin> If the sun exerts its radiance from its center, reinforced by the power of its entire body, it is necessary that the further its rays travel from it, the more they spread out. If this is so, you, whose eye is near the water that reflects the sun, see only a very small portion of the sun's rays carrying the form of that reflected sun onto the surface of the water. But if you were closer to the sun—as would be the case when the sun is at midday and the sea is toward the west—you would see the sun reflected upon said sea in a much larger form. This is because, being closer to the sun, your eye captures the rays closer to the <term>point<note>The source or convergence point of the light rays.</note></term> and thus captures more of them, resulting in greater brilliance. For this reason, one could prove that the moon is another world similar to our own, and that the part of it which shines is a sea reflecting the sun, while the part that does not shine is land.

How shadows blend together over a long distance is proven by the shadow of the moon, which is never seen <note>Leonardo is observing that because the moon is so far away, the shadow it casts into space (its umbra) tapers off and is not visible as a sharp shape against the heavens.</note>.

<margin>[4th fig.:] Where the shadow should strike the face</margin> Regarding objects that are above the eye and to the side, which you wish to make appear detached from the wall: between the <term>original shadow<note>original: "lonbra originale"; the shadow on the object itself (shading).</note></term> and the <term>derivative shadow<note>original: "lonbra di rivativa"; the shadow cast by the object onto the wall or floor.</note></term>, you must place a light in the middle; thus the object will appear detached from the wall.

On the members of the body: one must make a choice of all the parts for the purpose of painting <note>Leonardo frequently advised artists to select the most beautiful parts from various different models to create a "perfect" whole.</note>.

### ON LIGHTS AND SHADOWS

In every part of the body, and every tiny particle that possesses some degree of relief, I remind you to be careful to give them the primary masses <note>original: "principati"; the dominant or principal areas of light and dark that define the form.</note> of shadows and lights.

[1st fig.:] m n t u f Proposition [3rd fig.:] Conclusion
[Fig. near the text:] a d c e p n y s g f Example
**ON THE LIGHT WHICH ACTS WITH ALL ITS QUANTITY FROM A SINGLE LUMINOUS CENTER.**
If a large spherical light were to illuminate another spherical body much smaller than itself, it would follow—if the light rays were emitted from the surfaces of the light—that the smaller body would be enveloped and illuminated across more than half its surface. If this were so, the shadow, where it is intercepted further from its source, would be rendered smaller until it reached its end. However, experience shows the opposite: for the lights of candles, which are long and narrow, when they illuminate a small spherical body, the shadow which should be round on the wall would also appear wide and flat. For this reason, let us suppose that a c d e [Figure near the text] are the height and width of the light; if the surfaces are to act, a b [e] <note>The letter 'e' appears to be a label for the light source in the diagram.</note> illuminates the spherical body more than halfway—by as much as the distance from p to n or from y to s—and its shadow on the wall will appear much smaller than the one on the spherical body. The surfaces of the light’s thickness at c and d would illuminate the spherical body at p and y, that is to say, in the middle; consequently, this being so, the shadow on the wall will become as wide as the object itself. Therefore, the shadow on the ball would be wide and flat, and so would the shadow on the wall. Since experience demonstrates that this shadow is round in shape and always larger than its source, we must invalidate both the previous experiments and demonstrations and admit that the center of every light is the cause of shadows. Conduct the experience thus: [(Last fig.)] Let a b be the wall, c d the ball or a line; let e be the light. Measure the distance from the light to the wall a b along the line of light; then, measure the shadow and draw two lines that are similar to the distance between the wall and the light, and as wide as the shadow. In these lines, observe if the line e [c] d, at its distance, returns and is contained within the other lines.
[Last fig.:] a b cd e Experience.

The shadow will be of as much darkness as the part of the light that is seen by such shadow. <note>Leonardo is establishing a proportional relationship between the intensity of a shadow and the amount of the light source that is visible from that specific point.</note>

If the eye is at **.s.**, it is in the middle between the light and the sphere; therefore, it sees the half of the sphere that is illuminated by the light. And if this eye moves toward **.m.**, it will gradually see less light until it arrives at **.m.**, where it will then see no light at all.

Furthermore, if the eye moves toward **.o.**, it will always see more light until it reaches **.o.**, where then that eye will see the entire half of the sphere illuminated by the light **.o. .q.**

### [APPRENTICESHIP AND PRECEPTS OF PAINTING].

The young man must first learn perspective,
then the measurements of every thing;
then [copying] from the hand of a good master, to accustom himself to good limbs;
then from nature, to confirm for himself the reasons for the things learned;
then for a time, to see [study] the works of various masters;
then, to make it a habit to put into practice and work at the art.

— How the first painting was but a single line which surrounded the shadow of a man made by the sun on a wall. <note>Leonardo refers to the classical myth of the origin of painting, often attributed to the daughter of Butades, who traced her lover's shadow.</note>

— How painting must be seen from a single window <note>Meaning a single point of view or "eye."</note> as is evident by the reason of bodies made in this way [Figure] : . . . . . . . . . If you want to make a round ball at a great height, you must make it elongated in this manner, and stand so far back that, through <term>foreshortening</term> <note>original: "scortando"</note>, it appears round.

— How <term>narrative scenes</term> <note>original: "storie" — large-scale compositions depicting a historical, biblical, or mythological event.</note> should not be crowded and confused by many figures.

— How one should not give a cloth a confusion of many folds; rather, make them only where they are held by the hands or the arms, and let the rest fall simply where its nature pulls it, and let the nude [form] not be crossed by too many outlines or breaks in the folds.

— Draperies should be drawn from nature; that is, if you wish to make a woolen cloth, use the folds according to it; and if it is silk, or fine cloth, or that of peasants, or linen, or a veil, go about diversifying the folds for each. And do not make a habit, as many do, of using models covered in paper or thin leather, for you would be greatly deceived. <note>Leonardo is criticizing the use of stiff, artificial manikins instead of observing how real fabric drapes over the human body.</note>

— How old men should be made with sluggish and slow movements, with legs bent at the knees when they stand still, and feet parallel and spread apart, the back bent low, the head leaning forward and tilted, and the arms not too extended.

— How women should be depicted with modest gestures, legs squeezed together, arms gathered together, and heads low and tilted to the side.

— How old women should be depicted as bold and spirited, with angry movements like those of infernal furies; the movements should appear more spirited in the arms and the head than in the legs.

— Little children: with spirited and twisted gestures when they are sitting; and when standing, with timid and fearful gestures.

The rule of <term>finite lights</term> <note>original: "lumi finiti" — refers to light sources with a specific physical size, such as a window or a flame, rather than an infinitesimal point of light.</note> of varied size shall be that which is determined by the boundaries of the luminous body.
Because every point of its surface will send its rays throughout the space of the air, and through that same space, its entire shape can be perceived from each of those points.

---

Thus it may be concluded that the air will be full of light; from every side, that luminous body can be seen.

---

**How the shadow will be darker in the middle of its width than at its boundaries**
The reason is this: that part will be lighter which is seen by more parts of the luminous body. Therefore, the area *m o p* will be of equal brightness throughout because it is seen from every point of the light *a b*. But the area *q r s* will be the shadow, because the view of part of that luminous body is blocked; and that part of such a shadow will be darker which is seen by a smaller part of the luminous body. And conversely, that part will be lighter which is seen by a larger part of that light. <note>Leonardo is describing the phenomenon of the penumbra—the soft edge of a shadow where the light source is only partially obscured.</note>

---

**How the air between the shadow and the eye has no color, but is only a medium**
between the eye and the shaded body.

---

The air between the eye and the shaded body is mixed with the shadow of the aforementioned air, and it is lighter than the shadow of the body.

---

The center of the space positioned between two shadows—enclosed by the luminous body—will be that which is seen by the entire luminous body.

### ON THE THREE NATURES OF PERSPECTIVE
How perspectives are of three natures: The first relates to the rules of diminishing size, and is called <term>linear perspective</term> <note>original: "prospettiva diminutiva"</note>, concerning things that recede from the eye. The second contains within it the method of varying colors as they recede from the eye. The third and last relates to the explanation of how things should be less finished the further they recede. — The names shall be these: Linear perspective,
->Perspective of color,<-
->Perspective of disappearance.<- <note>original: "prospetiua dispeditione" — also known as the perspective of "loss of definition" or "clarity."</note>

### ON THE VISIBILITY OF COLORS
Which color is most evident? The thing that is brighter appears more from a distance, and the darker thing does the opposite.
->(On making a good choice.)<-

### ON HAVING FEW FOLDS IN DRAPERIES
How figures clothed in a cloak should not show the nude so much that the cloak appears to be directly upon the flesh, *seeing that* you would not want that cloak to be against the flesh. For you must consider that between the cloak and the flesh there are other garments which prevent the form of the limbs from being clearly seen through the cloak. And the limbs that you do make visible, make them thick enough so that it appears there are other garments under the cloak. But you shall show the near-true thickness of the limbs only for a <term>nymph</term> <note>In Renaissance art, "nymphs" were often depicted in "wet drapery" style to show movement and the female form.</note> or an <term>angel</term>, who are depicted dressed in thin garments, pushed and pressed against their limbs by the blowing of the winds.

### ON THE METHOD OF DEPICTING DISTANT THINGS IN PAINTING
It is clearly seen that the air is thicker than elsewhere where it borders the flat earth, and the higher it rises, the thinner and more transparent it becomes. For tall and large things that are far from you, their lower parts will be poorly seen because you see them through a line that passes through the thickest and most continuous air. The summit of these heights is seen through a line which, although it originates at your eye in the thick air, nevertheless, ending at the very top of the thing seen, ends in air much thinner than that at its base. And for this reason, as this line moves further from you point by point, it constantly changes quality from thin air to even thinner air. Therefore, you, the painter, when you make mountains, ensure that from hill to hill the bases are always lighter than the summits; and the further you make one from the other, make the bases lighter. 

<margin>And the higher they rise, the more they will show the truth of the form and the color.</margin>

How the air is filled in every part by all the <term>similitudes</term> <note>original: "similitudinj" — for Leonardo, these are the visual images or "species" that every object projects into the surrounding space, allowing them to be seen from any angle.</note> of the bodies found within it, and in every smallest part of said air. 
How is it possible that the air, though stirred, does not mingle the similitudes of the bodies moving through it? And if such air were still, without motion, is it possible for the similitudes of bodies to mingle with one another and create a mixing—either a mixing of colors or of other similitudes? 
And if it is true that the air is filled with them, is it possible that such fullness weighs more in one place than another? Or, if one eye looks at one similitude, can another eye see another in the same place—just as one would who looks into a mirror where another person also sees their own image?

---

How is it possible for the eye to see a multitude of images that are found in the air without them mingling or obstructing one another, or creating confusion in any way? This would happen if one motion crossed another, or if the similitude of one object struck that of another. 
And how can the air, without confusion, be a messenger to me of an object that is in one of the <term>four winds</term> <note>The four cardinal directions: North, South, East, and West.</note> and is near to its eye, while all the similitudes of all those bodies in the four winds come, mingled and placed in the winds to reach that eye—and yet they do not mingle or obstruct each other, so that the eye in the very same point sees all these similitudes without confusion?

---

->On the Similitude<-

If the air were filled everywhere with infinite similitudes of the bodies appearing in it, is it possible that such fullness exists in every smallest part of the air—filled with all these similitudes? Or are they spread throughout the whole air, or throughout each part of the air? Are they here or there? 
And why does one similitude not obstruct another? Or why does one eye look from one place and see such a similitude, and another eye look from another place and see another similitude, or even the same one—yet in seeing the same similitude, it will see it more from one side than the other? 
And how can it be that through every part of the air there pass such infinite similitudes of bodies of various forms, colors, sizes, and distances? 
And if it is true that the air is filled with these similitudes, do they have such power that in the mingling of the winds, these similitudes are not mixed? Instead, they preserve their power against one another, and pass through each other without confusion of their natures.

# [AIR, LIGHT AND SHADOW, SUN. — HOW TO REPRESENT THE NIGHT]

-> HOW THE AIR SHOULD BE MADE BRIGHTER THE LOWER YOU FINISH IT <-

Because this air is thick near the earth, and the higher it rises, the more it thins. When the sun is in the east and you look toward the west—observing the region between the south and the north—you will see that the thick air receives more light from the sun than the thin air, because the rays find more resistance. And if the sky, to your sight, ends at a low plain, that furthest part of the sky will be seen through that thicker and whiter air, *which* <note>The original manuscript has a slight repetition/correction: "ilquale laquale" / "qui qui".</note> will alter the true color of whatever is seen through it. There, the sky will appear whiter than it does above you, because your line of sight passes through a smaller quantity of air corrupted by thick <term>humors</term> <note>original: "grossi omori" — Leonardo refers to the heavy vapors and moisture near the earth's surface that create atmospheric haze.</note>. And if you look toward the east, the air will appear darker to you the lower it descends, because in that low air, the luminous rays pass through less.

-> ON THE DISCRETION OF SHADOWS, LOCATIONS, AND THE THINGS PLACED IN THEM <-

If the sun is in the east and you look toward the west, you will see all illuminated things to be entirely devoid of shadow, because you see what the sun sees. And if you look to the south or the north, you will see all bodies surrounded by shadow and light, because you see both what the sun does not see and what it does see. And if you look toward the path of the sun <note>Meaning, looking directly toward the sun (the east in this scenario).</note>, all bodies will show you their shadowed side, because that side cannot be seen by the sun.

-> ON THE MANNER OF DEPICTING A NIGHT SCENE <-

That which is entirely deprived of light is nothing but darkness. Since the night is of such a condition, if you wish to represent a story within it, you should arrange it so that there is a large fire. Then, the things closest to said fire should be most tinted by its color, because a thing that is closer to an object participates more in its nature. Making the fire lean toward a red color, you will make all things illuminated by it also appear reddish; and those things that are further from said fire, let them be more tinted by the black color of the night. 

The figures that are between you and the fire will appear dark against the brightness of that fire, because the part of the object that you see is tinted by the darkness of the night and not by the brightness of the fire. Those who are at the sides should be half-dark and half-reddish. Those who can be seen beyond the edges of the flames will be entirely illuminated by reddish light against a black field. As for their actions, make those who are close by shield themselves with their hands and cloaks as a defense against the excessive heat, turning their faces away as if fleeing. For those who are further away, depict many of them raising their hands to their eyes, pained by the excessive glare of the light.

---

<note>4. Corresponds to Manzi p. 92; Ludwig Vol. I, no. 146; Richter Vol. I, no. 604.</note>

# FOLIO 18 (verso). Ms 2038 BIB. NAT.

-> How the spirits are divided within the soul that is diffused through it <-
<note>This heading appears to be a philosophical or physiological title—perhaps a note for a different treatise—as the text immediately below returns to the study of optics and the atmosphere.</note>

Whoever desires to see the light within the darkness of the air by the force of the concavity <note>Leonardo uses "concavity" to describe the vast, dark void of space beyond the atmosphere.</note> of dense and dark bodies must know that the air, in itself, is without color. This darkness is nothing other than the void of non-transparent bodies. For this reason, the air by its own nature is very pure; that darkness is what we see as being blue in the air. The darkness generated in the air is caused by the force of the air itself, and the cause is the air that exists between the darkness and the eye. The thicker the air is, the whiter it appears; and the thinner it is, the more it mixes with that darkness and appears blue in color. The more transparent the air is, the more the air appears blue. This occurs in the air by the power of the sun’s light, which strikes the atoms <term>atoms</term> <note>original: "atomi" — in Leonardo's context, these are not subatomic particles but the tiny dust motes and vapors in the atmosphere that catch and reflect light.</note> of the air and gives them more color than the atoms of the air that are positioned in the darkness between the eye and the pure air.

-> On the painting of smoke <-

The shadow of the smoke that comes out of chimneys will be much darker the closer it is to the beginning from which it is born; and it will be much lighter the further away it is, because the thickness of the air comes between the eye and the smoke. Let this smoke be in clear air, from which it takes the imprint of its shadow; and this smoke will be lighter toward the air than toward the darkness of the plumes of smoke.

-> On the darkness of the air <-

The darkness of the air arises from the darkness of the earth, which is dark by its nature. In painting, the air is in itself white and luminous; and the thicker it is, the whiter and clearer it will be. And the thinner it is, the darker it will be near the darkness of the earth. The closer the air is to the "smoke" <note>Here Leonardo likely uses "fumo della terra" (smoke of the earth) to mean the low-lying mist or heavy atmosphere near the ground.</note> of the earth, the whiter and clearer it will be compared to the earth itself. Let the air be between the eye and the darkness of the earth; the darkness of the earth will be dark by its nature. The thicker the air is, the clearer it will be near the mist of the earth, because the air is white in itself. The darkness will be much darker near the mist of the earth because the air becomes much thinner toward the darkness of the earth. And as the air is thin, it will be much darker toward the darkness of the earth. And as the air is thicker, it will be much whiter near the mist of the earth. The air will be between the eye and the darkness of the earth, and the darkness of the earth will be dark by its nature; and the thicker the air is, the clearer it will be. Let the air be between the eye and the darkness of the earth, and the thinner the air is, the clearer it will be. <note>Leonardo is repeatedly refining a technical rule here: thickness of air adds "whiteness" (haze), while thin air allows the "darkness" of the background (the earth or space) to show through.</note> The air will be between the eye and the darkness of the earth, and the darkness of the earth will be dark by its nature, and the air will be thicker near the mist of the earth, because the air will be whiter.

<summary>Leonardo explains the optical phenomenon of the blue sky as a result of illuminated air particles seen against the darkness of space, while also providing rules for the atmospheric perspective of smoke and haze.</summary>

# [PAINTING, SCULPTURE, POETRY]

### WHY, BETWEEN TWO THINGS OF EQUAL SIZE, THE PAINTED ONE APPEARS LARGER THAN THE ONE IN RELIEF

This reasoning is not as easily demonstrated as many others, but I will nevertheless endeavor to satisfy the reader, if not in its entirety, then at least in part. Diminishing perspective <term>prospettiva diminutiva</term> <note>The branch of perspective dealing with how objects appear smaller as they recede into the distance.</note> demonstrates by logic that the further things are from the eye, the more they diminish; and these reasons are well confirmed by experience. 

Therefore, the visual lines that exist between the object and the eye, when they extend to the surface of a painting, are all cut at the same terminus <note>original: "termine" — the point where the lines of sight intersect the flat plane of the picture.</note>. But the lines that exist between the eye and a sculpture have different termini and lengths. The line that extends further to reach a part <note>original: "menbro" — literally "member" or limb, referring to a part of the statue.</note> that is more distant than others makes that part appear smaller. Because there are many lines longer than others, and because there are many small parts further away than others, it follows that they must appear smaller. By appearing smaller, their diminution makes the entire sum of the object appear smaller. 

This does not happen in painting, because the lines terminate at the same distance; it follows that they are without this physical diminution. Therefore, the parts do not diminish, and they do not reduce the sum of the object. For this reason, a painting does not diminish in the way a sculpture does. <note>Leonardo is arguing that because a statue is three-dimensional, its distant parts physically recede from the eye and "shrink" via perspective, making the whole statue seem smaller than a flat painting of the same size where every "part" sits on the same frontal plane.</note>

### HOW PAINTING SURPASSES ALL HUMAN WORKS BY THE SUBTLE SPECULATION BELONGING TO IT

The eye, which is called the first and principal window of the soul, is the primary way by which the "common sense" <term>commune senso</term> <note>In Renaissance psychology, the internal faculty where all sensory input was integrated and judged.</note> can most abundantly and magnificently consider the infinite works of nature; the ear is the second, which is ennobled by the description of things the eye has seen. 

If you historians, or poets, or other mathematicians <note>original: "matematici" — in this context, Leonardo refers to those who study the world through measurement and observation.</note> had not seen things with your eyes, you could poorly report them in your writings. And these very writings are born from painting <note>Leonardo suggests that written characters and the descriptive power of text are secondary to the visual image.</note>. If you, poet, describe a story with the "painting" of your pen, the painter with his brush will make it more easily satisfying and less tedious to understand. 

If you call painting "mute poetry," the painter may also call poetry "blind painting." Now consider which is the more grievous sting: to be blind or to be mute? Though the poet is as free as the painter in his inventions, his fictions do not give as much satisfaction to men as paintings do. For while poetry extends itself through words to figure forms, acts, and settings, the painter moves with the actual likenesses of those forms to replicate them. 

Now look at what is closer to man: the name of a man, or the likeness of that man? The name of a man changes in different countries, but his form is not changed except by death.

[Continued on Folio 19 verso]

<summary>Leonardo argues that painting appears larger than sculpture because it lacks physical depth that triggers perspective shrinkage, and he asserts painting's superiority over poetry by calling it a universal language of "forms" rather than "names."</summary>
<keywords>perspective, relief, sculpture vs painting, Paragone, window of the soul, common sense, mute poetry, blind painting, universal language</keywords>

<meta>This page transitions from Leonardo’s aesthetic arguments comparing painting and sculpture to his scientific investigations into optics. Here, he shifts from the theory of art to the physics of light and shadow, specifically examining how the anatomy of the eye and the nature of contrast influence our perception of boundaries and celestial bodies.</meta>

- FOLIO 19 (recto). - Ms 2038 BIB. NAT.

### why the boundaries of shadowed bodies
### appear among lights

Why the boundaries of shadowed bodies <note>original: "corpi ombrosi" — opaque objects that do not emit light themselves but cast or contain shadows.</note> appear with less definition <note>original: "diritura" — literally "straightness," but here referring to the sharpness or clarity of the edge.</note> than the boundaries of luminous bodies. I say that such an appearance occurs because the boundaries of lights are the extremities of their own bodies, which boundaries are in no other medium than the air; therefore, with their sharpness <note>original: "aspreza" — literally "roughness," implying a distinct, un-softened edge.</note> they end in the air. Furthermore, their rays strike nothing except the surrounding medium or the eye that looks at them. But the boundaries of the shadows of bodies do not end in the air, but in bodies just as dense as those that cause them, or in air as weak as its light; for which reason they are less defined than those of the lights. This is because the boundaries of the lights are between white and black, which are very different; but the boundaries of shadows are between shadow and darkness, which differ very little.

---

### how a star appears
### larger than it is
### to the sight

The reason a star appears larger than it is in its natural state is because its rays, striking the boundaries of the eyelids <note>original: "palpebre" — Leonardo refers here to the edges of the eyelids or the eyelashes.</note> of the eyes, bend upon striking those boundaries. This bending is projected into the back of the eye, just as the water of a river does when it strikes the piers <note>original: "pili" — the structural pillars or piles supporting a bridge.</note> of bridges, where it bends and "thickens" <note>Leonardo uses the term "ingrosa" to describe the visual accumulation or turbulence of water around an obstacle, a metaphor for optical diffraction.</note> around those piers. So does the light of the star at the boundaries of the hairs <note>original: "pili" — here meaning the eyelashes.</note> of the eye, which bends and spreads into the back of the eye. Between the rays that arrive directly and the rays that are bent, it seems that the star grows larger, because the eye does not judge the light of that star except by the space its rays occupy in the back of the eye. Thus, the star appears to grow larger because of the rays that bend at the boundaries of the eyelids.

<summary>Leonardo explains the optical reasons why shadows have softer edges than light sources and why stars appear larger than their physical size due to light diffracting around the eyelashes.</summary>
<keywords>optics, light and shadow, perception, astronomy, eye anatomy, diffraction, luminous bodies, shadowed bodies</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Leonardo’s "Paragone" (the comparison of the arts), specifically his defense of painting against poetry. While the previous page touched upon the physics of sight, this page uses those optical principles to argue that painting is a more direct and powerful medium than the written word.</meta>

- FOLIO 19 (verso). — Ms 2038 BIB. NAT. -

### [PAINTING IS SUPERIOR TO POETRY]

[Continued from folio 19 recto]
If the poet serves the sense through the way of the ear, the painter does so through the eye, which is the nobler sense. <note>Leonardo, like many Renaissance thinkers, ranked the senses; sight was considered the "prince of the senses" because it perceives the world directly.</note> I ask nothing more of such people than this: let a good painter represent the fury of a battle, and let a poet write of another, and let them be placed before the public together; you will see where the viewers will stop more, where they will consider more, where more praise will be given, and which will satisfy better. Certainly painting, being much more useful and beautiful, will please more. Write the name of God in one place and place His figure opposite; you will see which is more revered! If painting embraces within itself all the forms of nature, you have nothing but names, which are not universal like forms. If you have the effects of demonstrations, we have the demonstrations of the effects. <note>original: "se voi avete lieffetti delle dimostrationi noi abiano le dimostrationi deli effetti" — Leonardo argues that while poets describe the results of things, painters show the physical cause and appearance itself.</note>

Let a poet be taken who describes the beauties of a woman to her lover, and take a painter who depicts her; you will see where nature will turn the enamored judge. Certainly the trial of things should leave the sentence to experience. <note>Experience (sperientia) was the foundation of Leonardo's scientific and artistic method.</note> You have placed painting among the mechanical arts! <note>term: "mechanical arts" <gloss>In the Middle Ages and Renaissance, these were crafts involving manual labor, considered inferior to the "liberal arts" like rhetoric or music.</gloss></note> Certainly, if painters were as capable as you of praising their own works in writing, I doubt it would bear such a lowly name. If you call it "mechanical" because it is by hand—the hands figuring what they find in the imagination—you writers are also drawing with the pen manually what is found in your mind. And if you say it is mechanical because it is done for a price, who falls more into this error—if it can be called an error—than you? If you read for studies, do you not go to whoever pays you most? Do you do any work without some reward? Although I do not say this to blame such opinions, because every labor expects a reward. And a poet may say: "I will make a fiction that signifies great things"; the painter will do the same, as Apelles <note>Apelles was the most famous painter of ancient Greece, often cited by Renaissance artists as the ideal to emulate.</note> did with *Calumny*. 

If you say that poetry is more eternal, to this I say that the works of a coppersmith are more eternal, for time preserves them longer than your works or ours; nevertheless, they possess little imagination. And painting can, by painting on copper with glass colors <note>original: "colori di uetro" — likely referring to enamel or pigments that are fused like glass for durability.</note>, be made much more eternal. Through art, we may be called the grandchildren of God! If poetry extends into moral philosophy, this [painting] extends into natural philosophy. <note>term: "natural philosophy" <gloss>The study of nature and the physical universe, the precursor to modern science.</gloss></note> If that [poetry] describes the operation of the mind, this [painting] considers what the mind operates through movements. If that [poetry] frightens people with hellish fictions, this [painting] does the same with the same things in action. Let the poet be set to represent a beauty, a ferocity, a foul and ugly thing, or a monstrous one, alongside the painter; let the painter do it in his own way, changing forms as he wishes; will the painter not satisfy more? Have we not seen paintings have such conformity with the living thing that they have deceived men and animals? <note>Leonardo refers to classical anecdotes where birds tried to eat painted grapes or dogs barked at painted rivals.</note>

---

<summary>Leonardo argues for the superiority of painting over poetry, asserting that sight is the noblest sense and that painting, as "natural philosophy," captures the universal forms of nature better than words ever can.</summary>
<keywords>Paragone, painting vs poetry, mechanical arts, natural philosophy, Apelles, imitation of nature, experience, aesthetics</keywords>

- FOLIO 19 (verso). — Ms 2038 BIB. NAT. -

### [THE PRINCIPLES OF SIGHT AND PERSPECTIVE]

I have presented to you in many ways the nature of seeing. These modes of sight extend, one through the lines which show themselves by a principle of convergence <note>Leonardo refers to "concorsi," the way parallel lines seem to meet at a vanishing point in perspective.</note> extending from the eye to the object; another extends from the object to the eye. Another mode extends in such a way that the air placed between the eye and the object is traversed by its rays; another by rays and sight from above and from below; and likewise by rays and sight from one side and rays from the other.

And I will show you also how visual images blend with the air, and why this happens and how; and how the air acts as a tincture <note>original: "tignitura" — Leonardo views the air as a medium that can be "stained" or colored by the light and shadows of the objects within it, a concept fundamental to his technique of *sfumato*.</note> of what is seen; and how there is color in the air that exists between the eye and the object. 

And how the images <note>original: "spetie" — In Renaissance optics, "species" were the formal likenesses or "essences" of an object that were believed to radiate through the air to the eye.</note> seen extend through the air, and how the rays of the eye and the images intersect; and how one preserves its visual power as it passes through the paths of other images and rays, and how they leave an impression upon one another. 

And how you will see that in the convergence of these images, three types of images are formed: one which is the image enlarging itself more than the object seen; another being smaller; and the last <unclear>last</unclear> being an image equal to its cause <note>By "cause," Leonardo means the physical object itself that produces the visual image.</note>. 

And how the image of a body extends within the rays of the eye; and how you will see the air to be full of images, since a body is seen in every part of the air and its entire figure is seen from every side. And how you will likewise see every part of the body viewed through every part of the air; and how the air becomes clear through the images of that body, and how it takes on the tincture of that body's shadow.

And how it is that an image goes extending through the air and becomes the tincture and power of that body; and you will see how it extends along a line and then manifests itself to the eye; and how you will see again almost a power of seeing viewed through every part of the air, and how it extends so that the air is full of such power, and how it extends in such a way that the rays intersect; and how the image seen is understood through rays, and seeing is achieved through rays of sight.

<summary>Leonardo outlines a comprehensive scientific agenda for studying optics, focusing on how visual "species" (images) travel through the air, intersect, and change size relative to the viewer. He proposes that the air is saturated with the images of all objects, which a painter must understand to depict reality accurately.</summary>

<keywords>optics, perspective, species, rays of sight, atmospheric tincture, visual power, geometry of vision</keywords>

->LIGHTS. — PAINTING AND PHILOSOPHY. — LIMBS AND FIGURES].<-

### HOW WHITE BODIES SHOULD BE DEPICTED
If you represent a white body surrounded by a great deal of air, remember that white has no color of its own <note>Leonardo believed that white and black were not true colors, but rather the "extremes" of light and shadow; thus, white acts like a mirror for the colors around it.</note>, but rather takes on and transforms into a portion of the color of the objects facing it. If you see a woman dressed in white in the countryside, the part of her seen by the sun will be bright in color, such that it will partly cause the same discomfort to the eye that the sun does. But that part seen by the atmosphere—which is luminous because of the rays of the sun woven into it and penetrating it—will appear to lean toward a blue hue, because the air is itself blue. If on the nearby surface of the ground there are meadows, and the woman is found between the sunlit meadow and the sun, you will see all the parts of the folds that can be seen by the meadow take on the color of that meadow through reflected rays <term>riflessi: reflections of light and color from one surface onto another</term>. And so, she continues to be transformed by the colors of the nearby objects, whether they are luminous or non-luminous.

If you know how to reason and write the demonstration of forms, the painter will create them so they appear animated with shadows and lights, which compose the "air" <note>original: "aria" — here meaning the overall appearance, expression, or atmosphere of a face</note> of the faces; a point which you cannot reach with the pen, but which is reached with the brush.

->from nature: high or low,<-
->large or small, powerful and large,<-
->powerful and small, or large<-
->and weak, or small and weak?<-

### HOW HE WHO DESPISES PAINTING LOVES NEITHER PHILOSOPHY NOR NATURE
If you despise painting, which is the sole imitator of all the visible works of nature, you will certainly despise a subtle invention which, with philosophical and subtle speculation, considers all the qualities of forms: atmospheres and positions, plants, animals, grasses, and flowers, all of which are surrounded by shadow and light. And truly, this art is a science and the legitimate daughter of Nature, because painting is born of that very Nature. But to be more correct, we should call it the grandchild of Nature; for all visible things have been birthed by Nature, and from those birthed things, painting is born. Therefore, we shall rightly call it the grandchild of Nature and a relative of God <note>By calling painting a "relative of God," Leonardo elevates the artist from a mere craftsman to a creator who uses the same principles as the divine to generate a world.</note>.

### OF THE EYE WHICH, BECAUSE OF A GREATER LIGHT, CANNOT DISCERN LESSER ONES

### OF THE PLACEMENT OF THE LIMBS
Those limbs that endure fatigue, make them muscular; and those that are not used, you shall make without muscles and soft.

### OF THE ACTIONS OF FIGURES
You shall make the figures in such an action as is sufficient to demonstrate what the figure has in its mind; otherwise, your art will not be worthy of praise.

->HOW THE MIRROR LACKS ANY INHERENT IMAGE<-

This demonstration shows how the mirror lacks any inherent image <note>original: "spetie" — in Renaissance optics, "species" refers to the visual likeness or "phantom" of an object that travels through space to the eye</note> of its own, nor does it contain any within itself; rather, these images exist only on its surface and solely because of the eye that perceives them. For the eye sees the images of the bodies placed before it, and it does not see any image on the surface of mirrors except for the "shadow" <note>Leonardo here uses "shadow" to describe the ephemeral, non-material nature of a reflected image</note> of the image that travels through the air and settles upon the surface of the light of the glass. It forms itself with that same movement of the shadow produced by the vision of the eye within the air. The eye perceives the shadow of such vision through the air and creates the image of such vision; and if there were no air in the mirror, nor any likeness of an image, no image would be seen through the air except for shadow. And because the image is seen for every body that resembles a shadow, and because the likenesses of luminous bodies are seen—except that they exist within the air—the eye sees that image of shadow which comes from the air and accords with the movement of the bodies from which the likeness originates. Thus, the air retains no sight of any image, except as a shadow; and if you see any such image, it is because the air is still, without movement, and is not disturbed by any wind.
