->HOW THE AIR LACKS ANY INHERENT IMAGE<-
->THE AIR DOES NOT RETAIN ANY IMAGE<-

This demonstration is shown through the air, because it consists of shadow and is without a body, and images are resolved by its every movement. Therefore, the air settles in all its movement through the sight of such vision, just as the eye sees that image of shadow which comes from the air and is resolved by every movement without any movement of that air. No movement of the air remains; the air settles within the air and forms itself with that movement of air produced by the vision of the eye within the air, and the eye sees the shadow of such...

The air does not retain any image in itself except for the shadow; of its own accord, it possesses no image.

->OF THE MOVEMENT OF THE AIR<-
It is said that the air settles within the movement of the air, and it forms itself with that movement of the air produced by the vision of the eye within the air.

<note>Leonardo's repetitive language in these sections reflects his attempt to describe the invisible mechanics of "species" (visual information) passing through a medium (air) and hitting a surface (glass). He struggles to define whether the image "stays" in the air or is only created at the moment of perception.</note>

<summary>Leonardo argues that mirrors and the air have no inherent images but act as transparent or reflective mediums for "species" (visual likenesses). He posits that vision is a dynamic process where images are essentially "shadows" of objects perceived through the eye's interaction with the air.</summary>

->[LIGHTING OF FACES.
PEOPLE AND SHADOWS IN THE DISTANCE. — POSTURES].<-

### ON THE CHOICE OF LIGHT WHICH GIVES GRACE TO FACES
If you have a courtyard that you can cover at your will with a linen cloth, this light will be good. Or otherwise, when you want to paint a portrait, do so in bad weather or towards evening, placing the person you are portraying with their back against one of the walls of this courtyard. Take note in the streets, towards evening, of the faces of men and women when the weather is bad: what grace and sweetness can be seen in them! Therefore, you, painter, should have a courtyard arranged with walls tinted black, with a slight overhang of the roof over the wall; let it be 10 <term>braccia</term> <note>A "braccio" (plural "braccia") was a Renaissance unit of measurement, roughly equivalent to 23 inches or 58 centimeters.</note> wide, 20 long, and 10 high. When the sun is out, cover it with the cloth; otherwise, paint your portrait towards evening, or when it is cloudy or misty. This kind of atmosphere is perfect.

### WHY FACES APPEAR DARK FROM AFAR
We see clearly that all the <term>species</term> <note>original: "similitudine" or "spetie" — the visual images or "phantoms" cast off by objects that travel to the eye.</note> of visible things, both large and small, enter the senses through the small <term>pupil</term> <note>original: "luce" (light) — Leonardo uses this term to refer to the pupil or the opening of the eye.</note> of the eye. If the vast image of the greatness of the heaven and the earth passes through such a tiny entrance, the face of a man—being almost nothing among such great images—is diminished so much by distance that it occupies very little of that pupil, remaining incomprehensible. Furthermore, having to pass from the surface of the eye to the <term>imprensiva</term> <note>The "imprensiva" was considered by Leonardo to be the part of the brain where sensory impressions are first received and processed.</note> through a dark medium—that is, the hollow nerve <note>The optic nerve, which Renaissance anatomy often believed to be a hollow tube.</note> which appears dark—these images, not being of a powerful color, are stained by the darkness of their path, and once they reach the <term>imprensiva</term>, they appear dark. No other cause can be alleged; if that point in the pupil is black, it is because it is full of a transparent fluid that acts like air, performing the same function as a hole made in a board; when looking into it, it appears black, and things seen through light and dark air become confused in the darkness.

### HOW SHADOWS BEHAVE AT A GREAT DISTANCE
Shadows are lost at a great distance because the large quantity of luminous air found between the eye and the object tints the shadows of that object with its own color.

### WHY A MAN SEEN AT A CERTAIN DISTANCE IS NOT RECOGNIZED
Diminishing perspective shows us that the further away an object is, the smaller it becomes. If you look at a man who is a <term>crossbow-shot</term> <note>A common Renaissance unit of distance, roughly 200–300 yards.</note> away from you, and you place the eye of a small needle near your own eye, you will be able to see many men through that hole, sending their images to the eye, and all will fit into that small window at the same time. Therefore, if a man a crossbow-shot away sends his image to the eye, occupying only a tiny part of a needle's eye, how could you possibly discern or see the nose, the mouth, or any small part of that body in such a tiny figure? And not being able to see these, you cannot recognize the man, as you cannot distinguish the features that give men their diverse forms.

### ON POSTURE
The <term>pit of the throat</term> <note>original: "fontanella della gola" — the small depression at the base of the neck between the collarbones.</note> falls directly above the supporting foot. If an arm is thrown forward, the pit of the throat moves away from the vertical line of that foot; and if the leg is thrown backward, the pit of the throat moves forward; thus it changes with every posture.

->[REPRESENTATION OF A STORM AND A SPEAKER]<-

---

->HOW ONE SHOULD DEPICT A STORM<-

If you wish to properly depict a storm <note>The Italian "fortuna" here refers to a tempest or violent storm at sea.</note>, consider and observe its effects well. When the wind, blowing over the surface of the sea and the land, moves and carries away those things that are not firmly attached to the general mass. To properly depict this storm, you shall first show clouds, torn and broken, rushing in the direction of the wind, accompanied by sandy dust lifted from the sea shores, and branches and leaves lifted by the power of the wind's fury, scattered through the air, along with many other light objects. The trees and grasses should be bent to the ground as if showing a desire to follow the course of the winds, with branches twisted out of their natural growth and leaves ruffled and turned inside out. The men who are found there should be partly fallen and wrapped in their garments and the dust, looking almost unrecognizable; and those who remain standing should be behind some tree which they have embraced so that the wind does not drag them away; others with their hands over their eyes because of the dust, leaning toward the ground, with their clothes and hair streaming in the direction of the wind. Let the troubled and tempestuous sea be full of swirling foam between the raised waves, and the wind lifting into the embattled air a finer spray, appearing like a thick and enveloping mist. Of the ships that are within it, let some be shown with torn sails, the shreds of which flutter in the air along with some broken rope; some broken masts fallen with the ship turned on its side and broken among the tempestuous waves; some men shouting and embracing the remains of the vessel. You shall show clouds driven by impetuous winds against the high peaks of the mountains, making them wrap around in swirls similar to the waves striking the rocks; the air should be terrifying because of the dark shadows created by the dust, mist, and thick clouds.

->ON DEPICTING SOMEONE SPEAKING AMONG SEVERAL PEOPLE<-

You shall make the person whom you wish to speak among many people by considering the subject matter of which he is to treat, and by adapting his actions to that matter. That is, if the matter is persuasive, let the gestures be to the purpose; if the matter is explanatory with various arguments, let the speaker take two fingers of his right hand and hold one finger of the left, having the two smaller fingers separated <note>This specific gesture—holding the index or middle finger of one hand with the other—was a standard rhetorical sign in Renaissance art to indicate the "counting off" of logical points.</note>, and with his face turned toward the people, with the mouth somewhat open so that he appears to be speaking. If he is sitting, let him appear to rise somewhat, straight and forward with his head; and if you show him standing, make him lean a little with his chest and head toward the people. You shall depict the audience as silent and attentive, all looking at the face of the orator with admiring gestures. Also, make the mouths of some old men, out of wonder at the arguments they hear, hold their mouths with the corners pulled back, creating many folds in the cheeks; and with the eyebrows raised where they meet, creating many wrinkles across the forehead. Some who are sitting should have the fingers of their hands woven together, holding within them their left knee; others with one knee over the other, upon which they hold the hand that supports the elbow, which in turn supports the bearded chin of some bent old man.

---

->HOW ONE SHOULD DEPICT A STORM.<-

<note>This section is a translation of the French version provided in the OCR, which mirrors the Italian text above.</note>

If you want to represent a storm well, consider and set down its effects well, when the wind, blowing on the surface of the sea and the land, stirs and carries away things that are not immobile within the universal mass. And to represent this storm well, you will first make shredded and broken clouds move according to the course of the wind, accompanied by the sandy dust taken from the sea shores, and branches and leaves taken by the power of the wind’s fury, scattered in the air, and in their company many other light things. The trees and grasses having bent to the ground, appearing almost to want to follow the course of the winds, with branches twisted out of their natural direction, with their leaves overturned and reversed. The men who are found there are partly fallen and enveloped by their draperies, and almost unrecognizable because of the dust. And let those who remain standing be behind some tree they have embraced, so that the wind does not drag them away; others with their hands at their eyes because of the dust, leaning toward the earth, with their draperies and their hair following the course of the wind; let the troubled and tempestuous sea be full of turning foam between the high waves, and let the wind lift into the embattled air a finer [lighter] foam, in the manner of a thick and enveloping mist. Of the ships found there, let some be made with the sail torn and its rags agitated by the wind in the air at the same time as some broken rope; some broken masts, fallen with the ship turned sideways and broken by the tempestuous waves; some men who cry out embracing the rest of the ship. You will make the clouds driven by the impetuous winds struck against the high summits of the mountains, enveloping them in swirls similar to those of waves struck against the reefs; the air frightening from the dark shadows made in the air by the dust, the mist, and the thick clouds.

->ON REPRESENTING SOMEONE WHO SPEAKS AMONG SEVERAL PEOPLE.<-

You will have to make the one you want to speak among many people by considering what matter [subject] he has to treat, and to accommodate his actions so that they belong to that matter, that is to say, if the matter is persuasive, let the acts be according to the intention; if the matter is explanatory for various reasons, let the speaker take with the two [first] fingers of the right hand, a finger of the left, having separated the two smallest ones, with the face lively turned toward the people, with the mouth a little open which appears to speak. If he were sitting, let him appear to rise a little straight and forward with the head, and if you make him standing, make him lean a little with the chest and the head toward the people, whom you will represent as silent and attentive, all looking at the orator in the face with admiring acts. Also make the mouth of some old men, who, amazed by the sentences they hear, hold the mouth with its ends lowered, dragging many folds of the cheeks, with the eyebrows high at their junction which create many folds on the forehead; some sitting with the fingers of the hand interlaced, between which they hold the left knee; others with one knee over the other, on which they hold the hand that contains the elbow, whose hand goes to support the bearded chin of some bent old man.

# How one should draw nudes

<margin>x</margin>
When you draw nudes, ensure that you always sketch them as a whole and then finish the limb that seems best to you, and which has a good relationship with the other limbs. Take care not to make them over-muscular, so that they look like wood <note>Leonardo often warned against "woody" figures—drawings where muscles are so exaggerated and stiff that they lose the appearance of soft, living flesh.</note>; otherwise, the nudes will feel devoid of grace. In doing so, you would create nudes that look like sacks of walnuts <note>original: "sacchi di noci"</note>, regardless of how much they are filled with walnuts, or like sacks of melons <note>original: "sacchi di poponi"</note>, regardless of how much they are filled with melons. For this reason, let the muscles be kept in their proper measure, so that one does not bulge out merely to fill another, but rather let them appear as they are in those who provide the movement, in the manner that nudes should. But if you do not follow the proper measure, you will not be able to give the nudes grace, nor will you give the nudes the proper measure, nor will you maintain the balance of the weights in such a way that the limbs are filled from within; for it would not be given by the proper measure because the proper...

# [ON RELIEF IN PAINTING. — THE NATURE OF SHADOWS. SHADOWS FROM SPECIFIC LIGHT SOURCES].

->OF GIVING AID WITH ARTIFICIAL LIGHTS AND SHADOWS<-
->TO THE FEIGNED RELIEF OF PAINTING<-

To increase the relief in your painting, you should place—between the feigned figure and the nearby object that receives its shadow—a line of bright light that divides the figure from the darkened object. And on that same object, you shall make a light area after two light parts <note>This likely refers to a graduation of light where the shadow is "sandwiched" by brightness to make it pop.</note> that surround the shadow cast on the wall by the opposing figure. And take care to frequently do this for those limbs that you want to appear somewhat separated from their body; especially when the arms cross the chest, ensure that between the impact of the arm's shadow on the chest and the arm's own shadow, there remains a bit of light. This makes it appear as if the light passes through the space between the chest and the arm. And the more you want the arm to appear distant from the chest, the larger you should make that light. Always strive to arrange bodies against backgrounds so that the dark parts of the bodies end against a light background, and the illuminated parts of the body end against a light <gloss>dark</gloss> background <note>Leonardo corrects himself here: light should be set against dark, and dark against light, to create contrast.</note>.

->OF SURROUNDING BODIES<-
->WITH VARIOUS LINES OF SHADOW<-

Ensure that the shadows cast upon the surfaces of bodies by various objects always undulate with various twists, according to the variety of the limbs that create the shadows and of the thing that receives that shadow.

->OF THE NATURE OF SHADOW IN ITSELF<-

Shadow is of the nature of universal things, which are all more powerful at their beginning and weaken toward their end. I speak of the beginning of every form and quality, evident and non-evident, and not of things led from a small beginning to a great growth over time—such as a great oak which had a weak beginning from a small acorn. Rather, I would say the oak is most powerful at its birth from the earth, which is to say at its greatest thickness. Therefore, shadow—darkness is the first degree of shadow, and light is the last. Therefore, you, the painter, shall make the shadow darkest near its cause, and make its end convert into light, so that it appears to have no end <note>This describes "sfumato," Leonardo’s famous technique of smoky, blurred transitions where shadow dissolves into light without hard edges.</note>.

->HOW SHADOWS MADE BY SPECIFIC LIGHTS<-
->SHOULD BE AVOIDED BECAUSE THEIR ENDS ARE SIMILAR TO THEIR BEGINNINGS<-

Shadows made by the sun or other specific lights <note>By "specific lights," Leonardo means point sources like a candle or direct sunlight, which create harsh, unflattering edges.</note> are without grace for the body they accompany, because they leave the parts divided in a confused way with an evident boundary between shadow and light. And these shadows are of equal power at the end as they are at the beginning.

---

### OF GIVING AID, WITH ARTIFICIAL LIGHTS AND SHADOWS, TO THE FEIGNED RELIEF OF PAINTING.

To increase the relief in a painting, you shall take care to place—between the feigned figure and the neighboring thing that receives its shadow—a line of clear light that separates the figure from the obscured object; and on the same object, you shall make light after two light parts, between which lies the shadow cast on the wall by the opposing figure. And take care to often do this [for] the limbs that you wish to appear somewhat separate from their body, and especially when the arms cross the chest, ensure that between the place where the shadow of the arm strikes the chest and the arm's own shadow, there remains a little light which appears to pass through the space between the chest and the arm. And as much as you want the arm to appear more distant from the chest, so much larger shall you make the said light. And see that you strive to arrange bodies on their backgrounds in such a way that the part of these *bod* bodies which is dark ends in a light background and the part of the body that is lit ends in a light [dark] background ².

### OF ENCIRCLING BODIES WITH VARIOUS LINEAMENTS OF SHADOW.

Ensure that always the shadows made upon the surfaces of bodies by various objects are undulating, with various twists, by means of the diversity of the limbs that make the shadows and of the things that receive this shadow ³.

### OF THE BEING [manner of being] OF SHADOW IN ITSELF.

Shadow is of the nature of universal things, which are all more powerful at the beginning and weaken toward the end. I speak of the beginning of all forms and qualities, visible and invisible, and not of things led from a small beginning to a great growth through time, such as a great oak, which had the weak beginning of a small acorn; I will even say that the oak is more powerful at its birth from the earth, that is to say, at its greatest thickness. Therefore, *shadow and darkness are the first degree of shadow, and the bright light* ["luce"] *is the last; therefore, you, painter, shall make the shadow darkest near its cause, and its end, make it convert into bright light, that is to say, let it appear without end* ⁴.

### HOW THE SHADOWS MADE BY SPECIFIC LIGHTS SHOULD BE AVOIDED, BECAUSE THEIR ENDS ARE SIMILAR TO THEIR BEGINNINGS.

Shadows made by the sun or other specific lights are without grace for the body they accompany, given that they confusedly leave the parts separated with a visible boundary of shadow and light. And the shadows are of similar power at the end as at the beginning ⁵.

### Of the voice and how it is made
### Why the voice is resonant

The voice is produced by the winds of the lungs, which first send the air through the path of the windpipe <note>original: "gola de polmoni" — literally the "throat of the lungs."</note>; this air, by reason of its percussion within the cartilages and the larynx <term>guscio della gola<gloss>literally "the shell of the throat," Leonardo’s term for the larynx or voice box</gloss></term>, creates the sound. This sound will be more or less high-pitched or low depending on whether the opening of that larynx tightens or widens. This opening is closed or opened by means of the muscles that wrap around the rings of cartilage in the throat. This sound, having been made in the larynx, comes striking through the channel of the throat and, arriving in the mouth, takes the form of the voice with the help of the tongue and other muscles of the mouth. These muscles, through their various movements, vary the mouth's channel, the throat, and the interior of the mouth into various and diverse shapes, as will be shown in the treatise on the voice. And because such a voice resonates better in empty spaces than in full ones—and this will be proven by the principle of the reverberation <note>original: "rinchuossione" — the rebounding or echoing of air against a surface.</note> of the air—it is true that such a voice would be little heard if it were not for the emptiness of the mouth, because the air strikes within the mouth in various shapes and is thus reverberated in the larynx. This reverberation creates that vibration <note>original: "ronzo" — literally a hum or buzz.</note> that you feel in the chest and in the throat of one who speaks; the same thing happens in organs where the wind is struck in the mouth of the pipe.

---

### How the throat makes high and low sounds
### With the reverberation of the voice

The larynx, which is muscular and cartilaginous, tightens as it rises and makes a high-pitched sound; as it lowers, it widens and makes a low sound. This sound reverberates within the cavities of the larynx and, resonating in this way, comes out through the channel of the throat.

---

### On the lowing of oxen

Oxen have throat muscles of a different shape than those of man, and for this reason, they cannot speak with an articulated voice as man does. However, they have a very wide larynx; because of this width, the air reverberates for a long space of time, and in this reverberating, it generates the lowing, which is resonant and deep. This is because the air does not exit through a channel as narrow as that of a man, and for this reason, while resonating in the chest, it does not reverberate as frequently as that of a man. It reverberates infrequently because the throat muscles of oxen cannot tighten to such a thinness as those of a man, as their muscles are thick and powerful <note>original: "uirulenti" — likely meaning strong/fibrous rather than "virulent" in the modern sense.</note>. To allow the air to reverberate in diverse ways, the muscles of the throat must be agile and capable of diverse movements, so that the air reverberates against the muscles of the throat; this true sound will be discussed in the treatise on the voice of the throat and will be proven through the anatomy of oxen and men.

---

### How the voice is low and high

The voice will be higher the more the muscles of the throat are tightened, and it will be lower the wider the muscles are; it will be more resonant the firmer the muscles are. In the treatise on the voice, it will be seen that the muscles of the throat are of diverse kinds because the muscles are of various shapes; the muscles of the human throat are of different shapes than those of oxen, and the muscles of the throats of those who speak or sing are of various shapes, as are those of the throat of one who cries out or one who sighs.

<summary>Leonardo analyzes the anatomical mechanics of the human voice, attributing pitch to the tightening of the larynx and resonance to the reverberation of air in the mouth and chest, while comparing these structures to the anatomy of oxen.</summary>
<keywords>anatomy of the voice, larynx, vocal cords, acoustics, reverberation, comparative anatomy, oxen, phonetics, windpipe</keywords>

# [SHADOW AND LIGHT. — THE TRIANGLE WITHOUT SHADOW].

### WHAT SHADOW AND LIGHT ARE
Shadow is the privation of light and merely the opposition of dense bodies to luminous rays. Shadow is of the nature of darkness; light is of the nature of clarity. One is a privation, the other a demonstration. They are always in company, joined to bodies. Shadow has greater power than light, because it prohibits and entirely deprives bodies of light, whereas light can never totally drive away the shadow from bodies—that is, from dense bodies <note>Scholarly references: G. Manzi, p. 274; H. Ludwig, vol. II, no. 549; J.-P. Richter, vol. I, no. 119.</note>.

<margin>
[1st fig.:] Separated shadow and attached shadow.
[2nd fig.:] Separated shadow, invisible.
</margin>

### THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN SHADOW ATTACHED TO BODIES AND SEPARATED SHADOW
Attached shadow <note>original: "onbra congiunta" — the shadow that sits directly on the object itself, often called "form shadow" today.</note> is that which never departs from illuminated bodies, such as a ball which, when placed in the light, always has a part of itself occupied by shadow; this shadow never separates regardless of how the ball is moved. Separated shadow <note>original: "onbra separata" — what we now call a "cast shadow."</note> may or may not be created by the body. Let us suppose the ball is at a distance of one <term>braccio<gloss>An Italian unit of measurement, literally "an arm," approximately 23 to 27 inches.</gloss></term> from a wall, and the light is on the opposite side. This light will cast onto the wall exactly as much expansion of shadow as is found on the part of the ball facing the wall. The part of the separated shadow that does not appear occurs when the light is beneath the ball; in this case, the shadow goes toward the sky and, finding no resistance along its path, it is lost <note>Scholarly references: G. Manzi, p. 297; H. Ludwig, vol. II, no. 616; J.-P. Richter, vol. I, no. 125.</note>.

[3rd fig.:] g h l m n i p q k [4th fig.:] a b c d e c f

### THE OPINION OF SOME THAT A TRIANGLE CASTS NO SHADOW ON A WALL
There have been some mathematicians who have held for certain that a triangle with its base turned toward the light casts no shadow upon a wall. They prove this in the following way, saying: No spherical body smaller than the light can reach the halfway point with its shadow. Luminous lines travel in straight paths; therefore, let us say the light is **g-h**, the triangle is **l-m-n**, and the wall is **i-k**. They say the light at **g** sees the face of the triangle **l-n** and the part of the wall **i-q**, and likewise **h** sees, like **g**, the face **l-m**, and then sees **m-n** and the wall **p-q-k**. If the entire wall is seen by the light **g-h**, it follows that the triangle must be without shadow, and that which has no shadow cannot cast one. This seems believable in this case, unless the triangle **n-p-q** were seen by two lights **g** and **h**. But **i-p** and likewise **q-k** are each seen only by a single light; that is, **i-p** cannot be seen by **h**, and **q-k** will never be seen by **g**. Therefore, the area **p-q** will be twice as bright as the two neighboring spaces that contain shadow <note>Scholarly reference: J.-P. Richter, vol. I, no. 199. Richter notes that the end of this paragraph has been previously translated incorrectly in other editions.</note>.

<summary>Leonardo defines the fundamental relationship between light and shadow, distinguishing between "attached" (form) shadows and "separated" (cast) shadows. He then critiques a mathematical theory regarding why a triangle might appear not to cast a shadow when illuminated by two light sources.</summary>

<keywords>optics, cast shadow, form shadow, light source, geometry, triangle, braccio, mathematical proof, chiaroscuro</keywords>

# — FOLIO 22 (recto). — Ms 2038 BIB. NAT.

<margin>
On the motion of vision
</margin>

If a single thing is viewed through two <term>apertures<gloss>original: "spiracoli" — Leonardo uses this term to refer to the pupils of the eyes as openings through which light and images enter.</gloss></term>, that same thing will appear doubled, and it will be near the eye, as is demonstrated here. These two apertures are the two eyes of man. The object that appears doubled will be the one that is near the apertures, and the one that is remote will appear <term>single<gloss>original: "scempia" — an archaic term for simple or unpaired, the opposite of doubled.</gloss></term> for the reason illustrated below between *m* and *n*.

<margin>
apertures
apertures
pyramid of vision
eye of the observer
</margin>

If two eyes look at a single thing, any object that is between the eye and the thing being looked at will appear doubled. This occurs because it represents itself to each eye within two different rays—that is, between the line of sight of each eye and the thing being observed. This is seen in the figure below, where *f* is placed near the eyes and the thing being observed is *e*. *f* will be seen between *f* and *d* by one eye, while the other eye sees it between *f* and *c*; because of this, the object *f* appears doubled, being seen one toward *c* and the other toward *d*. The true cause is the straight line from the center of each eye to the object being observed, which is the line along which the object is seen as single.

---

<note>Geometrical diagrams illustrating the principles of binocular vision and diplopia (double vision). The diagrams show how an intermediate object (f or b) is projected onto different points of the background (c, d or k, m) when focusing on a distant point (e or c).</note>

---

That object which is placed in the middle of the <term>pyramid of vision<gloss>original: "piramide del uedere" — a fundamental concept in Renaissance optics where visual rays form a pyramid with the eye as the apex and the object as the base.</gloss></term> will be doubled. This is because it is seen by both of the central lines of each eye, which go to the object being observed; each of these lines sees the object that is interposed between itself and the center of the observed object in two different places.

For if eye *a* looks at object *c*, its central line *a-c* sees the interposed object *b* at the position *k*; and eye *d* looks at the same object *c*, and its central line *d-c* sees the object *b* at the position *m*. Because of this, it appears as two. And if you were to look at object *b* with both eyes, then object *c* would appear as two for the same reason, because the line *a-b* sees object *c* at position *p*, and the line *d-b* sees object *c* at position *f*.

<summary>This page explores the geometry of binocular vision, specifically explaining how objects appear doubled (diplopia) when they are positioned in front of or behind the point of focus. Leonardo uses precise diagrams to show how the intersection of visual rays from both eyes creates these shifting projections against a background.</summary>
<keywords>optics, binocular vision, diplopia, pyramid of vision, visual rays, central line, geometry of sight, perspective</keywords>

-> [IMAGINATION. — THE FUNCTIONS OF THE EYE. — COLOR PERSPECTIVE. — BALANCE]. <-

### WAY TO INCREASE AND AWAKEN THE MIND TO VARIOUS INVENTIONS
I will not hesitate to include among these precepts a new invention for speculation which, although it may seem small and almost worthy of ridicule, is nonetheless of great utility in awakening the mind to various inventions. And this is: if you look at certain walls stained with various spots or stones of mixed colors, and you have to invent some scene, you will be able to see in them the resemblance of various landscapes adorned with mountains, rivers, rocks, trees, great plains, valleys, and hills in diverse ways. You will also be able to see there various battles and the lively actions of figures, strange expressions of faces, and costumes, and infinite things which you can then reduce to their complete and proper forms. It happens with such walls and mixtures as it does with the sound of bells: in their ringing, you will find every name and word that you can imagine.

### OF THE 10 FUNCTIONS OF THE EYE, ALL PERTAINING TO PAINTING
Painting extends to all ten functions of the eye, that is: **light, darkness, brightness, body, color, shape, location, distance, proximity, motion, and rest**. This little work of mine will be woven from these functions, reminding the painter by what rule and method he must imitate with his art all these things—the work of Nature and the *ornament of the world*.

### HOW THE PAINTER MUST PUT THE PERSPECTIVE OF COLORS INTO PRACTICE
To put into practice this perspective of varying and losing, or diminishing, the proper essence of colors, you shall take objects placed in the countryside at intervals of one hundred <term>braccia<gloss>Original: "braccia." An Italian unit of measurement, approximately 23 inches, originally based on the length of an arm.</gloss></term>, such as trees, houses, men, and plains. As for the first tree, you shall have a pane of glass fixed firmly, and let your eye be fixed likewise. On said glass, draw a tree following the form of that first tree. Then, move it to the side until the natural tree almost borders your drawing. Then, color your drawing so that in color and form it matches the other, and so that if you close one eye, both appear to be painted on said glass and at the same distance. Follow this same rule for the second and third trees, from hundred to hundred *braccia*, one by one. Let these serve as your <term>authorities<gloss>Original: "autori." Leonardo refers to these calibrated studies as "masters" or standard references for his future work.</gloss></term> and masters, always using them in your works where they belong; they will make the work recede well into the distance. However, I find as a rule that the second diminishes by 4/5 from the first when it is 20 *braccia* away from the first <note>Leonardo is calculating the specific ratio of atmospheric degradation and size reduction as distance increases.</note>.

### ON THE SERPENTINE LINE AND THE BALANCE OF FIGURES AND OTHER ANIMALS
Whatever figure or graceful animal you make, remember to avoid "woodenness"—that is, they should go about counterpoising and balancing themselves so that they do not appear like a piece of wood.

*Those you wish to depict as strong should not be made this way, except for the turning of the head upon the shoulders.*

### ON LINEAR PERSPECTIVE
Linear perspective shall be divided into three parts: the first shall be the principles of the diminution <note>The perceived reduction in size as objects recede.</note> of bodies at various distances; the second shall be the diminution of colors and their variety at different distances; the third shall be the diminution of the definition <term>notizie</term> <note>Literally "notices" or "knowledge"; Leonardo uses this to mean the clarity or distinctness of an object's details and edges.</note> of bodies and their boundaries at various distances.

<margin>ø</margin>
**How one must paint the air and the smoke.**

<margin>ø</margin>
**Of misty and smoky air and of its colors and variety.**
Air mixed with smoke is of much greater variety than air alone, and when mixed with mist it will also have a varied diversity, because smoky and misty air takes on the nature of smoke and mist.

<margin>ø</margin>
**In what way the air must be made to appear.**

<margin>ø</margin>
**Of the variety of the colors of the air:**
That air will be clearer which is seen through a shorter line <note>Meaning the line of sight passing through a thinner layer of the atmosphere.</note>, and this is proved by the ninth proposition of this work which says that the air will be all the clearer the more it is mixed with light, and all the darker the more it is mixed with darkness. The reason is this: the thicker the air is, the whiter it will be because it is mixed with more light, and the thinner it is, the bluer it will be because it is mixed with more of the darkness of the cold air <note>Leonardo believed the blue of the sky was caused by the darkness of outer space seen through the illuminated atmosphere.</note> that is above it, as is seen in the height of the sky. And if you paint clear air over the darkness of a mountain it will appear blue, and if it is over another clear air it will be white.

**In what way clouds are to be made.**

O you painter, who wish to make something appear between the vision and the eye by means of smoke, know that smoke is of the nature of mist; and like mist, when mixed with more light it will be whiter.

of the sun in the smoke

-> ON LINEAR PERSPECTIVE <-

Linear perspective consists in the function of visual lines, proving by measurement how much the second object is smaller than the first, and how much the third is smaller than the second, and so on by degrees until the end of the things seen. I find through experience that if the second object is as far from the first as the first is from your eye, even if they are of equal size, the second will be exactly half the size of the first <note>original: "fia altrettanto minore" - Leonardo describes a 1:2 ratio here.</note>. And if the third object—of equal size to the second and positioned in front of it—is as far from the second as the second is from the first, it will be half the size of the second. Thus, by degrees at equal distances, they will always diminish by half, provided that the interval does not exceed the number of 20 braccia <term>braccia</term> <note>A Florentine "braccio" (plural "braccia") was a unit of measurement roughly equal to 23 inches or 58 centimeters, representing the length of an arm.</note>. Within those 20 braccia, a figure equal to your own height will lose 4/5 of its size; at 40 braccia it will lose 9/10, and then 19/20 at 60 braccia. Thus, from stage to stage, it will diminish, provided the wall <note>The "parieta" refers to the picture plane—the flat surface upon which the artist paints.</note> is distant from you by twice your height; for placing it at only one height makes a great difference between the first braccia and the second.

-> ON PLACING THE FIRST FIGURE IN A NARRATIVE PAINTING <-

You shall make the first figure in the narrative <note>original: "storia" - in Renaissance art, this refers to a complex composition depicting a historical, biblical, or mythological scene.</note> smaller than life-size according to how many braccia you imagine it to be distant from the front line, and then determine the others in comparison to that one using the rule above.

-> I ASSIGN DEGREES TO THINGS OPPOSITE THE EYE JUST AS THE MUSICIAN ASSIGNS THEM TO VOICES OPPOSITE THE EAR <-

Although objects opposite the eye touch one another continuously, I will nonetheless establish my rule in intervals of 20 braccia, just as the musician has done with voices. Although the voice is continuous and joined together, he has nonetheless established degrees from voice to voice, calling them first, second, third, fourth, and fifth; and thus, from degree to degree, he has given names to the varieties of the rising and falling of the voice.

-> METHOD FOR GIVING FIGURES SHADOW IN HARMONY WITH LIGHT AND THE BODY <-

When you are painting a figure and you wish to see if the shadow is in harmony with the light—ensuring it is not more red or more yellow than the true nature of the color you wish to shade—do this: cast a shadow with your finger over the illuminated part of your work. If the accidental shadow <note>A "shadow" cast by a physical object (your finger) onto the painting to serve as a real-world reference point.</note> you have made is similar to the painted shadow on your work, it is correct. Then, by moving your finger closer or further away, you can create darker or lighter shadows, which you should always compare with your painted ones.

---

-> ON LINEAR PERSPECTIVE. <-

<note>The following section translates the French transcription provided in the original manuscript's modern scholarly apparatus.</note>

Linear perspective consists in the function of visual lines, proving by measurement how much the second thing is less than the first, and how much the third is less than the second, and so on from degree to degree, until the end of things seen. I find by experience that if the second thing is as distant from the first as the first is from your eye, although they are of the same size, the second will be once smaller than the first; and if the third thing, of the same size as the second and situated in front of it, is as far from it as the second is from the first, it will have half the size of the second. And thus, from degree to degree, at equal distances, there will always be diminutions by half, the second [being half] of the first [and so on], provided that the interval does not reach the number of 20 brasses <note>French: "brasses" - equivalent to the Italian braccia.</note>; and at the said 20 brasses, the figure similar to you will lose 4/5 of its size, then at 40 it will lose 9/10, then 19/20 at 60 brasses; and so from step to step it will diminish, by distancing the wall from you at twice your size, for to do so [distance it] by only one makes [already] a great difference, from the first brasses to the second.

-> ON PLACING A FIRST FIGURE IN THE NARRATIVE. <-

You will make the first figure in the narrative smaller than nature by as many brasses as you represent it distant from the first line, and then you will take the others in comparison to this first one, with the rule above.

-> I GIVE THE DEGREES OF THINGS OPPOSITE THE EYE AS THE MUSICIAN [GIVES THOSE] OF THE VOICES [RESONANCES] OPPOSITE THE EAR. <-

Although things opposite the eye touch one another step by step, I will nevertheless make my rule from 20 to 20 brasses, as the musician has done for voices, who, although they are united and attached together, has nevertheless placed degrees from voice to voice, calling them first, and: 2nd, 3rd, 4th, and 5th, and thus from step to step and degree to degree has placed [given] names to the varieties of the raising and lowering of the voice.

-> MANNER OF MAKING THE SHADOW OF FIGURES IN ACCORD WITH THEIR LIGHT AND THEIR BODY. <-

When you make a figure and you want to see if the shadow is the companion of the light, [so] that it is not either more red or [more] yellow than is the essential nature of the color you want to shade, you will do thus: make the shadow with your finger on the lit part and if the accidental shadow made by you is similar to the natural shadow made by the finger on your work, it will be well, then with the finger closer or further, make darker or lighter shadows, always comparing them with yours.

f. 23r

# Of the nature of the air

Whether it is possible for the air to be condensed or not—let those who deny such a thing is possible explain. For if it were not possible to condense or rarefy <term>rarefy</term> <note>To make air less dense, the opposite of condensation.</note> the air, its nature would be such that motion could not take place through it. This is because, in motion, the air opens up before that which moves; and if the air did not condense, the moving object would have to push as much air ahead of itself as the space it occupies. Thus, it would continue pushing all the way to the edge of the atmosphere. If this were not possible, it would be necessary for the air moved by the object to push an equal amount of air in front of it, and that air to push the next, all the way to the end of the sphere of air—so that it would be necessary to move a mass as large as the entire atmosphere. Furthermore, if even a small amount of air were removed from a tiny space, it would be necessary for all the air in the world above it to move to fill that vacuum <note>original: "vacuo"</note>. This is contrary to reason. However, if air condenses, it moves within itself, fleeing the motion of whatever strikes it and condensing as it flees. Subsequently, that air flees and the neighboring air condenses likewise. In this way, step by step, the air fills the space left by the body moving through it. The air struck by the motion flees into itself and into the other air adjacent to it.

# Of the motion of the air

If air is forced out of a small hole, that air expands in great quantity through the surrounding air. Furthermore, the air moves in various directions among the branches of forests and inside houses.

# Whether air holds weight within itself or not

If it did not have weight, it would not offer the resistance it does to one who moves swiftly through it. Furthermore, if it were not condensable—if it were of a nature similar to water, which, although it does not condense <note>Leonardo correctly observed that water is nearly incompressible compared to air.</note>, still offers resistance to speed—then one who was in water could not move with as much speed as if they were in the air, because of the density of the material of water, which is impossible to condense. And the air would act in the same way if it did not condense.

# Whether air has weight

Proof of how air has weight: because if it did not have weight, a bird could not support itself upon it, nor would the surrounding air open to make room for the air moved by the flight of that bird. And if it did not have weight, it would not move from high to low, nor in any other direction, unless it were forced. Let them tell us, then, where the wind comes from—which is air moved from one part to another. Furthermore, if air were not heavy, it would be distributed equally throughout the entire world without being denser in one place than in another.

<summary>Leonardo argues for the physical properties of air, using logical deduction to prove that air must be both compressible and heavy to allow for motion, wind, and the flight of birds.</summary>
<keywords>air, physics, compression, weight, atmospheric pressure, resistance, flight, fluid dynamics, vacuum</keywords>

-> WHY AN OBJECT PLACED CLOSE TO THE EYE LEAVES ITS OUTLINES INDISTINCT <-

[3rd fig.:] a b c d
For all those things placed before the eye that are too close to it, it will happen that their <term>outlines</term> <note>original: "termini", referring to the edges or boundaries of an object.</note> cannot be discerned except confusedly. This is similar to what happens with objects close to a light source, which cast a large and blurry shadow. This same effect occurs when judging objects externally in all cases of linear perspective. It is similar to light; the reason is that the eye creates a <term>master line</term> <note>The central axis of vision where sight is sharpest.</note> which, with distance, widens and embraces with true knowledge large things far away, just as it does small things close by. 

But because the eye emits a multitude of lines that surround this principal median line—which are less powerful at perceiving the truth the further they are from the center of that circular path—it happens that an object placed very near the eye is not at a sufficient distance for the master line to encompass its outlines. Therefore, those outlines must fall upon the lines of weak perception. These lines serve the office of the eye much like <term>braques</term> <note>A type of pointing dog used in hunting.</note> in a hunt, which flush out the prey but cannot catch it; thus, these lines cannot "catch" the object but are the reason that the master line turns toward the things flushed out by those lines.

### How the limbs should be aided by the fading and wrapping of folds.

[1st fig.:] b a c
From b [to] a there is one head, and likewise from c [to] a; and this takes place when the elbow forms a right angle.

> [2nd fig.:] How 2 lights, between which a body is located from 2 sides, forming low pyramids, leave it without shadow.

Why the eye, having seen brightness, finds a place of medium light to appear dark, and similarly having come out of the darkness, a place of medium light appears very bright.

### WHY THE THING PLACED NEAR THE EYE LEAVES ITS OUTLINES INDISTINCT.

[3rd fig.:] a b c d
For all things facing the eye that are too close to it, it is necessary that their outlines are discerned only confusedly, as happens with things near the light, which cast a large and confused shadow; and thus it happens to one who is judging things outside. In all cases of linear perspective, it is similar to light, and the reason for it is that the eye creates a master line, which at a distance widens, and embraces with true knowledge large things from afar, as it does small things from nearby. But because the eye emits a multitude of lines that surround this principal median, which are all the less powerful to know the truth as they find themselves further from the center in this [conical] circulation, it happens that the thing placed near the eye—not being at that distance close to the master line capable of encompassing the outlines of the thing—these outlines must find themselves in the lines of weak comprehension. These are for the office of the eye like the pointing dogs in the hunt, which flush the game and cannot take it; thus these cannot take, but are causes for the master line to turn to the things flushed by these lines. Consequently, the things whose outlines are judged by these lines are blurred.

The entire nature of the eye is formed only for the straight line which departs from the eye and goes to the object; and along such a line the simulacra of things approach the eye. But of these simulacra there is only one that is straight among the <unclear>thousands</unclear> <note>original: "milite"; likely a variant of "migliaia" (thousands), referring to the infinite number of possible lines of sight.</note> of those lines, and this is the one that passes through the center of the light <note>referring to the pupil or the central axis of vision</note> of that eye. Lights do the same when they send their rays through small <term>spiracles</term> <note>original: "sspiracoli"; small openings or apertures.</note>, through which only one ray passes for each hole that is straight and passes through the center of that hole, which is inside the <term>camera</term> <note>original: "camera"; referring to a darkened chamber or room, the basis of the "camera obscura."</note> or upon the air. But why do the simulacra of things widen once they have passed through the holes? This occurs because the rays by which they are carried cross each other, and not because the images themselves expand.

<summary>Leonardo analyzes the linear propagation of light through small apertures, explaining that the apparent expansion of images (simulacra) after passing through a hole is caused by the crossing of rays at a central point rather than the light itself spreading out. This provides a geometric foundation for his understanding of both the human eye and the camera obscura.</summary>

### [EXERCISES FOR THE MEMORY — ACCURATE REPRESENTATIONS — GOOD POSES]

#### ON THE WAY TO LEARN WELL BY HEART
When you wish to know something you have studied well by heart, follow this method: when you have drawn the same thing so many times that it seems you know it by heart, try to do it without the model. On the other hand, have a tracing made on a thin, flat glass of your model, and place it over the thing you have reproduced from <note>original: "san ta sto", likely a corruption of "di fantasia" (from imagination)</note> without the model. Note well where the tracing does not match your drawing; and where you find you have erred, keep it in mind so as not to err again. Rather, return to the model to represent that erroneous part so many many times that you have it well in your <term>imagination</term> <note>In the Renaissance, the "imagination" was considered a specific mental faculty that stored and manipulated visual images.</note>. And if you cannot have flat glass to trace a thing, take a very thin piece of kidskin <note>parchment</note>, well-oiled and then dried; and when you have used it for one drawing, you can erase it with a sponge and make the second.

#### ON THE WAY TO REPRESENT A SITE CORRECTLY
Have a glass as large as half a "royal" sheet of paper and fix it well before your eyes—that is, between the eye and the thing you wish to represent. Then position your eye at a distance of 2/3 of a <term>braccio</term> <note>A "braccio" (plural *braccia*) was an Italian unit of measurement roughly equal to the length of an arm, approximately 23 inches or 58 cm.</note> from said glass and fix your head with an instrument in such a way that you cannot move your head at all. Then, close or cover one eye and, with a brush and some ground <term>hematite</term> <note>original: "matita" / "lapis"; refers to red chalk or iron ore used for drawing.</note>, mark on the glass what appears beyond it. Then trace from the glass onto paper, pounce it <note>A method of transferring a drawing by pricking holes in the outlines and dusting them with charcoal powder.</note> onto good paper, and paint it if you like, thereafter making good use of <term>aerial perspective</term> <note>The technique of representing distance by making objects paler, bluer, and less distinct.</note>.

#### TO LEARN TO MAKE A FIGURE POSE WELL
If you want to accustom yourself well to correct and good poses of figures, fix a square frame or chassis, divided on the inside into squares with thread, between your eye and the nude model you are representing. You shall make those same squares lightly on the paper where you wish to draw said nude. Then, place a small ball of wax in a part of the grid to serve as a sight-point which you will always align, when looking at the nude, with the pit of the throat <note>original: "fontanela della gola"; the suprasternal notch.</note>. And if the model is turned backward, align it with one of the "knots" <note>the vertebrae</note> of the neck. These threads will teach you all the parts of the body that, in every action, are found below the pit of the throat, below the angles of the shoulders, below the breasts, hips, and other parts of the body. The transverse lines of the grid will show you how much higher it is when posing on one leg than on the other, and likewise for the hips, knees, and feet. But always fix the grid by a perpendicular line, and in effect, make sure that all the parts of the grid occupied by the nude are taken up by your drawn nude within the drawn grid. The drawn squares can be as much smaller than those of the grid as you wish your figure to be smaller than life-size. Then, keep in mind for the figures you make the rule of the correspondence of the limbs as the grid has shown them to you. The grid should be 3 and a half <term>braccia</term> high and 3 wide, distant from you by 7 <note>The original manuscript is unclear on this number.</note> <term>braccia</term> and one <term>braccio</term> away from the nude.

<margin>24</margin>

### On the nature of the voice

The natural voice is produced when the trachea <note>original: "trāca"</note> is of a uniform width throughout its entire length and is free from any constrictions of the throat.
A forceful voice is produced when the trachea diminishes in its width, giving way to the larynx <note>original: "laringie"</note>, which width
diminishes in the same manner, only lacking the strength of the throat. A harsh voice is produced when the trachea
is made rough by viscous humor <note>In Renaissance medicine, "humors" were bodily fluids thought to govern health and physical properties; here, Leonardo refers to mucus.</note> or when it is affected by herbs or another fluid that, in passing, moves
upward, and which fluid hinders the motion of the air of the voice. A sweet voice is produced when the trachea
is clean and the humors are of a uniform consistency, which humors serve to sweeten the passages of the voice.
A <term>low</term> <note>original: "grue", meaning "grave" or deep-pitched.</note> voice is produced when the trachea is large and open in the passages of the throat; and likewise, it becomes <term>high-pitched</term> <note>original: "acuta", meaning acute or shrill.</note> by
lacking that width of the throat. And the voice will be low when it is driven with a vigorous motion of moist
air; and likewise, the voice will be high-pitched when it is driven with a swift motion of dry and thin air.

### On the nature of the modes of the voice

The first mode of the voice occurs when the voice lacks width of the throat and is pushed with a diminishing motion; and the 
<unclear>second</unclear> <note>The OCR reads "quāto" (how much/fourth), but the numerical sequence suggests this is the second mode.</note> mode of the voice occurs when the voice lacks length of the throat, lacks width, and is pushed with a diminishing
motion of air. The third mode occurs when the voice is grounded in the width of the throat and lacks air in the
motion of that voice. The fourth mode occurs when the voice lacks its width and lacks the motion of air, and
is grounded in the length of the throat. The fifth mode occurs when the voice lacks the length of the throat and is produced with
an eloquence of width of that throat and pushed with a swift motion of air. The voice that lacks width and lacks length
and is pushed by a lack of air produces the sixth voice. The seventh voice occurs when the voice is grounded in width.

### On the nature of the voice and its variety

The voice lacks power when it lacks velocity in the motion of the air through the passages of
the throat, and lacks the width of that throat, and lacks the length of that throat. The voice is grounded in
power when it is pushed out of the throat with a swift motion of air, with width of the throat, and with length of that throat.
The voice lacks power when it lacks the length of that throat, lacks width, and lacks the
motion of air. Another voice occurs when the voice lacks length and lacks the motion of air, and is grounded
in its width. Another voice occurs when the voice lacks width and is grounded in length, and lacks the
motion of air. Another voice occurs when the voice lacks width and lacks length, and is grounded in the
motion of air. Another voice occurs when the voice is grounded in its length and grounded in its width, and
lacks the motion of air. Another voice occurs when the voice is grounded in length and grounded in the motion
of air, and lacks its width. Another voice occurs when the voice is grounded in its width and 
grounded in the motion of air, and lacks its length. Another voice occurs when the voice is grounded in its
length and grounded in its width, and grounded in the motion of air. The voice is of little power when it lacks
width, lacks length, and lacks the motion of air; and the more the voice is of little power, the more it lacks
motion of air, lacks width, and lacks length.

<summary>Leonardo categorizes the various qualities of the human voice—such as sweetness, harshness, and pitch—by analyzing the physical dimensions of the trachea and the behavior of air and "humors" within the throat.</summary>
<keywords>acoustics, anatomy, voice production, trachea, larynx, humors, vocal pitch, Leonardo da Vinci, physiology of sound</keywords>

## [PAINTING IS SUPERIOR TO SCULPTURE. — THE MIRROR AS THE MASTER OF PAINTERS].

<margin>4</margin> [Continued from folio 25 recto:] We know well that he who is practical and skilled will not make such errors; on the contrary, with sound rules, he will remove so little at a time that he will guide his work well. Furthermore, if the sculptor works in clay or wax, he can remove and add; and when the thing is finished, it is easily cast in bronze. This is the final and most permanent operation that sculpture has; for that which is only of marble is subject to ruin, but not bronze. Therefore, painting done on copper—which, as I told you regarding painting <note>The original text says "painting" here, but Leonardo likely meant "sculpture," as corrected in the French notes.</note>, allows for removing and adding—is equal to bronze. For when you first made the work in wax, you could still remove and add. If this sculpture in bronze is eternal, this [painting] on copper and glass is most eternal. If bronze remains black and ugly, this painting is full of various and charming colors and infinite varieties, as I have said above. And if you wished to speak only of painting done on wood panels, I would be content to judge between it and sculpture, saying that painting is more beautiful, possesses more imagination <note>original: "fantasia"</note>, and is more abundant, while sculpture is more durable, but nothing else. Sculpture shows what it is with little effort; painting seems a miraculous thing, making impalpable things appear palpable, flat things appear in relief, and near things appear distant. In fact, painting is adorned with infinite speculations <note>In this context, "speculations" refers to deep intellectual study and scientific observation of the natural world.</note> that sculpture does not employ.

->HOW THE MIRROR IS THE MASTER OF PAINTERS<-

When you want to see if your painting as a whole conforms to the thing portrayed from nature, take a mirror and reflect the living thing within it. Compare the reflected object with your painting and consider well if the subject of both likenesses conforms with one another. Above all, the mirror should be taken as your master—specifically the flat mirror—because on its surface, things have a resemblance to painting in many aspects. That is to say, just as you see a painting made on a flat plane show things that appear in relief, the mirror on a flat plane does the same. The painting is a single surface, and the mirror is the same. The painting is impalpable, in that what appears round and detached cannot be surrounded by the hands, and the mirror does the same. The mirror and the painting show the likenesses of things surrounded by light and shadow. Both appear to exist far beyond their surfaces. And if you realize that the mirror makes things appear detached through the use of outlines, shadows, and lights—and if you have among your colors shadows and lights more powerful than those of the mirror—certainly, if you know how to compose your painting well, it too will appear as a natural thing seen in a large mirror.

***

<note>3. References: G. Manzi, p. 205; H. Ludwig, vol. I, no. 408; J.-P. Richter, vol. I, no. 529.</note>

<summary>Leonardo argues that painting is superior to sculpture because it can intellectually represent depth and atmosphere, and he promotes the flat mirror as the ultimate objective tool for artists to verify the realism of their work.</summary>

<meta>On the previous page (folio 24 recto), Leonardo concluded a comparison between painting and sculpture, arguing that while sculpture is more durable, painting is more mentally sophisticated and capable of representing a wider variety of natural phenomena. <page-num>f. 24v</page-num>
<header>Ms 2038 — FOLIO 24 (verso). — National Library</header>

One cannot say that, in the eye, the space of the object <term>vanishes<note>original: "anichilli" — literally 'annihilates' or turns to nothing; Leonardo uses it here to describe how objects appear to disappear at a distance.</note></term> because of distance in the same way the object itself vanishes. For if you keep the eye steady, just as in the air the <term>likenesses<note>original: "similitudine" — the visual images or "species" that Leonardo believed objects radiate through the air to reach the eye.</note></term> of things become invisible due to distance, the air that is between the eye and the thing does not become invisible. Yet the air between the eye and the object is a thing just like the object, and it too has its own likeness which extends through the air between the eye and itself. And if those likenesses that depart from this air between the eye and the object do not <term>vanish<note>original: "anichilāno"</note></term>, why should those vanish that come from that object through that same air? 

And you see that if you keep the eye steady, the air does not vanish because of distance; therefore, neither will the likenesses of things vanish through that air. Thus, the air is the cause of such obscuring of the object, as it is that which, with its thickness, makes the space of said air the same color as the air at the same distance. Therefore, the object is seen less according to how much more air there is between itself and the eye.

->**How one should write about seeing**<-

When you render, by virtue of perspective, the air thicker than ordinary air, ensure that you make a space of air of the same thickness at one mile of distance from each other, and do the same for another two miles, and another three, and so on step by step. And let this ball <insert>M</insert> be a ball of mist, or of smoke, or of other dense, veiled bodies, and always keep doubling its thickness mile by mile. 

And if it is mist, at one mile's distance make it as clear as possible; and at two miles' distance make it thicker, and so on step by step make it thicker until the distance of a mile becomes so thick that the thing you see through it would be as light in color as ordinary air. Therefore, at three miles' distance there will be as much mist as is required to cover an object so that it becomes invisible, and so on, always doubling from one mile to the next in the same wind; and let there be a space of mist with less wind than would be needed to cover an object.

<summary>Leonardo discusses the physics of aerial perspective, arguing that objects disappear at a distance not because their "likenesses" cease to exist, but because the increasing density and thickness of the intervening air obscures them. He provides a practical rule for painters on how to systematically increase the density of mist or smoke over distances to achieve a realistic sense of depth.</summary>
<keywords>optics, aerial perspective, atmospheric density, likenesses, similitude, visibility, painting technique, mist, distance</keywords>

->[THE WRETCHED EXCUSE OF PAINTERS. — PAINTING IS SUPERIOR TO SCULPTURE].<-

---

ON THE WRETCHED EXCUSE MADE BY THE *wretched* WHO FALSELY AND UNWORTHILY CALL THEMSELVES PAINTERS.

There is a certain generation of painters who, because of their lack of study, must rely on the beauty of gold and <term>azure<note>original: "azuro" — Referring to lapis lazuli blue, which, like gold leaf, was an expensive material often used to compensate for poor technical skill.</note></term>. With the greatest foolishness, these men claim they do not produce good work because of the poor payments they receive; they pretend they would know how to do as well as any other if only they were well paid. Now look at these foolish people! Such men do not know how to produce a single good work and then say: "This one is for a high price, this one for a medium one, and this one is a cheap sort," thereby showing that they have work available for every price.

HOW SCULPTURE REQUIRES LESS <term>GENIUS<note>original: "ingiegnio" — This refers to the inventive power, intellect, or creative talent of the artist.</note></term> THAN PAINTING, AND LACKS MANY NATURAL ELEMENTS.

Engaging myself no less in sculpture than in painting, and practicing both to the same degree, it seems to me that I can, with little bias, give a judgment on which is of greater genius, difficulty, and perfection. First, sculpture is subject to certain lights—that is, from above—whereas painting carries its own light and shadow with it everywhere. Light and shadow are of the highest importance; therefore, in this case, the sculptor is aided by the nature of the <term>relief<note>original: "rilieuo" — The physical three-dimensional form of the statue.</note></term>, which generates these shadows for itself. The painter, however, creates them through "accidental art" <note>artificial technique</note> in the places where Nature would reasonably produce them. 

The sculptor cannot diversify the various natures of the colors of things; painting does not fail in any part. The perspectives of sculptors do not appear true at all; those of the painter appear to reach hundreds of miles beyond the work itself. <term>Aerial perspective<note>original: "prospettiva aerea" — The technique of representing distance by modifying colors and clarity to simulate the effect of the atmosphere.</note></term> is far from their work; they cannot represent transparent bodies, they cannot represent luminous things, nor reflected lines, nor shining bodies like mirrors and similar lustrous things, nor mists, nor dark weather, nor an infinite number of things that are not mentioned so as not to be tedious. 

As for the claim that sculpture is more resistant to time: although painting has a similar resistance when done upon thick copper covered in white <term>enamel<note>original: "smalto"</note></term>, and painted upon with enamel colors and returned to the fire to melt; this, for eternity, surpasses sculpture. One might say that where they <note>enamel painters</note> make an error, it is not easy to repair it; this is a wretched argument to try to prove that an irremediable mistake makes the work more worthy! But I will say plainly that it is more difficult to repair the genius of the master who makes such errors than it is to repair the work he has ruined. <note>The rest continues on folio 24 verso.</note>

### On birds that sustain themselves in the air
### and on the reason for their <term>flight<note>original: "uolita" — A term Leonardo used to describe the act or power of flying, derived from the Latin "volitare."</note></term>

Let there be a weight of air as great as the weight of the bird, just as the weight of a flying bird is of the air, just as the weight of that bird itself; because if the air did not move, the bird could not sustain itself there, because since that air offers no <term>resistance<note>original: "resistētia" — A fundamental concept in Leonardo's studies; he realized that air acts as a fluid medium that can be pushed against.</note></term>, the bird would immediately fall. Therefore, it can be sustained by nothing other than moved air which creates weight beneath the bird, just as the air above the bird is without weight, or truly is of lesser weight.

---

The flight of the bird is achieved through the swirling of the air, because the bird would not fly if the air did not give it resistance with its movement.

---

Because when the bird moves its wings, the air found beneath those wings becomes compressed; and by its nature, this air being <term>compressible<note>original: "cōpressibile" — Leonardo was among the first to recognize the elasticity and compressibility of air, comparing it to a spring.</note></term>, it desires to return to its original state and thus offers resistance to the bird's wings. This resistance made by the air pushes the bird upward, and this is the <term>foundation<note>original: "fōdamēto"</note></term> of all flight. The bird, therefore, by the movement of its wings, compresses the air beneath them; and the air, being by its nature compressible and wanting to return to its original state, gives resistance to the wings of the bird. 

And this is the foundation of all flight; and this can be seen in birds of great weight and small wings, such as a **crow**; or truly a bird of great weight and great wings, such as an **eagle**; or truly another bird of great weight and small wings, such as a **goose**; or truly another bird of great weight and great wings, such as an **eagle**; or truly another bird of great weight and small wings, such as a **goose**; or truly another bird of great weight and great wings, such as an **eagle**; or truly another bird of great weight and small wings, such as a **goose**; or truly another bird of great weight and great wings, such as an **eagle**; or truly another bird of great weight and small wings, such as a **goose**; or truly another bird of great weight and great wings, such as an **eagle**; or truly another bird of great weight and small wings.

<note>The repetitive nature of the final paragraph reflects Leonardo's process of refining his observations or perhaps a rhythmic quality to his drafting as he considers different species (crow, eagle, goose) as examples of the ratio between body mass and wing surface area.</note>

<summary>Leonardo explains the mechanical basis of flight, arguing that birds stay aloft by compressing the air beneath their wings, which then provides an upward resistance. He notes that this principle applies to various birds regardless of their weight or wing size, such as eagles, crows, and geese.</summary>

<header>[AERIAL PERSPECTIVE. — THE PAINTER MUST BE UNIVERSAL].</header>

### ON AERIAL PERSPECTIVE
There is another kind of perspective which I call aerial, because through the variations in the atmosphere one can recognize the distances of various buildings that are anchored at their base to a single line. This is like seeing many buildings beyond a wall, where all appear to rise above the distant edge of said wall at the same height. If you wished to make one appear further away than the other in a painting, you must represent an atmosphere that is somewhat <term>thick<note>original: "grossa" — Referring to atmospheric density or haze, which scatters light.</note></term>. You know that in such an atmosphere, the furthest things seen within it, such as mountains, appear <term>azure<note>original: "azura" — Leonardo was among the first to scientifically explain why distant mountains appear blue due to the thickness of the air between the eye and the object.</note></term>, almost the color of the air when the sun is in the east. Therefore, you should paint the first building beyond the wall in its own color; the one further away should be less defined and more azure. That which you want to be even further away, make it proportionally more azure; and that which you want to be five times further away, make it five times more azure. This rule will ensure that buildings appearing on a single line and of the same size will be clearly distinguished as to which is more distant and which is larger than the others.

### WHY THE PAINTER IS NOT PRAISEWORTHY 
### IF HE IS NOT UNIVERSAL
It can be clearly said that some are mistaken when they call a painter a "good master" who only does a head or a figure well. Certainly, it is no great feat if, by studying a single thing for the duration of one's life, one reaches some perfection in it. But we know that painting embraces and contains within itself all things produced by nature, all that results from the accidental actions of men, and ultimately, everything that can be perceived by the eyes. Therefore, he seems to me a <term>poor master<note>original: "tristo maestro" — Literally "sad" or "wretched," here meaning mediocre or limited in skill.</note></term> who only does one figure well. Do you not see how many and what kind of actions are performed by men alone? Do you not see how many different animals there are, as well as trees, herbs, flowers, landscapes, varieties of mountainous and flat sites, springs, rivers, cities, public and private buildings, tools suited to human use, various garments, ornaments, and arts? All these things should be executed with equal skill and quality by the one you wish to call a good painter.

### ON DRAWING
Which is better: to draw from nature or from the <term>antique<note>original: "anticho" — Referring to classical Greek and Roman sculptures, which were the standard for beauty and proportion during the Renaissance.</note></term>? Or: which is more difficult—the outlines or the shadows and lights? <note>Two crossed-out ovals appear before the first text and before the second title; a bar appears before the final sentence.</note>

# OF PAINTING

Why the **shadows** above the line of the **depth of the eyes** are darker than any other part of the face is proven thus: because the eyes are placed in such deep locations within the face that almost no light can reach into the dark recesses of those places. And because no light can penetrate into the depth of said eyes, no <term>species<note>original: "sspetie" — In Leonardo's time, "species" referred to the visual images or "likenesses" emitted by objects that travel through the air to the eye.</note></term> can be produced there, because no strike of light is possible. And because in those dark places no species is possible for the eyes, it is evident to you that where no species arrives, there is no line of vision; therefore, where there is no line of vision, the shadows appear dark. Because where no species is seen, the shadows appear black. Where no species is seen, there is the highest darkness which we call **black**, because where no species comes, no species is seen there; and where no species is seen, there is the maximum darkness which we call black, because where no species comes, no species is seen there.

**Vision**

### OF THE LIGHT THAT MUST BE SEEN IN THE EYES FROM MIRRORS

In the eye, no species of any thing is seen by itself unless it turns toward that part from which such species comes; therefore, the eye would always come to see the locations from which it [the species] comes into said eyes. If there were life in those species, the eye would then come to always see the parts of the eye, and the eye would see nothing there, because the eyes do not see except the object standing before them in a **straight line**, through which the darks can be seen as darks and the shadows as shadows. Because no species is seen there—and just as in the eye no species is seen where there has been no line of vision—so where a line of vision cannot come, no species can be seen, because light is not seen except by a **straight line**. Therefore, no species is seen in the greatest shadows, whereby the shadows appear black.

The mirrors [reflections] come to the light of the eye, or truly from the eye toward the eye seen; there is no true experiment of this.

<summary>Leonardo explains the optical reasons why eye sockets appear as the darkest parts of the face, arguing that light cannot reach these deep recesses to reflect an image or "species" back to the observer. He further details that vision only occurs along straight lines, which dictates how shadows and reflections are perceived in the human eye.</summary>
<keywords>optics, eye sockets, shadows, species, vision, straight lines, painting theory, light and shadow</keywords>
