### OF STUDYING WHILE YOU ARE AWAKE 
### OR BEFORE YOU FALL ASLEEP IN BED IN THE DARK

I have experienced it to be of no small benefit when you find yourself in the dark in bed to go over in the imagination the surface outlines of the forms previously studied, or other notable things encompassed by subtle <term>contemplation<note>original: "speculatione" — Leonardo uses this to mean deep, analytical observation or mental processing.</note></term>. And this is a truly laudable act and useful for confirming things in the memory.

### HOW THE PAINTER OUGHT TO BE DESIROUS TO HEAR 
### THE JUDGMENT OF EVERY MAN WHILE DOING HIS WORK

Certainly, one should not refuse the judgment of anyone while he is painting. For we know clearly that a man, even if he is not a painter, will have knowledge of the form of another man and will judge well if he is hunchbacked, or has one shoulder high or low, or if he has a large mouth or nose or other defects. And if we know that men can truly judge the works of Nature, how much more should we confess that they can judge our errors! For you know how much a man deceives himself in his own work; and if you do not recognize it in yourself, consider it in others and learn *at others' expense*, and you will profit from others' errors. So be eager and patient to hear the opinions of others. Consider well and think well if the critic has a reason or not to criticize you. If you find that he does, correct it; if you find he does not, act as if you did not hear him, or show him the reason—if he is a man you esteem—why he is mistaken.

### HOW IN WORKS OF IMPORTANCE A MAN SHOULD NOT TRUST 
### SO MUCH TO HIS MEMORY THAT HE DOES NOT DEIGN TO DRAW FROM NATURE

That master who would suggest that he can retain within himself all the forms and effects of Nature would certainly seem to me to be adorned with much ignorance, since said effects are infinite and our memory is not of such capacity that it suffices. Therefore, you painter, see to it that the greed for gain does not surpass in you the honor of the art, for the gain of honor is much greater than the honor of riches. So, for these and other reasons that could be said, you will first attend to giving the eye—through drawing—the demonstrative form of the intention and invention first made in your imagination. Then, go on removing or adding until you are satisfied. Afterward, have men arranged, clothed or naked, in the manner you have ordained for the work; and ensure that by measure and size subjected to perspective, nothing passes into the work that is not well-advised by reason and by natural effects. And this shall be the way to make yourself honored in your art.¹

That thing which is painted in white or black will appear in better <term>relief<note>original: "rilievo" — The quality of appearing three-dimensional or standing out from the flat surface.</note></term> than any other. Therefore, I remind you, painter, to clothe your figures in the lightest colors you can; for if you make them of dark color, they will have little relief and little evidence from a distance. And this is because the shadows of all things are dark. If you make a dark garment, there will be little variation between the lights and the shadows; but in light colors, there will be a great variation.

---

->OF STUDYING WHILE YOU ARE AWAKE OR BEFORE YOU FALL ASLEEP, IN BED, IN THE DARK.<-

I have experienced for myself that it is of no small utility, when you are in the dark in bed, to go on repeating in the imagination the surface outlines of forms previously studied, or other notable things understood through subtle contemplation; and this is an act properly laudable and useful for confirming things in the memory².

->HOW THE PAINTER OUGHT TO BE DESIROUS TO HEAR, WHILE DOING HIS WORK, THE JUDGMENT OF EVERY MAN.<-

Certainly there is no reason to refuse, while a man paints, the judgment of everyone, for we know well that a man, though he is not a painter, has a true notion of the form of another man, and will judge well if he is hunchbacked or has a high or low shoulder, or if he has a large mouth or nose [similarly], or other defects. And, if we know that men can judge with truth the works of Nature, how much more will it be appropriate to confess that they can judge our errors! For you know how much a man is mistaken in his own works, and if you do not know it in yourself, consider it in others and learn at the expense of others and you will profit from the errors of others. Be therefore desirous to hear with patience the opinions of others; and consider well and think well if he who blames has a cause or not to blame you. If you find that yes, correct; and if you find that no, make the appearance of not having heard him; or show him by reason, if he is a man you esteem, the reason for which he is mistaken³.

->HOW FOR WORKS OF IMPORTANCE, A MAN OUGHT NOT TRUST SO MUCH TO HIS MEMORY THAT HE DOES NOT DEIGN TO REPRESENT FROM NATURE.<-

The master who would give it to be understood that he can remember all the forms and effects of Nature would appear to me assuredly adorned with much ignorance; seeing that the said effects are infinite and our memory is not of such capacity that it suffices. Therefore, you painter, take care that the greed for gain does not surpass in you the honor of Art, for the gain of honor is much greater than the honor of riches. So that, for these reasons and others that could be said, you will apply yourself first with drawing, to give by a demonstrative form, to the eye, the intention and the invention which were first in your imagination; then, go removing or adding until you satisfy yourself, then have men arranged, clothed or naked, in the manner that you have ordered in the work, and see that in measures and sizes submitted to perspective, nothing passes into the work which is not advised by reason and by natural effects. This is the way to make yourself honored by your Art⁴.

The thing that will be painted in white or black will appear in better relief than any other work. I remind you, painter, to cover your figures with the lightest colors you can, for if you make them of dark color, they will be of little relief and little visibility from afar. This is because the shadows of all things are dark; and if you make a dark garment, there will be little difference between the lights and the shadows, and in light colors, there will be great differences⁵.

In what way a star appears at an offset angle: as
or rather through the air which appears to be at an offset angle.
How the eye does not see the true position of a star, but it will be at an offset angle
because the path of such a star crosses the horizons of that eye. In such a way
that if the eye were at the center of the earth, that star would be in its true position in the middle of the

Wherefore, if such a star is in the middle of the sky <note>i.e., at the zenith</note>, it will be in its true position, because the air

and thus, by an equal ray, it will be at an offset position from the true one of that star.

wherefore, by consequence, if the air is visible through the rays of the sun, it will appear to be
an offset sun. Wherefore, if it is visible through the rays of the sun, it will appear to be at an offset
toward the sun. Wherefore, if it is visible through the rays of the sun, it will be of equal thickness between

The true position of that star will be the air visible through the rays of the sun.

### FOLIO 26 (verso) — Ms 2038 / BIBL. NAT.

->[FACES LEARNED BY HEART. — GAMES FOR DRAFTSMEN. — DRAWING IN COMPANY.]<-

->ON THE METHOD OF RETAINING THE FORM OF A FACE IN MEMORY<-

If you wish to have the facility to keep the expression of a face in your mind, first learn by heart many types of heads, eyes, noses, mouths, chins, throats, necks, and shoulders. Let us take noses as an example. Noses are of 10 types: straight, hooked, concave, with a prominence higher or lower than the middle, aquiline, uniform, snub, round, and sharp. These are the types seen in profile. From the front, noses are of 12 types: those that are thick in the middle, thin in the middle, thick at the ends, thick at the tip and thin at the attachment <note>The "attachment" refers to the bridge of the nose where it meets the brow.</note>, thin at the tip and thick at the attachment, with wide or narrow nostrils, high or low, with the openings exposed or hidden by the tip. And so you will find diversity in the other features, which you should draw from nature and commit to memory. Or, when you have to create a face from memory, carry a small notebook with you where such features are noted. Once you have glanced at the face of the person you wish to represent, look afterward in private to see which nose or mouth resembles theirs, and make a small mark there to recognize it later at home. Of monstrous faces <note>original: "visi mostruosi" — Likely referring to "grotesque" heads or those with extreme physical deformities, which Leonardo famously studied.</note> I do not speak, because they are kept in the memory without effort.

->ON GAMES THAT DRAFTSMEN SHOULD PLAY<-

When you draftsmen wish to find some useful recreation in your games, you should always do things related to your profession—that is, developing a good <term>judgment of the eye<note>original: "bono ivditio dochio" — The ability to estimate proportions and distances accurately without tools, a vital skill for a Renaissance artist.</note></term>, knowing how to judge the truth of the widths and lengths of things. To accustom the mind to such things, let one of you draw a straight line at random on a wall; then let each of you hold a thin stalk or straw in your hand, and let each person cut theirs to the length that the first line appears to be while standing at a distance of 10 <term>braccia<note>The "braccio" (plural "braccia") was a standard Florentine unit of measurement, roughly equivalent to an arm's length or 23 inches.</note></term>. Then let each one go to the model to measure their estimated length against it. He who comes closest with his measure to the size and length of the model shall be the winner and receive the prize previously agreed upon by all. One should also take measurements in <term>foreshortening<note>original: "misure schortale" — Referring to the visual compression of an object when viewed at an angle.</note></term>; that is, take a dart or other rod and look at a certain distance in front of you, and let each person estimate how many times that measure fits into that distance. Furthermore, see who can better draw a line one *braccio* long, and let it be tested with a pulled string. Such games are the cause of developing a good judgment of the eye, which is the principal act of painting.

->WHETHER IT IS BETTER TO DRAW IN COMPANY OR NOT<-

I say and confirm that drawing in company is much better than alone, for many reasons. The first is that you will be ashamed to be seen as insufficient among the number of draftsmen, and this shame will be the cause of good study. Secondly, a healthy envy <note>Leonardo uses "invidia bona" to mean "emulation" or "productive competition."</note> will stimulate you to be among those more praised than yourself, for the praise of others will spur you on. Another reason is that you will learn from the techniques of those who do better than you; and if you are better than the others, you will profit by avoiding their faults, and the praise of others will increase your own merit.

### [THE PAINTER IN THE STUDIO — TIME FOR STUDYING ATTITUDES — THE HUMAN BODY — CHOOSING BEAUTIFUL FACES]

[Continued from folio 27 verso:] If you nonetheless desire company, take it from your studio. <note>Leonardo often weighed the benefits of solitude versus the collaboration of a workshop.</note> And this [company] can be beneficial to you for the confirmation that comes from various speculations. Any other company could be very harmful to you. <note>original: "esse pure vorai chonpagnia. pigliala deltuo. isstudio... ognialtra conpagnia. tipotrebbe. essere assai danosa"</note>

#### AT WHAT TIME ONE SHOULD STUDY THE SELECTION OF SUBJECTS
The winter evening vigils should be used by young people for the study of things prepared in the summer; that is, take all the nudes you have made in the summer and bring them together, and make a selection of the best limbs and bodies from among them, and put them into practice and commit them well to memory.

#### OF ATTITUDES
Then, in the following summer, you shall choose someone who is well-proportioned in life and who has not been brought up wearing doublets <note>A doublet was a tight-fitting jacket; Leonardo believed tight clothing distorted the natural form or movement of the body</note>, so that the person is not estranged from their [natural] nature. To such a person, you shall have them perform graceful and elegant actions. And if they do not show the muscles clearly within the outlines of the limbs, it matters not; let it suffice you to get the good attitudes from them, and you shall correct the limbs with those [anatomical studies] you conducted in the winter.

#### WHY IT IS NECESSARY FOR THE PAINTER TO KNOW THE INTRINSIC FORM OF MAN
That painter who has knowledge of the nature of the nerves, muscles, and tendons <term>lacerti: an archaic term for bundles of muscle fibers</term> will know well, in moving a limb, which nerve, how many, and which nerves are the cause of it; and which muscle, by swelling, is the cause of the shortening of that nerve; and which cords, converted into very thin cartilages, surround and contain said muscle. Thus, he will be a diverse and universal demonstrator of various muscles through the various effects of the figures, and he will not act like many who, in diverse actions, always make those same things appear in the arms, backs, chests, and legs—which things should not be counted among small errors.

#### OF THE SELECTION OF BEAUTIFUL FACES
It seems to me no small grace [is possessed by] that painter who gives a good "air" <note>In art, "aria" (air) refers to the expression, character, or noble spirit of a face</note> to his figures. This grace, if one does not have it by nature, can be acquired through incidental study in this way: look around for the good parts of many beautiful faces, whose beauty is confirmed more by public reputation than by your own judgment; because you could deceive yourself by choosing faces that have a similarity to your own, for it often seems that such similarities please us. And if you were ugly, you would choose faces that are not beautiful, and you would create ugly faces, like many painters whose figures often resemble the master. Therefore, take beauties as I say and commit them to memory.

### Ms 2038 — FOLIO 27 (verso). — NATIONAL LIBRARY.

->[COMPOSITION. — ON CARE RATHER THAN SPEED. — THE LIFE OF THE PAINTER IN THE STUDIO.]<-

**ON THE METHOD OF LEARNING TO COMPOSE FIGURES WELL TOGETHER IN NARRATIVE PAINTINGS**

When you have learned perspective well and have committed to memory all the parts and bodies of things, you should take pleasure, as you go about for recreation, in seeing and considering the positions and actions of men as they talk, dispute, laugh, or come to blows with one another; what their own actions are and what actions are made by the bystanders, the mediators, or the onlookers. Note these down with brief marks <note>Sketch placeholder in original manuscript</note> [(Figures:)] in this manner in a small notebook of your own, which you should always carry with you. It should be of tinted paper so that you do not have to erase it, but rather move from an old one to a new one; for these are not things to be erased, but rather preserved with great diligence. This is because there are such infinite forms and actions of things that the memory is not capable of retaining them; therefore, you shall keep these [notebooks] as your authors and masters.

**HOW ONE MUST FIRST LEARN DILIGENCE RATHER THAN RAPID PRACTICE**

If you, as a draughtsman, wish to study well and profitably, accustom yourself to drawing slowly, and judge among the lights which ones and how many hold the first degree of brightness; and similarly among the shadows, which are darker than the others, and in what manner they blend together. Compare the proportions of one with another; observe toward which part the outlines are directed, and which part of the lines twists in one direction or another, and where they are more or less evident, and likewise where they are thick or thin. Finally, ensure that your shadows and lights are united without strokes or marks, in the manner of smoke <term>sfumato: a technique of blending colors and tones so subtly that there is no perceptible transition</term>. And when you have trained your hand and your judgment to this diligence, speed will come to you so quickly that you will not even notice it.

**OF THE LIFE OF THE PAINTER IN HIS STUDIO**

In order that the prosperity of the body does not spoil that of the intellect, the painter or draughtsman should be solitary, and especially when he is intent on speculation and consideration <term>speculation: the act of deep mental observation and theorizing about natural forms</term> of those things which, appearing continually before his eyes, provide material for the memory to be well preserved. If you are alone, you will be all your own; and if you are accompanied by even one companion, you will be only half your own—and even less so depending on the indiscretion of his conduct. And if you are with more people, you will fall further into this same disadvantage. If you should say: "I will do it my own way, I will withdraw to one side so as to better speculate on the forms of natural things," I say this is difficult to do, because you could not help but often lend an ear to their chatter. And as one cannot serve two masters, you would perform the duty of companionship poorly and the effect of artistic speculation even worse. And if you say: "I will withdraw so far apart that their words will not reach me and will not disturb me," I tell you that you would then be considered a madman; but see, in doing so, you would still be alone.

[Continued on folio 27 recto]

# How light does not consume itself,
# nor how it mixes.

<note>Leonardo discusses how light rays from different sources or reflected in mirrors do not interfere with or "consume" one another as they pass through the same space in the air.</note>

Observe that luminous rays within the air do not mix with one another for any other reason than that which the eye and the light have shown us. For when many mirrors <term>spechi</term> are placed in such a way that each one sees a single object, each mirror will show that same object whole; and the rays of sight from one of the said mirrors will not be lost because of another in the eye that sees them all. There is no doubt that the rays from the many mirrors do not join together in the air along the same path toward the eye. And if they were to join in the air, there would be reason to lose [the clarity] of one because of another, according to the ratio of the union of so many rays of the object in the eye and in the air; because of the many mirrors, each one renders <note>original: "rāde," a contraction for "rende" (renders or gives)</note> the object in the eye by itself in its entire form through that ray.

---

# ->How the rays of light do not consume themselves<-
# ->by the interposition of another light.<-

Because one light does not consume itself through another, when sending their rays to the same place, one through the other, the rays of one light and another will not double the light where the light is not already doubled, but will only double the reasoning of the shadows. And one light and another will not interfere with each other, nor does one light render the shadow of the other unless it was in the line of the eye. And do not be deceived, for where there is a doubling of light, it will not double the rays of the said lights in themselves; only because of the way those rays have of traveling through one another, they do not double nor will they be lost because of themselves, nor because of the other; it does not render like air does to air <note>This likely refers to the idea that light rays pass through each other without resistance, much like air moving through air.</note>.

---

# ->How objects are seen through a very small aperture<-

<note>This section describes the "camera obscura" effect and the persistence of light rays passing through a small aperture (spira/spiraculo) without mixing.</note>

Since through the smallest opening <term>spira</term> <note>Leonardo uses "spira" or "spiraculo" to refer to a small hole or aperture, essentially describing the principle of the camera obscura or the pupil of the eye.</note> of the eye, the rays of the said objects render entire figures and images; these rays will cross within the eye. For all the reasons of traveling one through the other, they are not lost in the eye, nor does one ray mix with another. The rays will not be lost by traveling through the air along the same path, one through the other, and one does not render as air does. If there is a doubling of light, do not be deceived, because if there is a doubling of light, it will not double the rays of the said lights in themselves; only because of the way those rays have of traveling one through the other, they do not double, and they will not be lost because of themselves, nor because of the other; it does not render like air does to air. ### [JUDGING ONE'S OWN PAINTING. — RULE FOR THE BEGINNINGS OF PAINTERS].

---

ON JUDGING YOUR PAINTING.

We know clearly that errors are recognized more easily in the works of others than in our own; and often, by rebuking the small errors of others, you will ignore your own great ones. To avoid such ignorance, first ensure that you are a good perspectivist <note>original: "prospectiuo," one who understands the mathematical laws of perspective</note>; then, have a thorough knowledge of the measurements of man and of other animals. Also, [be] a good architect—that is, in what pertains to the form of buildings and the other things that are upon the earth, which are of infinite forms; the more knowledge you have of these, the more praiseworthy your work will be. And in those things for which you have no practice, do not refuse to draw them from nature. 

But to return to the promise made above, I say that in your painting you should hold a flat mirror and frequently look at your work inside it. There, it will be seen in reverse, and it will appear to be by the hand of another master; thus, you will judge the errors better than in any other way. It is also good to get up often and take a bit of some other recreation <note>original: "solã zõ," meaning solace or relaxation</note>, because when you return to the work, you will have better judgment; for staying fixed upon the work causes you to be greatly deceived. It is also good to move further away, because the work then appears smaller and can be comprehended better in a single glance, and one better recognizes the discords and disproportionate limbs and colors of things.

THE RULE TO BE GIVEN TO YOUNG PAINTERS.

We know clearly that the sight of the eye is one of the swiftest operations that exists, seeing infinite forms in a single moment; nevertheless, it understands only one thing at a time. Let us take a case: you, the reader, will look at this whole written page in one glance and immediately judge it to be full of various letters, but you will not know in that moment which letters they are, nor what they mean; therefore, you must go word by word, line by line, if you wish to have knowledge of these letters. 

Furthermore, if you wish to climb to the top of a building, you must ascend step by step; otherwise, it will be impossible to reach its height. So I say to you, whom Nature turns toward this art: if you wish to have true knowledge of the forms of things, begin with their individual parts <note>original: "parti cule," small details or particulars</note>, and do not move to the second until you have the first well in your memory and in practice. If you do otherwise, you will waste your time and truly prolong your study. And remember to learn diligence before speed. <margin>A crossed-out oval appears after the titles.</margin>

---

### [ON THE PHYSICS OF LIGHT AND SHADOW]

<margin><note>Small circular symbol with a horizontal bar and a vertical tick, likely representing a light source</note></margin>
**What the position of lights and bodies is**

No part of an opaque body is in such great darkness as that part where no portion of the luminous body <note>a light source, such as the sun or a lamp</note> can be seen; and such a place is the beginning of the "shadows of the air" <note>original: "onbre d’aria"; this refers to the volume of shadowed space between the object and the surface it falls upon</note>. This shadow is as wide as the luminous body itself, and its path follows a straight line through the diameter to the center of the points of that luminous body. That part of the shadow will be of the greatest darkness when it is the sum of many shadows; and these shadows are created by as many opaque bodies as are placed between the luminous body and the shadow. These are the bodies that prevent the shadow from "seeing" <note>Leonardo frequently uses the metaphor of "seeing" to describe whether a surface is directly exposed to light rays</note> the whole of the light. In such a case, a point in that shadow will be darker the less it is able to see the light; and if it sees some portion of the light, its darkness will decrease in proportion to the part of the light it sees. The shadow will continue to diminish in darkness as the view of the light falling upon it from above increases. This is why the primary part of the shadow diminishes in darkness, and the next part is less dark than the previous one, because it "sees" more of the light.

---

<margin><note>Small circular symbol with a cross and tick mark</note></margin>
**How the shadow diminishes toward the end**

In the same way that a shadow diminishes toward its end, the luminous body likewise diminishes toward its end. If we take a luminous body and an opaque body and bring them together so closely that they almost touch, we will see that the place near the point of contact will be of such darkness that it will almost equal the "proper shadow" <term>proper shadow: the shadow on the object itself, as opposed to the shadow it casts on another surface</term> of the luminous body. This occurs because it lacks the sum of all the shadows, being struck <note>original: "rigorigato," likely meaning "re-radiated" or intersected by light rays</note> by one of the many rays of the luminous body. That luminous body will be more luminous the less shadow there is toward its own summit. You can see this by the shadow made by the thickness of the hand when it is near the shadow of a wall; if you hold your hand so close to the wall that they almost touch, you will see that in the very space of the wall's shadow from which the hand was moved, there remains a shadow less dark than in the rest of the wall.

<summary>This folio explores the mathematical relationship between the size of a light source and the intensity of the shadows it creates, explaining that darkness is a result of the partial or total obstruction of light rays. Leonardo uses a practical observation of a hand's shadow against a wall to demonstrate how proximity and light exposure change the depth of a shadow.</summary>
<keywords>optics, shadow of the air, luminous body, opaque bodies, light rays, shadow intensity, physics of art</keywords>

# [THE PROPORTIONS OF THE LIMBS — CHILDREN AND MEN — LIGHTS].

### ON THE PROPORTIONS OF THE LIMBS
*As...*
And I remind you again to take great care, when giving limbs to your figures, that they appear to be in harmony, not only with the size of the body, but also with its age. Thus, for young people, there should be limbs with few muscles and veins, and delicate, rounded surfaces of a pleasing color; for men, they should be sinewy and full of muscles; for old men, they should have wrinkled, rough, and veiny surfaces, with the <term>nerves</term> <note>original: "nerbi"; in Renaissance anatomy, this term often referred to tendons or ligaments as well as nerves</note> very prominent.

### HOW INFANTS HAVE JOINTS CONTRARY TO MEN IN THEIR THICKNESS
Small children have all their joints thin, while the spaces between one joint and another are thick. This happens because the skin over the joints is alone, without any other flesh, and is of the nature of a <term>nerve</term> <note>original: "neruo"; meaning a ligament or sinew</note>, which binds and ties the bones together. The moist, fleshy matter is found between one joint and the next, enclosed between the skin and the bone. But because the bones are thicker at the joints than between the joints, the flesh, as a man grows, loses that excess that was between the skin and the bone; consequently, the skin draws closer to the bone and makes the limbs appear thinner. On the joints themselves, because there is nothing but cartilaginous and sinewy skin, it cannot shrink, and by not shrinking, it does not diminish. For these reasons, children are thin at the joints and thick between the joints—as can be seen in the joints of the fingers, arms, and shoulders, which are thin and have deep dimples—whereas a man, on the contrary, is thick at all the joints of the fingers, arms, and legs; and where children have pits, men have relief <note>i.e., protruding muscles or bone structure</note>.

### ON THE DIFFERENT MEASUREMENTS BETWEEN INFANTS AND MEN
Between men and small children, I find a great difference in the length from one joint to another; for a man has, from the shoulder joint to the elbow, and from the elbow to the tip of the thumb, and from one shoulder blade to the other, two heads for each section, while the child has only one. This is because Nature composes for us the size of the "house of the intellect" <note>the skull/brain</note> before that of the vital spirits <note>the rest of the body's systems</note>.

### ON APPLYING THE LIGHTS
First, apply a universal shadow to the entire containing part that does not see the light; then apply the medium shadows and the principal ones, comparing one to the other.
And likewise, apply a general medium light to the illuminated part, then adding the middle and principal lights, similarly by comparison.

---

And I remind you again to have great attention, in giving limbs to figures, that they appear to be concordant, not only with the size of the body, but also with the age; that in young people there are limbs with few muscles and veins, and delicate and round surfaces, of a pleasant color; that in men there are nervous and muscle-filled ones; that in old men they are with wrinkled, rough, and veiny surfaces, and very apparent nerves.

#### HOW SMALL CHILDREN HAVE JOINTS CONTRARY TO [THOSE OF] MEN IN THEIR THICKNESS.
Small children have all the joints fine, and the spaces between one and the other are thick. This takes place because the skin over the joints is alone, without other pulp, and is of the nature of nerve, which girds and binds the bones together. The fleshiness full of humor is found between one and the other joints and is included between the skin and the bone; but because the bones are thicker at the joints than between the joints, the flesh, during the growth of man, comes to leave this superfluity which is made between the skin and the bone; from then on, the skin approaches the bone more and comes to thin the limbs. And on the joints, because there is only cartilaginous and nervous skin, it cannot dry, and, not drying, it does not diminish. Therefore, for these reasons, children are delicate at their joints and thick between the joints, as one sees the joints of the fingers, arms, and shoulders, delicate and with deep holes; man, on the contrary, is thick at all the joints, fingers, arms, legs, and where children have hollows, they [MEN] have relief.

#### OF THE DIFFERENT MEASUREMENTS THAT THERE ARE FROM CHILDREN TO MEN.
Between men and small children I find a great difference in length from one to the other joint, given that man has, from the joint of the shoulder to the elbow and from the elbow to the tip of the big finger, and from the humerus of one of the shoulders to the other, two heads per piece [each time], and that the child has one, because Nature composes for us the size of the dwelling of intelligence before that of the vital spirits.

#### OF GIVING THE LIGHTS.
Give first a universal shadow to all the containing part which does not see the light, then give there the medium shadows, and the principal ones, comparatively one to the other.
And likewise, give the containing light of medium light, giving there next the mediums and principals, likewise comparatively.

# FOLIO 28 (verso)

If a lead ball of 2 <term>ounces</term> <note>original: "once"; a unit of weight roughly equal to 28 grams</note> is thrown by a force that directs it through the air, it would come to penetrate the air with a force of 10 <term>degrees</term> <note>original: "gradi"; Leonardo often used "degrees" as a generic unit to quantify abstract powers like force, heat, or speed</note>; and if it breaks a wooden board one <term>finger</term> <note>original: "deto"; a unit of thickness approximately equal to 1.8 cm</note> thick, having been broken by such force, I say that by sending through the same air a lead ball of 1 ounce with the same [initial] force, the air will be penetrated with the same force of the motion of that ball; [but] the one-ounce ball will penetrate the air with 5 degrees of force, and it will break the same wooden board with half the power of the 2-ounce ball.

->How the ounces are to be divided into minutes<-
->with measurement and the ratio of time<-

By how many minutes the air is to be penetrated by the 2-ounce ball shall be of a determined quantity of time; and what shall be the determination of the time during which that ball will traverse the space of one <term>braccio</term> <note>original: "braccio"; a "cubit" or "arm's length," approximately 58–62 cm depending on the city</note>. I say that if the air is penetrated with 10 degrees of power, and within the time of one minute that ball traverses the space of one braccio in length, then the ball of 1 ounce will penetrate the air with 5 degrees of power, and within the time of two minutes, that ball will traverse the space of one braccio. I say, by such reasoning, that if the 2-ounce ball penetrates the air and, within the time of one minute, that ball traverses the space of one braccio, the ounce will be of half the weight, or less than half the weight; therefore, it will be less powerful in penetrating the air, or less of that ball will be penetrated. Logic dictates that the air penetrated by a ball of 1 ounce will be of 5 degrees; and if that [distance] is less than a braccio, the air it traverses will be the space of one braccio within the time of 2 minutes, or fewer minutes. For logic dictates that with that power by which the air is penetrated, sending the ball of 1 ounce will be of a power of 5 degrees; and with this same power, that ball will penetrate the air for the space of one braccio within the time of 2 minutes.

I say that if, in sending the ball of 1 ounce, it penetrates the air with 5 degrees of power and within the time of one minute, that ball will traverse the space of one braccio. Therefore, a ball of 2 ounces and that of 1 ounce will follow the same ratio as was said above.

If, in sending the ball of 2 ounces, it penetrates the air with 10 degrees of force, and within the time of one minute that ball traverses the space of one braccio; then sending the ball of 1 ounce, it will penetrate the air with 10 degrees of force. Therefore, it is logical that within the time of 1 minute, the space of one braccio will be covered.

To make a head so that its features are in accord with the turning and bending [inclining] of a head, follow these methods: you know that the eyes, eyebrows, nostrils of the nose, the corners of the mouth and the sides of the chin, the jaw, cheeks, ears, and all parts of a face are placed in equal alignments upon the face. # FOLIO 29 (recto).
### Ms 2038 - BIB. NAT.

The air between the eye and the object moves so that it may be charged with that <term>likeness</term> <note>original: "similitudine"; in Renaissance optics, this refers to the visual form or "image" of an object traveling through space.</note>.

<margin>n</margin>
If it were possible for the air between the eye and the object to be displaced by the command of the <term>species</term> <note>original: "spetie"; the "species" are the visual images or rays emitted by an object that allow it to be seen.</note>, rendering that part a vacuum, such a logic would not hold because it is impossible for a vacuum to exist in nature. And if we were to take it as a true hypothesis that the likeness of the object reaches the eye in less time—being moved less through a vacuum than through the air—then such a motion would be instantaneous. For logic would dictate that if it were moved through the air, it would take time, and logic also dictates that where there is no medium, there should be no time.

<margin>n</margin>
How the sight dies away—not in the air—would follow a certain ratio if there were no smoke, because the likeness of the object would not be lost [in] very pure air.

->size . air . object . darkening . distance<-
->dark . light . truth . whiteness . blackness<-
->shadows . light . weak . strong . small . large<-
->distance . proximity . finite . infinite<-

<margin>let it move</margin>
Let the air move on every side by the sight in such a way that the eye will always be in the center of a <term>sphere</term> <note>Leonardo often conceptualized the propagation of light and sound as expanding spheres, similar to ripples in a pond.</note> of likeness of a certain ratio. This being granted forever, the sight does not change if the air does not change in every direction, returning the species to the sight. And because they are not fixed in the middle of the moved air, the species changes. Such a logic would apply in every direction, returning the species to the sight, because the species of these things are throughout all the air, and the air is everywhere. Let the <unclear>air</unclear> move, therefore, in every direction <unclear>and</unclear> <unclear>it</unclear> does not change the sight.

In every point of this sphere there is every point of the likeness of a body, rendering to the sight every point of that likeness; being produced in every point of that air without giving either impulse or hindrance to one another.

# [THE INTEREST OF FIGURES. — ANGER. — DESPAIR. — GRACE OF LIMBS. — SHADOWS].

A figure is not praiseworthy if it does not display an action that expresses the <term>passion</term> <note>original: "lapassione"; in Leonardo’s time, "passion" referred to the internal movements of the soul or intense emotional states.</note> of its mind and soul.

That figure is more praiseworthy which best expresses the passion of its spirit through its action.

### HOW TO DEPICT AN ANGRY FIGURE
For an angry figure, you should show him holding someone by the hair, with their head twisted toward the ground, and with one of his knees on the victim's ribs, raising his fist high with his right arm. This man should have his hair standing up, his eyebrows low and knit together, his teeth clenched, and the two corners of his mouth arched. His neck should be thick and leaning forward over the enemy, and it should be full of wrinkles.

### HOW TO DEPICT A DESPERATE PERSON
For a desperate man, you should show him striking himself with a knife, having torn his clothes with his hands; and let one of those hands be in the act of tearing at his own wound. Make him with his feet wide apart and his legs somewhat bent, and his body likewise leaning toward the earth, with his hair torn and scattered.

### ON THE GRACE OF THE LIMBS
The limbs must be fitted to the body with grace, according to the purpose of the effect you wish the figure to achieve. If you want to make a figure that shows elegance, you must make the limbs slender and extended, and without showing too many muscles; and those few that you do show for your purpose, make them only soft—that is, with little evidence—and with shadows that are not harsh. The limbs, especially the arms, should be "unlocked" [(Figure :)] <note>original: "disnodate"; meaning the joints should appear flexible and relaxed rather than stiff.</note>—that is, no limb should be in a straight line with the limb that joins it. And if the hips—the poles of the man—are positioned so that the right is higher than the left, you shall make the joint of the upper shoulder drop in a perpendicular line over the most prominent part of the hip. Let that right shoulder be lower than the left, and let the <term>pit of the throat</term> <note>original: "fontanella"; the hollow at the base of the neck.</note> always be above the middle of the joint of the foot that supports the weight. Let the leg that does not support the weight have its knee lower than the other, and close to the other leg. The attitudes of the head and arms are infinite, therefore I will not extend myself in giving any specific rule; only let them be easy and graceful, with various twists and turns at the "unlocked" joints, so that they do not look like pieces of wood.

### HOW THE SEPARATE SHADOW IS NEVER
### EQUAL IN SIZE TO ITS CAUSE
If the rays of light are, as experience confirms, caused by a single point and travel in a circular path from their source, they go on diverging and spreading through the air. The further they go, the more they widen; and the object placed between the light and the wall is always represented by a larger shadow, because—

### how rivers should be

The clearing of rivers that are full of gravel is done in this way: you must have the gravel opened up just enough to create a small channel <note>original: "righagnolo"</note> through which the water can begin to pass. Then, dam the river in such a way that its water all flows through the said channel; and thus the water of the river, with its own power, will carve it back out as wide and deep as shall be necessary.

---

### how rivers should be

Continuing the method mentioned above, it says that above the bank of gravel, the water should be diverted once more and made to take another path; by doing this, all the gravel will be carried into the sea, and the bed of said river will be leveled.

---

### how the bed of a river should be raised

This must be done to remedy the great flow of the river so that it does not consume the <term>embankment</term> <note>original: "argine"; the raised bank or levee of the river.</note>. It is done in this way: you make a dam in the bed of said river so that the water stops within that bed, and then you will open an exit on the side of the embankment through which the water spreads onto the plain of said embankment. In this way, the water will leave all its earth <note>i.e., silt and sediment</note> there and will return to the sea clear through its exit. You shall do this in many places along its course. And if you wish to raise the bed of said river, it is done by the method mentioned above: you block the course of said river and make the water stop in the riverbed, and then you will open the exit on the side of the flat embankment so that the water spreads over the plain of that embankment; there it will leave its earth, and thus you will have the bed of said river raised and leveled.

---

### how the motion of water is

-> the motion of water in a straight line is <-
faster in the middle than at the sides; and this occurs because the water that touches the sides is hindered by the friction <note>original: "frotamento"</note> of said sides, and because of this its flow slows down. Thus it happens that the water in the middle is faster than the water at the sides.

### [ARRANGEMENT OF THE LIMBS. — LIGHT AND SHADOW].

#### ON THE CONVENIENCE OF THE LIMBS
Regarding the convenience <note>or "suitability," referring to the natural ease of movement</note> of the limbs, you must consider that when you wish to represent someone who, by some circumstance, has to turn backward or to the side, you should not make them move their feet and all their limbs in the direction where the head turns. Rather, you shall distribute this turning movement across 4 joints: namely those of the foot, the knee, the hip, and the neck. And if you rest the weight on the right leg, make the left knee bend inward, and let its foot be slightly raised on the outside; and let the left shoulder be somewhat lower than the right; and the nape of the neck should align with that same place locho <note>original: "locho locho," a repetition in the manuscript</note> where the outer ankle of the left foot is turned. And if the left shoulder is there, it will be perpendicularly above the tip of the right foot. And always arrange your figures so that the chest does not turn in the same direction as the head, for Nature, for our convenience, has made the neck so that it can easily serve various needs, as the eye wishes to turn toward various places. The other joints are also partially obedient to this same principle. And if you depict a man sitting, and his arms must sometimes be employed in some transverse action, make it so that the chest turns upon the hip joint.

#### ON THE SHADOW PRODUCED BY A BODY PLACED BETWEEN 2 EQUAL LIGHTS
That body which is located between 2 equal lights will cast 2 shadows from itself, which will be directed in a line toward the 2 lights. And if you move said body away or bring it closer to one of the lights, the shadow that is directed toward the nearer light will be of less darkness than the one directed toward the more distant light.

#### THE BODY THAT IS CLOSER TO THE LIGHT MAKES A LARGER SHADOW AND WHY
If an object placed before a particular light is in close proximity, you will see it cast a very large shadow on the opposite wall; and the more you move said *light* object <note>Leonardo corrected himself here</note> away from the light, the more the size of that shadow will decrease.

#### WHY THE SHADOW LARGER THAN ITS CAUSE IS PRODUCED WITH DISCORDANT PROPORTIONS
The discordance in the proportion of the shadow that is larger than its cause <note>original: "chagione," referring to the object casting the shadow</note> arises because the light, being smaller than the object, cannot be at an equal distance from the extremities of that object. And the part that is more distant grows more than the parts that are near, and therefore it increases more.

#### WHY THE SHADOW LARGER THAN ITS CAUSE HAS BLURRED EDGES
That air which surrounds the light is almost of the same nature as that light in its clarity and heat; and the further it moves away, the more it loses its similarity. The thing that casts a large shadow is close to the light and finds itself illuminated by both the light and the luminous air; therefore, this air leaves the boundaries <note>original: "termini"</note> of the shadow blurred ¹.

---

### ON THE ARRANGEMENT OF THE LIMBS.
Regarding the arrangement of the limbs, you will have to consider that when you wish to represent someone who, by some circumstance [accident], has to turn backward or to the side, you do not make them move their feet and all their limbs toward the side where they turn their head, but *you shall* shall make this movement act and be distributed across 4 joints, that is to say, those of the foot, the knee, the hip, and the neck. And if you pose the weight on the right leg, you shall make the left knee bend inward; and let its foot be a little raised on the outside, let the left shoulder be a little lower than the right, and let the nape of the neck meet at the same *place* place where the outer ankle of the left foot is turned *and if*, and the left shoulder above the tip of the right foot, by a perpendicular line. And always arrange the figures in such a way that where the head turns, the chest does not turn there, for Nature, for our convenience, has made the neck such that it can serve with ease in various cases, the eye wanting to turn toward various places. And to the same, the other joints are partially obedient; and if you make the man sit and sometimes his arms have to be employed in something transverse, make the chest turn upon the hip joint ².

### ON THE SHADOW MADE BY A BODY SITUATED BETWEEN 2 EQUAL LIGHTS.
The body that is found placed between 2 equal lights will emit 2 shadows, which will be directed equally by the line of the [will be formed according to equal lines as to the] 2 lights. And if *you move* said body away or approach it to one of the lights, the one of its shadows which is directed toward the closer light will be of lesser darkness than that which is directed toward the more distant light ³.

### THE BODY WHICH IS CLOSER TO THE LIGHT MAKES A LARGER SHADOW, AND WHY.
If an object opposite a particular light is of great proximity, you will see it make a very large shadow *c* on the opposite wall, and the more you move *the light* said object away from the light, the more the form of the shadow will decrease ⁴.

### WHY THE SHADOW LARGER THAN ITS CAUSE IS MADE OF DISCORDANT PROPORTION.
The discordance of the proportion of the shadow larger than its cause arises because the light, being smaller than the object, cannot be at equal distances from the extremities of the object, and the part which is more distant grows more than those which are near; for that reason, it grows more ⁵.

### WHY THE SHADOW LARGER THAN ITS CAUSE HAS CONFUSED [BLURRED] TERMS [CONTOURS].
The air which surrounds the light is almost of the nature of this light in clarity and heat; the more it moves away, the more it loses its resemblance; the thing that makes a large shadow is close to the light and finds itself illuminated by the light and by the luminous air; therefore, this air leaves the terms of the shadow confused ⁶.

### ON THE BREAKING OF WOODS

If a plank one cubit <note>original: "braccio," a traditional Italian unit of measure roughly equal to the length of an arm, approx. 58-62 cm</note> long and one finger <note>original: "duto/dito," a small unit of measure, approx. 1.8-2 cm</note> thick breaks with a weight of one finger-unit, and another plank of the same length and thickness is two fingers wide, how much more weight will it hold than the first? I say that because its width is doubled, its resistance is also doubled. Therefore, the rule for a plank of the same length and thickness is: the wider it is, the more weight it will hold. So, if it is 2 times wider, it will hold 2 times the weight; and if it is 100 times wider, it will hold 100 times more weight.

->ON THE BREAKING OF BEAMS<-
->WHEN THEY ARE SUSPENDED AT THE ENDS<-

<note>Geometric diagram on the right showing three vertical segments of increasing length, illustrating the relationship between length and strength of beams.</note>

If a beam of a certain length and thickness breaks with 10 weights, and it were twice as long, it would break with 5 weights. If it were 3 times longer, it would break with the 3rd part <note>one-third</note> of the weight. Thus, the rule is that as much as it is longer, so much is it weaker; so that if it were 100 times longer, it would hold the 100th part of the weight that the first one held.

->ON THE BREAKING OF A BRANCH<-
->WITH TWO WEIGHTS, OR OF A BEAM<-

A branch or beam will be so much weaker when loaded with two weights as the weights are more distant from one another. If one weight is at one finger-width and the other weight is at another finger-width, it will be stronger the closer they are together.

->ON THE BREAKING OF A BRANCH<-
->OF A TREE<-

If a tree branch is 1 cubit long and it breaks with a weight of 10 pounds <note>original: "lb" for "libbre"</note>, if it were 2 cubits long, it would break with 5 pounds; and if it were 3 times longer, it would hold the third part of the weight. It becomes weaker as it becomes longer.

The rule for a beam that is of the same finger-width in width and length, but is thicker: I say that if it is 2 times thicker, it will hold 4 times more weight. And if it is 100 times thicker, it will hold 10,000 times more weight. Thus, in proportion to the thickness, its power is squared <note>Leonardo uses "raddoppia" (doubles), but his calculations describe a geometric square (n²)</note>. I say when it is 2 [units] thick, it is multiplied: I say 2 times 2 makes 4; and if it is 3 thick, it will be 3 times 3 which makes 9; and if it is 10, it will be 10 times 10 which makes 100; and if it is 100, it will be 100 times 100 which makes 10,000.

<summary>Leonardo outlines the proportional relationships between the dimensions of a wooden beam (length, width, and thickness) and its structural strength, correctly identifying that strength decreases linearly with length but increases with the square of the thickness.</summary>
<keywords>structural mechanics, beam strength, proportions, physics of wood, breaking point, Leonardo's laws of motion, statics</keywords>

It has been said by many that it is not good for a painter to know well how to draw the forms of the limbs of man in all the attitudes and gestures that a man can perform, and that this is a superfluity <note>unnecessary or excessive</note> because there have been those such painters who have done without this knowledge of **anatomy** and yet were noble painters, and that this work <note>anatomical study</note> is not esteemed by them to be of any utility. 

To this, I respond that if those such painters had been rare <note>of exceptional quality</note>, they would have had even more need to know this such knowledge, and that they do not realize that the good painters and sculptors have always practiced it. And if no memory of it has reached us, it is not the fault of their ignorance, but of time which consumes all things, and of their successors who have not known how to understand the value of such knowledge. If those successors had known how to understand its value, they would have acted in such a way that the memory of such knowledge would not have been lost; because they did not know of such knowledge, they fled from the labor <gloss>original: "fatcha," toil or effort</gloss> and gave no notice of it to posterity in their books. 

Many have fled from such knowledge out of boredom, and many for not knowing how to draw the lines of **anatomy**, because it seems to them a thing of melancholy <note>Leonardo refers to the grim nature of dissection and the "melancholy" of studying corpses</note>. But they do not realize that if they only knew how it ought to be done, they would have the greatest pleasure from it; for a man of noble genius <term>noble ingniegno: the innate intellectual capacity of a high-minded artist</term> ought to carry love for those things which are of utility to his practice. And this is a thing that properly belongs to the painter or sculptor.

If you wish to see the **anatomy** of a horse, you need nothing more than a single horse, because all horses are of one and the same form; but it is not so with the limbs of man, because they are infinitely varied. As you see, one shoulder may be higher than the other, or one arm longer than the other, or one leg thicker or thinner than the other, and so it is with all the parts of the body of man. It is not so with the horse, because all horses are of the same form, and so it is with all other brute animals <note>non-human animals</note>. 

But in man there is the greatest variety that exists in any other species of animals; for you will see one who will have a thick and short neck, and another thin and long; one will have a wide chest and another narrow; one will have long arms and another short. So it is with all the parts of the body, and therefore it is necessary that the **painter** knows the **anatomy** of all the parts of the human body, so that he knows how to change the forms of the man according to the different attitudes and gestures that the man can make. This is so that he is not like many who always make the man in one and the same attitude and gesture; and if they do change him, they change him in such a way that it seems to be the very same man in all his attitudes. This is a great vice <note>a flaw or artistic defect</note>, and therefore it is necessary that the painter knows the **anatomy** of all the parts of the human body so that <unclear>not</unclear>

### [HEIGHT OF THE POINT OF VIEW. — REPRESENTATION OF A BATTLE].

**HOW HIGH ONE SHOULD PLACE THE POINT [OF VIEW]**
The point [of view] should be elevated to the height of the eye of an average man. The end of the plain which borders the sky should be made at the height of the boundary of the flat earth with the sky, except for the mountains, which are free <note>original: "libere libere"; Leonardo means mountains are not bound by the horizon line of the flat plain and can rise to any height</note>.

**WAY TO DEPICT A BATTLE**
First, you shall make the smoke of the artillery <term>artillery: heavy weaponry or cannons</term> mixed into the air along with the dust stirred up by the movement of the horses and the combatants. You shall treat this mixture in this way: dust, because it is an earthly and heavy thing, even though it rises easily and mixes into the air due to its fineness, nevertheless naturally returns downward. Its highest ascent is made by its finest part; therefore, it will be least seen there and will appear almost the color of the air. The smoke that mixes with the dusty air, the higher it rises to a certain height, the more it will appear as a dark cloud. And at its summit, one will see the smoke more clearly than the dust. The smoke will lean toward a somewhat bluish color, and the dust will keep to its own color. On the side from which the light comes, this mixture of air, smoke, and dust will appear much brighter than on the opposite side. 

As for the combatants, the more they are within the said turbulence, the less they will be seen, and the less difference there will be between their lights and their shadows. You shall make the faces and the people flush red, as well as the air around them, and the musketeers <term>scoppettieri: soldiers armed with an early form of handgun or light cannon called a scoppietto</term> together with those near them. The further this redness moves from its source, the more it is lost. The figures that are between you and the light, being distant, will appear dark against a light background; and their legs, the closer they are to the ground, the less they will be seen, because the dust there is thicker and denser. 

If you depict horses running out of the crowd, make little clouds of dust distant from one another, at the same interval as the jumps made by the horse. The cloud that is furthest from the said horse should be seen the least—instead, it should be high, spread out, and thin—and the one nearest should be more evident, smaller, and denser. Let the air be full of flights of arrows of various kinds, some rising, some descending, and some following a flat line. The bullets of the muskets should be accompanied by a bit of smoke following their path. You shall make the figures in the foreground dusty, on their hair and eyebrows and other flat areas suited to holding dust. You shall make the victors running with their hair streaming and other light things scattered to the wind, with their eyebrows low <note>indicating a focused or fierce expression</note> and with their teeth clenched and the ¹ [Continued on folio 30 verso].

-> ### ON THE PRINCIPLES OF SHADOWS AND LIGHTS <-

Shadows: both primary shadows and derived shadows. Primary shadows <note>original: "onbre per se"; these are shadows that exist on the dark side of an object itself, rather than being cast onto a surface</note> are those which contain within themselves the cause of their shadow; that is, the light does not strike them due to the intervention of their own body. These bodies contain within them the derived shadows <note>original: "onbre dirivate"; these are cast shadows</note>, which are those cast from another body placed between the light and the space that receives the shadow. And derived shadows are of 3 types <note>original: "ragioni"; literally 'reasons' or 'categories'</note>: one is equal to its body, another is larger, and the other is smaller. The equal one is that which is cast by a light equal [in size] to its body; the other is larger, being cast by a light smaller than the body; and the smaller one is that which is cast by a light larger than the body.

This shall be proved by experience with lights placed at different thicknesses <note>Leonardo likely refers to the diameter or width of the light source</note>. For a circular light shall be considered throughout its entire space as a single light. A body that is smaller than the light will produce a shadow smaller than the body; a light that is smaller than the body will produce a shadow larger than the body; and that light which is equal to the body will produce a shadow equal to the body.

Derived shadows are divided into two categories: namely, shadow and penumbra <term>penumbra: Leonardo uses the term "preonbra" to describe the partial shadow or "fringe" created when a light source is not a single point</term>. The shadow is that which is caused by the center of the light, and the penumbra is caused by the entire circle of the light source. This shall be proved in the chapter on the intersection of light rays. Furthermore, it shall be proved that the equal shadow will never be [exactly] equal except at great distances, but will always be [slightly] larger. 

The shadow that is derived from bodies smaller than the light is a pyramidal shadow <note>meaning it tapers to a point</note>. The shadow that is derived from bodies equal to the light will be a columnar shadow. And the shadow that is derived from bodies larger than the light will be an inverted pyramid shadow <note>meaning it widens as it moves away from the object</note>. This occurs because throughout the circle of the light, both shadow and penumbra are created, as will be proved below.

<summary>Leonardo defines the three types of cast shadows (tapering, cylindrical, and widening) based on the size of the light source relative to the object, and introduces the concept of the penumbra.</summary>
<keywords>optics, light and shadow, primary shadow, cast shadow, penumbra, pyramidal shadow, columnar shadow, geometry of light</keywords>

### HOW SMALL FIGURES SHOULD NOT, BY REASON, BE HIGHLY FINISHED

I say that for things of small size <note>original: "pichole"; here meaning figures viewed at a distance</note> which appear diminished in form, it arises because that thing is far from the eye. When this is the case, it is inevitable that between the eye and the object there is much air; and this "much air" prevents the clarity of the form <note>original: "evidentia della forma"</note> of these objects, so that the minute details of these bodies become indiscernible and unrecognizable. Therefore, you, the painter, shall make small figures only sketched <note>original: "acciennate"; suggested or indicated</note> and not highly finished; if you do otherwise, you will be acting against the effects of Nature, your mistress.

The object remains small because of the great distance between the eye and the object; this great distance encloses within itself much air; and much air forms in itself a dense body <note>Leonardo views air as a physical medium that accumulates density over distance, a concept essential to his theory of "atmospheric perspective"</note> which obstructs the eye and takes away the minute details of the objects.

### WHAT BACKGROUND THE PAINTER SHOULD USE FOR HIS WORKS

Since we see from experience that all bodies are surrounded by shadow and light, it is necessary that you, the painter, arrange things so that the part which is illuminated ends against a dark background, and likewise, the shaded part of the body ends against a light background. This rule will give a great boost in making your figures stand out in relief <note>original: "arileuare"; the illusion of three-dimensionality</note>.

<margin>
**ON PORTRAYING**
When you have to portray from nature, stand at a distance three times the size of the object you are portraying.
</margin>

<margin>
**Why a painting looks better in a mirror than outside it.** <note>Leonardo frequently advised using a mirror to provide a "fresh eye" on a composition, as the reversal helps the artist spot imbalances.</note>
</margin>

<margin>
**ON SHADOWS**
Where shadow borders light, take note of where it is lighter or darker, and where it is more or less "smoky" <term>sfumato: the technique of blending tones so subtly that they transition like smoke</term> toward the light. Above all, I remind you that in young people you should not make the shadows end sharply like stone, because flesh has a bit of transparency. This is seen by looking at a hand held between the eye and the sun, which appears to glow red and be luminously transparent. You should place the part with the most color between the lights and the shadows. And if you wish to see what shadow is required for your flesh tones, cast a shadow upon it with your finger; and according to whether you want it lighter or darker, hold your finger closer or further from your painting, and then imitate that.
</margin>

<margin>
**HOW ONE CAN LEARN ON EVERY JOURNEY**
This kindly Nature has provided for us in such a way that throughout the whole world you find something to imitate.
</margin>

<margin>
**ON DEPICTING A WILD SITE**
Trees and plants that are more branched with thin limbs should have less darkness in their shadow. The tree and the plants that have larger leaves will be the cause of greater shadow.
</margin>

->HOW ONE SHOULD RECOGNIZE<-
->WHICH PART OF THE BODY SHOULD BE<-
->MORE OR LESS LUMINOUS THAN THE OTHERS<-

If **f.** is the light and the head is the body illuminated by it, that part of the head which receives the ray upon itself at the most equal angles <note>Leonardo is referring to the angle of incidence; "equal angles" implies a perpendicular strike, where the angles on either side of the light ray are 90 degrees</note> will be the most illuminated. And that part which receives the rays at less equal angles will be less luminous. And this light performs its office in a manner similar to a physical blow; for a blow that falls between equal angles is of the first degree of power, and when it falls between unequal angles, it will be as much less powerful than the first as the angles are more dissimilar. For example: if you throw a ball at a wall whose ends are equidistant from you, the blow will fall between equal angles. But if you throw the ball at said wall while standing at one of its ends, the ball will fall between unequal angles and the blow will not take hold <note>original Italian: "nonsi appichera"; French editorial note: "déviera" (will deflect). Leonardo suggests the energy of the light "glances off" if the angle is too shallow</note>.

[Figure 2:] l o f d
->HOW BODIES ACCOMPANIED BY SHADOW AND LIGHT<-
->ALWAYS VARY THEIR BOUNDARIES ACCORDING TO THE COLOR AND LIGHT<-
->OF THE THING THAT BORDERS THEIR SURFACE<-

If you see a body where the illuminated part is set against a dark background, the part of that light which will appear of the greatest brightness will be that which terminates against the darkness at **d**. And if said illuminated part borders a light background, the boundary of that illuminated body will appear less bright than before, and its highest brightness will appear between the boundary of the background at **f** and the shadow. And this same thing happens to the shadow; for the boundary of that part of the shadowed body that is set against a light place at **l** will appear of much greater darkness than the rest. And if said shadow terminates against a dark background, the boundary of the shadow will appear lighter than before, and its greatest darkness will be between said boundary and the light at point **o**. <note>This describes the phenomenon of "simultaneous contrast," where the eye perceives values as more intense when placed next to their opposites</note>

[Figure 3:] b c d n a
->ON THE PEAKS OF LIGHT THAT TURN AND SHIFT<-
->ACCORDING TO THE SHIFTING OF THE EYE SEEING THE BODY<-

Let us suppose that the body is this circle figured here to the side, and that the light is point **a**, and that the illuminated part of the body is **b. c.**, and that the eye is at point **d**. I say that the <term>highlight<gloss>original: "lustro"; a specular reflection or "glint" that moves across a surface as the observer moves, distinct from the fixed illuminated area</gloss></term>, because it is "all in all and all in the part," if you are at point **d**, the highlight will appear at point **c**; and as much as the eye moves from **d** to **a**, so much will the highlight shift from **c** to **n**.

Ms 2038 National Library — FOLIO 33 (recto). — [LIGHTING THE FIGURES — METHOD OF DRAWING — NORTH AND SOUTH LIGHT — BEAUTY OF COLORS].

### HOW LIGHT SHOULD BE GIVEN TO FIGURES
Light must be used according to the natural environment where you imagine your figure to be. That is: if you imagine it in the sun, make the shadows dark and the highlights broad, and imprint the shadows of all surrounding bodies and their shadows upon the ground. And if you represent it in overcast weather <note>original: "tristo tenpo," literally "sad weather," referring to a cloudy or dull day</note>, make little difference between light and shadow, and do not create a distinct shadow at the feet. And if you represent it inside a house, make a great difference between lights and shadows, including a shadow on the floor. And if you represent it with a screened window <note>original: "finestra inpanata," a window covered with oiled cloth or parchment to diffuse light</note> and a white-walled room, there should be little difference between lights and shadows. 

And if it is illuminated by fire, you shall make the lights reddish and powerful, and the shadows dark. The edges of the shadows striking against the walls or the floor should be sharp; and the further the shadow gets from the body, the wider and larger it should become. If a figure were lit partly by fire and partly by the air <note>meaning natural daylight</note>, make the light from the air more powerful and the firelight almost red, in imitation of fire. Above all, ensure that your painted figures have a large light source coming from above—that is, the living models you observe—because the people you see in the streets all have their light from above. Know that even with a close acquaintance, if they were lit from below, you would find it difficult to recognize them.

->THE ORDER OF DRAWING<-
<margin>d</margin>
When drawing an animal <note>Leonardo often uses "animal" to refer to living beings, including humans</note>, draw first from the drawings of a good master made with art from nature, and not from habit <note>original: "praticha," referring to drawing from memory or formula rather than observation</note>. Then draw from a relief <note>a three-dimensional model or sculpture</note> in the company of a drawing made from that same relief. Then, draw from a good natural model, which you must put into practice.

### AT WHAT HEIGHT THE LIGHT SHOULD BE FOR DRAWING FROM NATURE
The light for drawing from nature should be from the North, so that it does not change <note>North light is preferred by artists because it remains consistent throughout the day, unlike the shifting sun in the South</note>. And if you use a South light, keep the window screened with cloth, so that as the sun illuminates it all day, the light does not shift. The height of the light should be situated so that every body casts a shadow on the ground that is as long as the object is high.

### HOW THE BEAUTY OF COLOR MUST BE IN THE HIGHLIGHTS
If we see that the quality of colors is recognized through light, it must be judged that where there is more light, there the true quality of the illuminated color is most visible; and where there is more darkness, the color is stained by the color of that darkness. Therefore, you, painter, remember to show the truth of colors on the illuminated parts. ¹

***

### HOW ONE MUST GIVE LIGHT TO THE FIGURES.
<note>This section is a French translation of the Italian text above, included in the original manuscript's transcription.</note>
One must make use of light according to what would be given by the natural situation where you pretend your figure is; that is to say: If you pretend it is in the sun, make the shadows dark and large areas of light, and imprint the shadows of all surrounding bodies, their shadows on the ground. And if you figure it in bad weather, make little difference between the lights and the shadows, and without making any other shadow at the feet. And if you figure it in a house, make a great difference between the lights and the shadows, and shadow on the ground. And if you figure a window there covered with canvas and a white dwelling, little difference from lights to shadows. And if it is lit by fire, you will make the lights reddish and powerful, and the dark shadows. And let the shadows be finished [sharp] when hitting the walls or on the ground, and as they move further from the body, let them become broader and larger. If a part of it were lit by fire and a part by the air, make that of the air more powerful and that of the fire almost red, like fire. And especially make your painted figures have a great light, and from above, that is to say, those that you represent as living, given that the people you see in the streets all have the light from above; and know that you do not have such great knowledge that if the light were giving from below, you would not endure fatigue in recognizing them ².

### ORDER [METHOD] FOR DRAWING.
To draw from an animal: Draw first from the drawings of a good master, made with art from nature, and not from habit; then from relief in the company of the drawing taken from this relief, then from a good natural [model], which you must put into use ³.

### AT WHAT HEIGHT THE LIGHT SHOULD BE FOR DRAWING FROM NATURE.
The light for drawing from nature must be in the north, so that it makes no change; and if you make it in the south, keep the window covered with canvas, so that the sun, lighting it all day, does not make changes. The height of the light must be situated in such a way that each body makes its shadow on the ground as long as its height is ⁴.

### HOW THE BEAUTY OF THE COLOR MUST BE UPON THE LIGHTS.
If we see that the quality [nature] of colors is known by means of light, it is to be judged that where there is the most light, one sees more the true quality of the illuminated color, and where there is more darkness, the color will hold to the color of these darknesses. Therefore, you, painter, remember to show the truth of the colors on the illuminated parts ⁵.

***

Ms 2038 BIB. NAT.
— FOLIO 33 (recto). —

## How the true likenesses of bodies are seen in the eye

<margin>
It is seen through 
experience 
that every object 
that the clear air 
sees, which is 
tinted blue, 
will have the 
shadows of white 
bodies tinted 
with blue.
</margin>

If the air were transparent in itself and was not mixed with the vapors of the water it contains, the <term>likenesses</term> <note>original: "simulacri," referring to the optical images or representations of objects reaching the eye</note> of bodies would tint the eye that sees them with their own color. If there were a white ball in the air mixed with vapors, and the air were tinted with blue, and the light of the sun’s rays came from the east and struck the ball, the part of the ball turned toward the sun would be tinted with whiteness. However, the part that does not see the sun would be tinted by the color of the air. This air, being <term>blue</term> <note>original: "turchino," a deep sky-blue or turquoise color</note>, tints that part of the ball not facing the sun with its blueness. Furthermore, if the light of the air is turned toward the east and the air is blue, this air will be brighter toward the east than toward other parts. On the opposite side, the shadow of the ball will appear, which will be tinted blue; and its shadow upon the ball itself will be tinted blue, but it will be darker. The closer one gets to the ball, the darker the blue will be, reaching its greatest darkness as it nears the ball itself.

---

## HOW ONE MUST LEARN TO PRACTICE

First learn the <term>science</term> <note>original: "sciẽza," meaning the underlying theoretical principles or laws of nature</note>, and then follow the <term>practice</term> <note>original: "praticha," meaning the applied skill or execution</note> born from that science. The painter must study with a system and not leave anything out of his memory. He should see what difference there is between the shadows of trees of the same species, and which are more or less dark, or more or less light. You shall do the same with plants, grasses, stones, the air, clouds, and animals. You will see such a degree of competition and benefit to the spirit that the path to painting will be made short.

---

### How one must first learn diligence rather than speed

If you, the painter, wish to study well and fruitfully, when you go walking, carry a small book of tinted paper. With a <term>silverpoint stylus</term> <note>original: "stile d'ariento," a traditional drawing tool using a silver rod on prepared paper, which creates fine, permanent lines</note>, note with brevity the <term>movements</term> <note>original: "moti," referring to the physical motions and emotional gestures of people</note> and actions of men, and the circumstances of the <term>bystanders</term> <note>original: "astãti"</note> and their compositions. This will teach you the diligence required to know how to portray natural bodies, which is better than the speed of trying to learn them by heart.

<summary>Leonardo explains why shadows on white objects appear blue due to atmospheric light and urges artists to master the "science" of nature through diligent observation and sketching before focusing on speed.</summary>
<keywords>optics, blue shadows, color theory, artistic practice, science vs practice, silverpoint, sketching from life, observation of nature</keywords>
