[REFLECTIONS. — MAXIMS. — CHOICE OF FIGURES. — LIGHT AND SHADOW].

---

# OF SHADOW AND LIGHT
Every part of the surface surrounding a body is transformed partly into the color of the object placed opposite to it.

### EXAMPLE
If you place a ball—a spherical body—in the midst of various objects; that is to say, on one side there is sunlight, and on the opposite side there is a wall illuminated by the sun, which is green or some other color; let the floor where it rests be red, and let the two <note>The original OCR reads "12," likely a transcription of the Roman numeral "ii" for two.</note> transverse sides be dark. You will see that the natural color of said body participates in the colors of the objects placed opposite it. 

The most powerful will be the light source. The second will be that of the illuminated wall. The third will be that of the shadow. There remains then a quantity that participates in the color of the extremes.

That light which strikes between equal angles is the most powerful.
*Example of the blow.* <note>Leonardo often compared the behavior of light to the physics of a physical strike or a bouncing ball.</note>

He who paints a figure, if he cannot "be" it <note>original: "essere lei," meaning the painter must mentally inhabit or embody the character of the figure they are drawing</note>, cannot properly place it.

(It is a supreme misfortune when one’s opinion exceeds one’s work.)

<margin>In the choice of figures, let them be graceful rather than dry or woody <note>original: "secho o legnioso," terms used to describe a stiff, stiffly-contoured, or lifeless style of painting.</note>.</margin>

## ON THE QUALITY OF THE AIR REGARDING SHADOWS AND LIGHTS
That body will show the greatest difference between its shadows and its lights when it is seen under the strongest light, such as sunlight, or, at night, the light of a fire. This is to be used sparingly in painting, because the works remain harsh and without grace.

A body found in moderate light will have little difference between its lights and its shadows; and this occurs towards evening, or when it is cloudy. These works are soft and bring grace to every kind of face. Just as in all things extremes are a vice: too much light makes things too harsh, and too little light does not allow them to be seen. The middle ground is good.

## ON SMALL LIGHTS
<margin>from windows</margin>
Furthermore, small lights create a great difference between lights and shadows, especially if the room illuminated by them is large; and this is not good to use.

---

<summary>Leonardo explains how objects reflect the colors of their surroundings and advises painters to use soft, moderate light (like twilight or cloudy days) to achieve "grace" rather than the "harshness" caused by direct sunlight or small windows.</summary>

# ON ATMOSPHERIC PERSPECTIVE

The more the eye looks through air that is thicker and more dense, the more the objects seen through that air will appear to it darker in color and less distinct, as if you were seeing something in the middle of a fog. Conversely, the clearer the air and the less thick it is, the more clearly things will be seen, and the less they will be tinted by the color of the air. Furthermore, the thinner, clearer, and more subtle <term>subtle (sottile)</term><note>Leonardo uses "subtle" to describe air that is pure and lacks the heavy vapors of fog or dust.</note> the air is, the more things will appear brighter and of a color different from that of the air.

---

<margin>
The eye that looks into the clear air.
</margin>
<margin>
Right hand, smoke, left hand. <note>original: "māno drita fumo mācha." Leonardo likely refers to the positioning of elements in a potential experiment or drawing.</note>
</margin>
<note>The following paragraph is crossed out with a large X in the original manuscript.</note>
Or place it inside a denser smoke, and you will see the things that are inside said smoke appear darker and less distinct.

---

<margin>
Smoke or thick and dark air. Eye.
</margin>
Or arrange it so that the eye sees things through the smoke, and that those things must mingle with the said smoke; where the air is dense and thick, less subtle, and darker, you will see even more clearly that the things inside said smoke appear darker and less distinct.
<note>To the right is a small circle diagram labeled 'a'.</note>

---

Or if you were within thin, clear, and subtle air, and you saw a thing that was inside a dense, thick, and dark air, certainly that thing would appear to you darker, denser, and more tinted <note>original: "tēta," meaning stained or colored by the medium</note> than other things that are within said dense and thick air. This is because that dense and thick air sits between the eye and the object, and the clear air around you cannot grant the object its own clarity.
<note>To the right is a small circle diagram with marks resembling 'o' and 'd'.</note>

<margin>
Left hand, smoke, left.

Or if you were within dense, thick, and dark air, and you saw a thing that was within clear, subtle, and thin air, certainly that thing would appear to you to be of a clear color, as if it were illuminated by the sun, and it would appear less tinted by the density of the air.
<note>To the right is a small circle diagram labeled 'o'.</note>

<summary>Leonardo examines how the density of air, smoke, or fog acts as a filter that darkens objects and blurs their details, a fundamental principle of what is now called atmospheric perspective. He notes that the appearance of an object depends significantly on whether the viewer and the object are in the same or different atmospheric conditions.</summary>

### MS 2037 NATIONAL LIBRARY — FOLIO 1 (recto)¹ , ².

### [DETECTING A MINE. — DROWNING THE ENEMY].

If you want to know where a tunnel <note>original: "cha [cava]" - an excavation or mine</note> is taking its course, place a drum <note>original: "tanburo"</note> in all those places where you suspect the tunnel is being made. And upon said drum, place a pair of dice <note>original: "paio di dadi"</note>; and when you are near the place where they are digging, the dice will jump slightly upon the drum, due to the blow given underground in excavating the earth.

There are some who, having the convenience of a river or marsh on their lands, have made a large reservoir of water near the place where they suspect the tunnel is being made; and having dug toward the enemy and found them, they have opened the sluice and drowned a great many people in the mine.

If you wish to know where a mine is making its way, place a drum at all the locations where you suspect the mine is being made, and on the said drum, place a pair of dice; and when you are near the place where they are mining, the dice will jump a little above the drum, by the blow that is given underground while mining the terrain³.

Some, having the convenience of a river or ponds on their lands, have made, near the place where they suspected the mine was being made, a large reservoir of water, then dug toward the enemy and having found them, they opened the reservoir and drowned many people in the mine⁴.

---

1. Folio 100 [?] recto of Manuscript B; see below, note 2.
2. According to the deed of the Arconati donation in 1637, involving twelve manuscripts by Leonardo da Vinci given to the Ambrosian Library in Milan, the third—which became Manuscript B of the Institute (appearing as it is now in the second volume of this publication)—contained exactly one hundred leaves. However, the first was missing, and on the second, there were some cherries <note>Leonardo often doodled in margins; these cherries appear on what is now the third leaf</note>. Furthermore, five leaves of drawings, mostly polearms, had been inserted, and at the end, another small volume on mathematics and birds consisting of eighteen leaves. <term>Libri<gloss>Guglielmo Libri (1803–1869), a mathematician and notorious book thief who stole many of Leonardo's papers</gloss></term> removed the five inserted leaves, the 18-leaf booklet, and then leaves 84 to 87 and 91 to 100. These last ten constitute the current booklet, reproduced as it is now, numbered in red ink from 1 to 30 below the old pagination at the National Library, whose stamp this page bears along with three other marks. When these removed leaves were sold by Libri to <term>Lord Ashburnham<gloss>An English collector whose estate eventually returned many stolen manuscripts to their rightful national libraries</gloss></term>, the pagination in large, non-autograph figures was crossed out; but several of these figures can still be read, including those of folio 96 and folio 95 [recto]. The original placement of the others can be guessed by comparing subjects. In short, the concordance of the old end of Manuscript B with the current pagination is as follows: 3 [recto] = 91 recto, 5 = 92, 6 = 93, 4 = 94, 2 = 95, 9 = 96, 7 = 97, 10 = 98, 8 = 99, 1 = 100. Following this booklet are six leaves of drawings without text, mostly polearms, which precede it at the National Library.

<margin>
Italy 2037
</margin>

<note>Drawing of a long rectangular trough or conduit in perspective, with a small cylindrical bucket or joint to the right.</note>

When you have leveled the ground so that the base is flat, make a single conduit <term>canello: a tube, pipe, or channel</term> out of oak planks or other hard, thin wood. From these, make sections 4 cubits <term>bra [braccia]: a Renaissance unit of measurement, approximately 23 inches or 58 centimeters</term> long. One conduit must fit inside the next, and they should be joined with mastic <note>a resinous waterproof putty</note> and pitch. To ensure the conduit is strong, wrap it with hemp ropes and coat it with pitch, and it will be durable.

<note>Drawing of a horizontal pipe with water pouring out of a spout on the left end.</note>

Furthermore, you can make the conduits from pieces of swamp reeds. Join them to one another with mastic and pitch; at these joints, a small tube should be placed inside and another small one outside, joined as I described above. It will be strong and long-lasting.

If ships and galleys are in combat, the ships being victorious because of their high fighting tops, one must *put* pull the yard almost to the top of the mast; and let there be attached [suspended] at the extremity of said yard—that is, the one that is attached projecting toward the enemy—a small fighting top wrapped, underneath and around, with a thick mattress full of cotton, so that it is not damaged by small cannons. Then, pull down the opposite part of the yard with the capstan, and the opposite fighting top will go so high that it will far surpass the fighting top of the ship, and one can easily drive out the men who are inside. But it is necessary that the men who are in the galley go to the opposite side, so that they act as a counterweight to the load of the men placed in the fighting top of the yard¹.

When giving the assault with ladders, let two curtals be taken, let them be placed at the same window, let them be fired at the same time, and let there be a thick, new, and wet rope from one ball to the other. <note>This describes a "chain-shot" tactic where two cannonballs are linked by a rope to sweep away ladders or groups of enemy soldiers during a siege.</note>

---

<margin>1. J.-P. Richter, vol. II, no. 1115 (“4b”). <note>This refers to Jean-Paul Richter’s 1883 compilation of Leonardo’s writings.</note></margin>

<note>Top-left drawing: A crane arm or derrick with a bucket suspended by ropes, showing how Leonardo envisioned transferring loads between ship and shore.</note>
<note>Top-right drawing: A boat equipped with a vertical support and a hanging weight or vessel, illustrating the center of gravity and stability during lifting.</note>

If one wishes to lift weights by way of water, let a small boat <term>burchiello: a shallow-draft boat or barge common in Italian rivers and lagoons</term> with a wide hull be made, with several vessels <unclear>p</unclear>laced within, some filled with water and others empty. Let those vessels full of air pull upwards and those of water pull downwards. This should be done with winches <term>argani: heavy-duty winches used for hoisting</term>, screws <term>uiti: likely worm gears or threaded lifting mechanisms</term>, and wheels, and with counterweights; thus, those weights will be raised with ease because the system has great force. In the same way, we shall place terracotta vessels <note>Leonardo often suggests using "vasi di terra cotta" (earthenware jars) as ready-made air tanks or floats.</note> filled with air under the water; and when we want the weights to be raised, we will open the terracotta vessels so that the air escapes and the water enters them. Thus, they will become heavy <note>By letting water into the air-filled jars, they lose buoyancy and sink, acting as a falling counterweight to lift a connected load.</note> and the water will come over them, and the weight will rise. This can also be used if we want to lift weights from one boat to another.

To pull timbers <note>original: "legni", referring to logs or wooden beams.</note> out of the water, it is done with the boat filled with empty vessels tied to the sides of those boats; these should be full of air so that they pull upwards from the bottom of those boats <unclear>which are empty</unclear>.

<note>The following is the translation of the French commentary provided by the manuscript's editor.</note>

When you make ditches, throw the earth into the city, so that you then create a support against the hits of the bombards.

And never raise the rampart [too high], because it then becomes a shield [a defense] for the enemy.

When one gives the assault to a fortress, one first throws to the ground, with bombards, a part of the walls; then, one fills the ditch with fascines, from where those of the fortress throw bombard powder by hand. Or else, by blowing with bellows, one does good work; then one throws fire there with a ball of [with] fire-wicks.

Some were accustomed to throwing beehives down from the walls against the enemies; others [threw] boiling <unclear>[?]</unclear>.

A type of wall resistant to bombards; that is to say: Make wing-walls with buttresses every 10 braccia, and between one and the other, fill with earth ².

When you want to preserve a tower or another wall from bombards, make in front of it a thick bastion full of hay, or litter [manure], [or] fascines ³, and on the outside, put the wet litter, re-wetting it often, because of the fire that the enemy can throw.

---

2. J.-B. Venturi, *Essai, etc*, p. 28, § XII; Dr. Max Jordan, *Das Malerbuch des L. da V.*, p. 73.
3. Cf. hereafter, folio 4 verso, 2nd line.

### [A CART THAT MOVES BY ITSELF].

---

Just as a man runs across a frozen river without moving his feet <note>Leonardo is likely describing the phenomenon of gliding or sliding across ice, where momentum carries the body forward</note>, so it is possible to create a cart that can run by itself.

A method for a cart that is easy to pull. Test this weight, and observe how its behavior changes as it moves from an inclined position to a horizontal one.

[6th figure:] 10 [Figure below the previous one:] This is better than the large wheel.
[Last figure, on the right:] from **a** to **M**

If this wheel is 6 <term>braccia: an Italian unit of measurement (literally "arms"), roughly equivalent to 23 inches or 58 cm</term> in diameter, there are 3 <term>braccia</term> from the center to the ground. If the axle <note>original: "polo," referring to the central spindle or hub of the wheel</note> is 1/6 of a <term>braccia</term> thick, its radius <insert>the half</insert> will be 1/12—which is to say, one inch <note>original: "oncia"</note>. Since there are 36 inches in 3 <term>braccia</term>, you have 36 inches of lever against one inch of counter-lever <note>Leonardo is calculating mechanical advantage: the ratio between the radius of the wheel and the radius of the axle</note>. In this way, one thousand units of force can lift thirty-six thousand. But there is only one defect: if the wheel sinks <insert>into the ground</insert>, it becomes difficult to move the perpendicular line of the wheel from **a** to **M**.

---

<note>original: J.-P. Richter, Vol. II, No. 1120</note>

<summary>Leonardo explores the physics of self-propulsion and mechanical advantage, calculating how a large wheel paired with a narrow axle can multiply force by a factor of 36. He notes the practical limitation of this design when encountering soft or uneven ground.</summary>
<keywords>self-propulsion, mechanics, lever, wheel and axle, mechanical advantage, braccia, physics of motion, friction</keywords>

If the weight you pull is 1,000 <term>libbre: Italian pounds, which varied by city but generally weighed about 12 ounces</term> and the force that pulls it is 10, the wheel of motion <note>the larger driving wheel or crank circle</note> will be 100 times larger than the wheel of the rope <note>the smaller axle or drum where the rope winds</note>. ### [NAVAL FORCES].

3. [1st fig.:] M

->METHOD OF...<-

If you want to create a naval fleet <note>original Italian: "armata marittima"</note>, use these vessels to smash through ships; that is, make vessels 100 feet long and 8 feet wide. But ensure that the oars on the left have their rowers <note>original: "motori," literally "movers"</note> on the right side of the vessel, and likewise those on the right on the left side,

->as appears in M<-

so that the levers of the oars may be longer. And let the said vessel be one and a half feet thick—that is, made of sturdy beams fixed on the outside and the inside with planks of opposing grain <note>original: "contrari liniamenti." This refers to cross-laminated timber or alternating the direction of the wood fibers for maximum structural strength to withstand the impact of ramming</note>. and let this vessel have, attached one foot below the water, an iron-pointed ram <note>original: "spuntone ferato"</note>, having the weight and the size of an anvil. And this vessel, by the force of the oars, once the first blow is given, will be able to pull back, then drive itself forward again with fury and give the second blow, and then the third, and as many as are needed to break the target ship.

---

3. [1st fig.:] M

->MANNER OF...<-

If you wish to create a maritime force, make use of these vessels for smashing ships, which is to say: Make vessels 100 feet long and 8 feet wide. But make it so that the left-hand oars have their rowers on the right side of the vessel, and similarly the right-hand ones on the left, as is seen in M [(1st fig.:)], so that the levers of the oars are longer. And let the said vessel be one and a half feet thick—that is, of beams fixed on the outside and the inside with planks in contrary directions. And let this vessel have, attached at one foot under the water, an iron-shod ram, of the weight and size of an anvil. And this ship will be able, by the force of the oars, the first blow having been given, to retreat, then move itself violently forward and give the second blow, and then the third, and so many others until it breaks the said vessel².

---

<note>The following text is transcribed from Leonardo's mirror writing, written right-to-left. The subject is the physics of buoyancy and water resistance as applied to swimming and nautical propulsion.</note>

->**swimming**<- <note>original: "nuoto"</note>
->**it moves**<- <note>original: "muova"</note>

<note>The following passage explores the concept of water resistance and displacement. Leonardo uses the word "substance" to describe the physical support water provides.</note>

If one part <note>referring to a body or a limb</note> is inside the water, it will be easier to move than if that part were outside, because the water supports it and gives it the strength to support the other part. And this is what I mean: you will see that the water with which a man helps himself <note>as in, pushes against to swim</note> has as much **substance** <term>substance (sustantia): Leonardo's term for the density or resistive force of a fluid that allows a body to push against it for propulsion</term> as that which the man has beneath himself through his own strength. 

And if the man were above the water, it <note>the water</note> would have as much substance as the strength of said man. And because the water that the man has beneath him through his strength cannot escape through the sides of the man—because the water that is above the man holds it firm—likewise, the water that is along the sides of the man has as much substance as the strength of the man who is below.

<note>Leonardo's sketches here illustrate these principles in practice:</note>

*   **Mechanical Paddle:** A study of a hinged oar designed to open and catch the "substance" of the water during the power stroke and fold to reduce resistance during the return.
*   **The Galley:** A long, narrow vessel designed to maximize the "strength" of many rowers pushing against the water simultaneously.
*   **Hull Displacement:** Sketches showing how different shapes sit in the water, demonstrating how the "substance" of the water supports the weight of the vessel and its occupants.

<summary>Leonardo analyzes the physics of buoyancy and resistance, arguing that water provides a physical 'substance' or counter-pressure that allows a swimmer or an oar to generate propulsion.</summary>
<keywords>hydrodynamics, buoyancy, swimming, naval engineering, water resistance, substance, propulsion, Leonardo da Vinci</keywords>

# Ms 2037 NAT. LIB. — FOLIO 6 (verso) —

### [NAVAL WARFARE — SHIP PLANKS]

<note>This page contains Leonardo’s sketches and notes on naval combat, focusing on how to maintain footing on slippery decks and a clever sabotage device for sinking enemy vessels.</note>

[Fig. 1:] Soap [Fig. 2:] <term>Caltrops<note>original: "triboli." These are multi-pointed metal spikes designed to always have one point facing up to injure the feet of soldiers or horses.</note></term> [Fig. 3:] Small planks [Fig. 4:] Articulated iron sole

->ON THE REMEDY IF THESE WERE THROWN UPON SHIPS BY THE ENEMIES<-

->SOFT SOAP, OR CALTROPS, OR NAILED BOARDS OR SIMILAR THINGS<-

You shall do this: when you go to battle, wear under your shoes iron soles divided in the middle—as shown in the drawing above—so that you can bend your foot. Let the bottom of these soles be like a <term>rasp<note>original: "raspa o scuffina." Woodworking tools with coarse surfaces used for shaping.</note></term> or file, or filled with short nail points, so that the soap does not cause the foot to slip and the man to fall flat. Because these soles are made of iron, the nailed boards and caltrops will also be thrown in vain.

<margin>[Fig. 5:] Armor that should be used in maritime battles so that the blows descending from the <term>fighting tops<note>original: "gagie" (Italian) / "hunes" (French). These are the platforms near the top of a ship's masts used by lookouts and archers.</note></term> do not strike their mark.</margin>

<margin>[Fig. 7:] n f &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; r &nbsp;&nbsp; a &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; g</margin>

[Fig. 6:] QUICK INSTRUMENT TO DETACH A PLANK FROM THE BOTTOM OF A SHIP WITH A SMALL BLOW.

The screw **n. f.** is the one that enters and grips the <term>plank<note>original: "lasse."</note></term>; the screw **r. a.** is the one that has tightened the steel. Having struck it with a hammer, or attached a rope from point **g** to the <term>rudder<note>original: "timone."</note></term>, as soon as the rudder moves, the screw **r. a.** releases the <term>spring<note>French: "ressort." Leonardo's Italian implies a tensioned component or "steel" (laciaro).</note></term> and the screw **n. f.** detaches the plank.

# Ms 2037 NAT. LIB. — FOLIO 6 (verso) —

## Manuscript Facsimile

<note>This page, from the Ashburnham 2037 codex (originally part of Paris MS B), contains Leonardo's philosophical definitions of force alongside technical designs for artillery and a sketch of a guard. The text is written in Leonardo's characteristic mirror script.</note>

Force is a <term>spiritual virtue<note>original: "uertù spirituale." In Leonardo's physics, this refers to an immaterial or incorporeal power, rather than something religious.</note></term>, an invisible power which, through <term>accidental violence<note>original: "acidentale uiolētia." A term from Aristotelian physics referring to motion that is forced upon an object, as opposed to its "natural" motion toward its resting place.</note></term>, is consumed and infused into bodies where the natural use and essence of those bodies have been removed. This gives life and growth to sentient and non-sentient bodies. This is of short life and always desires death, and when it dies, it extends itself. This is fast and always of varied nature, never of one kind, except that it desires nothing but to be consumed; it conquers by force and becomes life.

<margin>
<note>Text next to the cannon drawing on the left</note>
By this method, one can fire more shots from the same <term>culverin<note>original: "cholubrina." A long-barreled, relatively light artillery piece used from the late Middle Ages through the Renaissance.</note></term> without having to raise or lower it.
</margin>

# Ms 2037 NAT. LIB. — FOLIO 7 (recto)¹ —

## [INFANTRY SHIELDS. — ROWED SHIP. — NAVAL BATTLES].

Infantry shields should be made of spun cotton and formed into cords; these are to be woven tightly in a circle in the manner of a <term>rotella<note>original: "rotella." A small, circular shield typically carried by infantry or light cavalry during the Renaissance.</note></term>. And if you want it to be strong, soak the threads thoroughly before you make cords of them, and then smear them with pulverized <term>iron dross<note>original: "spuma di fero." Literally 'iron foam' or 'scum,' this refers to the slag or scale produced during the smelting or forging of iron, likely used here to add a hard, metallic grit to the fabric.</note></term>. Then make the secondary cords in two strands, then four, then eight; and each time, soak them in <term>borax<note>original: "borace." A mineral salt used in metallurgy and as a cleaning agent; here it may act as a preservative or fire-retardant.</note></term> water, or linseed water, or <term>quince<note>original: "pomicotogni." Quince seeds were famously used to create a thick, glue-like mucilage for sizing and stiffening fabrics.</note></term> water. Once you have made your cord, weave the shield. If you make a <term>doublet<note>original: "givbone." A snug-fitting jacket. Leonardo is proposing a form of "soft armor" similar to modern ballistic vests.</note></term> from this material, it will be flexible, light, and impenetrable.

<margin>[1st fig.:]</margin> Method for making a ship that, in case of need, can assist itself with oars.

<margin>[Last figures:]</margin> These are for situations where one must take small boats and make <term>mantlets<note>original: "mantelletti." Large, mobile protective screens or shields used to cover soldiers or artillery.</note></term> out of heavy planks, and place small <term>bombards<note>original: "bonbardelle." Small-caliber cannons or mortars.</note></term> beneath them to fight large vessels from a distance. ²

---

<note>The following notes refer to the source manuscript's history:</note>
1. Folio 97 [?] recto of Manuscript B of the Institute.
2. The words above the last figures are not by Leonardo (they are a Spanish transcription).

<keywords>infantry shields, cotton armor, rotella, naval warfare, bombards, military engineering, protective clothing</keywords>

Every <term>heavy body<note>original: "grave." In Renaissance physics, this refers to any object with weight or the force of gravity acting upon it.</note></term> approaches the center by the shortest path, and never by an oblique path if it were not impossible [to do so] by a straight line.

Because if the air were of varying density, at no time would the rays of sight travel in a straight line, but in a curve, following the <term>thinner air<note>original: "aria piu rada." Leonardo is observing atmospheric refraction, where light bends as it passes through air of different temperatures or densities.</note></term> and distancing themselves more from it.

184. In what manner air of varying nature reveals itself to the sight.
